But if it updates one table in place, today's date is added twice, and every later day inherits the damage. Retention and churn counts then drift silently.

show.title: In place update, run twice
show.text:
run 1: [10-21, 10-20]
run 2: [10-21, 10-21, 10-20]
later days copy the duplicate

beats.say: So keep one partition per day, overwrite that partition, and never read the table you are writing. Dedupe dates before prepending. A late event for an old day means rebuilding that day and every day after it.

check.q: What makes a cumulative job safe to rerun?
opts: Updating the table in place
Reading day N minus 1 and overwriting only day N
Running it twice and averaging
check.why: Fixed input and overwritten output give the same result however many times it runs.

work: Check your job writes by overwriting a dated partition, not appending.
Add a test that no date appears twice in any list.

m01.title: Should you build it at all?

beats.say: When is a cumulative table the wrong choice?

It shines for long lived entity questions: retention, resurrection, days since last active. If you only need yesterday's active count, a plain daily aggregate from events is simpler, with no chain of dependencies.

The cost is storage that grows per entity, and a chain that forces sequential backfills. Cap the list at ninety days, or store a bit mask in one integer, where each bit is a day. Thirty one days fit in a thirty two bit integer.

show.title: Keep it bounded
items: Bit mask: one bit per day

beats.say: Alternatives: partitioned event scans with pruning when data is small, or slowly changing dimensions when you need attribute history with validity ranges. Choose cumulative when scans would be huge and the same questions repeat daily.

check.q: You only need yesterday's total active users and data is modest. Best choice?
opts: A cumulative table with date arrays
A simple daily aggregate over partitioned events
A map column per user
check.why: No long entity history is needed, so a plain aggregate avoids the dependency chain and backfill cost.

work: List your repeated entity-level questions and see which truly need history per entity.
Decide a cap or bit mask size and a pruning rule before launch.

m01.title: The address book that remembers

beats.say: If your friend moves house, should every old letter you sent be relabeled with their new address?

Of course not. A good address book keeps every address, with the dates they lived there. Each line says: from this day until that day, this address. That is a type two slowly changing dimension. A dimension is just the descriptive facts about something.
Now someone asks: where did Sam live when I sent the March letter? You find the line whose dates cover March. That is an as-of lookup. The current address is simply the line with no end date yet.
So old letters keep their true story, and new letters get the new one. History stays honest.

check.q: Sam moved in June. Which address belongs to a letter sent in March?
opts: The newest address, since it is current
The address whose date range covers March
The average of all addresses
check.why: An as-of lookup picks the version valid on the event date. Using the current address would rewrite history.

work: Pick one dimension you own and list which attributes someone might ask about as they were then.
Check whether your current dimension keeps old values or overwrites them.

m01.title: Backfill with the streak trick

beats.say: You have one row per rider per day, three hundred rows saying free, free, free. How do you squash that into a few rows with start and end dates?
First, flag a change. Put one if today's tier differs from yesterday's, otherwise zero. The very first day counts as one.
Next, take a running sum of those flags. That number is the streak. It holds steady while the tier holds steady, and goes up by one at every change.

Group by rider and streak. Each group is one version, with its first date as the start. Free, then plus, then free gives three rows, not two. Group by tier alone and the two free runs would merge, erasing the upgrade.

check.q: A rider goes free, plus, free. Why group by rider and streak instead of rider and tier?
opts: Grouping by tier is slower
Grouping by tier merges the two free runs into one row
Streak is required by the warehouse
check.why: The streak increases at every change, so the two free runs get different numbers and stay separate versions.

work: Write the backfill with a lag comparison, a running sum, then a group by, and test it on a rider who returns to an earlier value.
Handle the first day per key so it counts as a change.

m01.title: The nightly incremental load

beats.say: Every night you receive a snapshot of two million drivers, but only two thousand changed. How do you update history without rewriting it all?

Compare today's snapshot with the current rows only, not the whole history. That sorts everything into five piles: old history untouched, current rows unchanged, changed rows to close, their new open versions, and brand-new keys.

Closing a row means setting its end date to today. In a warehouse, a merge closes the old rows, then an insert adds the new versions. Run both in one transaction, so a crash never leaves a closed row with no replacement.
Finally, make it idempotent. Run the same day twice and no rows are added, because the second run finds no differences against the current rows.

check.q: The nightly job is accidentally run twice for the same day. What should happen?
opts: Duplicate versions are added
The second run adds no rows
The second run deletes history
check.why: After the first run, current rows already match the snapshot, so the comparison finds no changes and nothing is added.

work: Compare snapshots to current rows only, never the full history table.
Run the merge and insert in one transaction.
Rerun a day in a test and assert the row count does not change.

m01.title: Why is_current gives wrong revenue

beats.say: Your revenue by tier report says plus riders bring in the most money. Why might it be wrong, and grow more wrong every month?

Joining trips to the dimension on is current gives every trip the rider's tier today. A rider who was free in March and upgraded in June has their March trips relabeled as plus. More riders change over time, so the error grows.
The fix is an as-of join. Match on the rider key, and require the trip date to be on or after valid from, and before valid to.
Use a half-open window. A trip on the exact change day then lands in exactly one row. If both ends are inclusive, that trip matches two rows and its revenue is counted twice.

show.title: Window edges
items: Both inclusive double counts the change day

check.q: Why does joining facts to the dimension on is_current distort revenue by tier?
opts: It drops rows with no match
It assigns today's tier to past trips
It counts the change day twice
check.why: is_current has one row per key, the latest, so all history is labeled with today's attributes.

work: Replace any is_current joins on historical facts with as-of joins.
Add a test that each fact row matches exactly one dimension row.
Use half-open validity windows everywhere.

m01.title: Late-arriving dimensions

beats.say: A trip arrives for driver 912, but the driver table has never heard of 912. Do you drop the trip?
No. Insert an inferred member: the driver id, with everything else marked unknown. Now the trip loads with a valid key and the revenue is not lost.
When the real driver record arrives, update that placeholder in place. The unknown row was never a true state of the driver, so it should not become a history version.
The trap: if the load treats the real record as a normal change, it closes the placeholder and adds a second row. Monitor how many inferred members stay unknown for days.

check.q: A trip arrives before its driver exists in the dimension. What is the best handling?
opts: Drop the trip until the driver arrives
Insert an inferred member, then update it later
Point the trip to the first driver row
check.why: An inferred member keeps the key valid and the fact loaded, and the real record later fills it in.

work: Add an inferred flag column to your dimension.
Write a check that lists inferred members older than one day.

m01.title: When SCD2 is the wrong tool

beats.say: Should every dimension be type two? Not at all. History has a price in rows, joins, and complexity.
Take driver location changing hourly. One million drivers times twenty-four changes is twenty-four million new rows every day. The dimension stops being small, and every as-of join gets slower.
Better options: overwrite with type one when nobody needs the past, like fixing a typo. Put fast-changing values on the fact table. Or split them into a small mini-dimension of banded values.

show.title: Instead choose
items: Fast values live on the fact

beats.say: If queries are rare and storage is cheap, plain daily snapshots can win on simplicity. SCD2 wins when changes are rare and as-of queries are common. Ask: will anyone need the value as it was, and how often does it change?

check.q: Driver location changes hourly and nobody queries old locations. What do you choose?
opts: SCD2 on location
Overwrite or keep it on the fact table
Daily snapshots forever
check.why: SCD2 would create millions of rows for a value no one needs historically. Overwriting or storing it on the fact is far cheaper.

work: Estimate daily new rows per attribute as keys times change rate before choosing type two.
Decide per column, not per table, which attributes need history.

m01.title: Pins and string: what a graph is

beats.say: How would you find every friend of a friend of yours, without asking each person one by one?
Picture a wall covered in pins and string. Each pin is a thing, like a person or a driver. Each string is a relationship, like referred or rated. Pins are called vertices. Strings are called edges.
To find friends of friends, you start at your pin and follow the strings twice. You are not adding up totals. You are walking connections.
And a new kind of relationship, like shares a phone, needs no new wall. You just tie a different coloured string.

show.kicker: Just a new kind of string

check.q: In a graph model, what is an edge?
opts: A thing such as a rider or driver
A relationship between two things
A total such as revenue per city
check.why: Vertices are the things; edges are the relationships connecting them, such as referred or rated.

work: List three questions your team asks that are about connections, not totals.
Sketch those questions as pins and strings on a whiteboard.

m01.title: Two tables hold a whole network

beats.say: How do you store an entire network in just two plain tables?

One table holds vertices: an identifier like rider colon one, a type, and a map of properties, such as city Pune. The other holds edges: a subject, an object, an edge type, and properties. For example, rider one referred rider two on April fourteenth.
Because the schema is generic, a new relationship type is just a new value in the edge type column. No new table and no migration.

show.title: Why generic works
items: New relationship equals new edge type value

beats.say: To ask who rider one referred, then who those people referred, you use a recursive query. It starts with rider one's edges, then joins the edges table to its own results, once per hop. Two hops means two joins.

check.q: A team wants to add a new relationship called shares_device. What does the generic schema need?
opts: A new edges table for that relationship
A new edge type value in the existing edges table
A new column on every vertex
check.why: Edges carry a type column, so a new relationship is simply new rows with a new type value.

work: Write a recursive query that finds referrals up to two hops from one rider.
Check what indexes exist on subject and object in your edges table.

m01.title: Cycles and supernodes

beats.say: What happens if rider A refers rider B, and B refers A?
The recursive query never finishes. It walks A to B to A forever, and the rows keep growing. Two fixes: stop at a maximum depth, say five hops, or keep a visited set so you never revisit a vertex.

show.title: Fixing cycles
items: Depth limit, for example five hops
Visited set, never revisit a vertex
Without either, the query loops forever

beats.say: The second trap is the supernode: one vertex with millions of edges, like a promo code that every rider used. Any traversal touching it explodes, because one hop fans out into millions of rows.

chip.text: One hop becomes millions of rows

beats.say: So you cap the fan out, sample its edges, or skip that vertex in the traversal. Otherwise one hub turns a cheap query into an hours-long job.

show.text: Cap, sample or skip the hub

check.q: Your recursive referral query never finishes on real data. What is the most likely cause and fix?
opts: A cycle in the data; add a depth limit or visited set
Too few columns; add a properties map
The edges table is too small; add rows
check.why: Cycles such as A refers B refers A make the recursion loop forever unless depth is limited or visited vertices are tracked.

work: Add a depth limit to every recursive graph query you own.
Count edges per vertex and list the top ten supernodes.

m01.title: When SQL stops being enough

beats.say: When should you stop answering graph questions in SQL?
Recursive queries are fine for two or three hops on a warehouse you already run. But each hop is a self join, so cost grows with fan out, and deep traversal gets slow.

Move to Neo4j, Neptune or GraphFrames when you need many hops, shortest paths, community detection for fraud rings, or answers in milliseconds. A graph store follows pointers instead of joining tables.

show.title: Reach for a graph engine when

beats.say: The price is another system to run, load and keep in sync. If your questions are sums by category, stay dimensional. Choose graph only when relationships are the question.

chip.text: Sync, ops and cost to maintain

check.q: Which need most clearly justifies a dedicated graph engine over recursive SQL?
opts: Monthly revenue by city
Interactive fraud ring detection across many hops
Listing each rider's last referral
check.why: Deep multi-hop traversal, community detection and interactive speed are where graph engines beat repeated self joins.

work: Measure how many hops your slowest graph question really needs.
Prototype the question in SQL first and note where latency breaks down.
Estimate sync and operating cost before proposing a graph database.

m01.title: The address book that remembers

beats.say: Your friend moves from Leeds to Bristol. Do you scratch out the old address in your book, or keep both?
Scratching it out is called overwrite. It is simple, but the past is gone. Old birthday cards you sent to Leeds now look like they went to Bristol.

Keeping both means adding a new line with dates. Leeds until March, Bristol since. Now every card matches where your friend lived then. That is a slowly changing dimension: a detail about a thing, like a rider's plan, that changes now and then, and you choose how much history to keep.
You choose per detail. Keep the birthday forever, overwrite typos, track addresses.

check.q: Why would you keep a new dated line instead of overwriting a friend's address?
opts: It uses less storage
Old events still match where the friend lived at the time
It makes the book faster to write
check.why: Overwriting rewrites the past. Dated lines let old events be explained with the value that was true then.

work: List the attributes in one dimension you own and mark which ones people ask about historically.
Find one report whose old numbers changed after an attribute was overwritten.

m01.title: Type 2: one row per version

beats.say: A rider upgrades to Plus on October third, then drops back to free on October fourteenth. How does one rider end up with two rows?

Type 2 never edits history. When the tier changes, the pipeline closes the old row by setting its valid to date, then inserts a new row with a fresh surrogate key, which is just an id the warehouse makes up. Rider four gets key seven, then key eight.

show.title: dim_rider_tier
show.text:
rider_key rider_id tier valid_from valid_to  is_current
7         4        plus 2026-10-03 2026-10-14 false
8         4        free 2026-10-14 NULL       true
show.note: Close the old row, insert the new one

beats.say: Intervals are half open. Valid from is included, valid to is excluded. So October fourteenth belongs only to key eight, and a report for any date matches exactly one row.
The open row has a null valid to and current true, so today's queries simply filter on the flag.

check.q: With valid_from <= d < valid_to, which row owns October 14 in the example?
opts: Key 7, the Plus row
Key 8, the Free row
Both rows
check.why: Key 7 ends exclusive at October 14, so that date falls only inside key 8's interval.

work: Write the as-of join for one fact table using valid_from <= event_date < valid_to.
Check your SCD tables use half-open intervals, not between.

m01.title: Picking an SCD type per column

beats.say: There are six SCD types, but you rarely pick one for a whole table. Which one fits which column?
Type zero keeps the original forever, like signup date. Type one overwrites, good for typo fixes. Type two adds rows, for city, tier or plan, anything a report must show as it was then.

Type three keeps current and previous in two columns, handy for one reorganisation. Type four keeps only the current row in the dimension and puts history in another table, for wide or fast changing data.
Type six is type two rows plus a current value column on every row, so one query can show the then-value and the now-value together.

show.sub: then-value and now-value in one query

check.q: Which type fits a report that must group by a rider's tier at the time of the trip and also by their tier today?
opts: Type 1
Type 3
Type 6
check.why: Type 6 keeps versioned rows plus a current-value column on each, so both views come from one query.

work: Annotate each column in a key dimension with its SCD type.
Document why each Type 1 column is safe to overwrite.

m01.title: Where SCD 2 bugs hide

beats.say: Your report says a rider was Plus on October fourteenth, but they were already free. Where did that bug come from?

Often from closed intervals. If valid to is inclusive and the next valid from is the same date, that day matches two rows and counts double. If valid to is a day early, it matches none. Half open intervals fix both.
Also guard the current row. Two rows flagged current for one rider will duplicate every join, so add a test that each natural key has exactly one.
And facts must use the version in force at event time. A late arriving change means re-cutting the intervals, and fixing surrogate keys on facts already loaded.

show.title: Late arriving changes
items: Join on event date, not today

check.q: Valid_to is inclusive and equals the next row's valid_from. What happens on that boundary date?
opts: It matches no row
It matches two rows and double counts
It matches exactly one row
check.why: Both the closing and the opening row include that date, so a join returns two matches.

work: Add a test that each natural key has exactly one current row and no overlapping intervals.
Add a test for gaps between consecutive versions of the same key.
Plan how late arriving changes will be backfilled.

m01.title: When Type 2 is the wrong call

beats.say: Type 2 everywhere sounds safe. So why do big teams avoid it?

show.sub: safe on paper, costly at scale

beats.say: A fast changing column, like a driver's last seen location, adds a row per change. A ten million row dimension can balloon into billions, and every fact join gets slower. That is when you use type four: a small current table, with history pushed to a side table.
If only a few reports need history, a daily snapshot of the dimension may be simpler than merge logic. Type six costs more, since every old row is rewritten whenever the current value changes.
Default to type two for business critical attributes, type one for the rest, and decide per column with the analyst who asks the question.

check.q: A column changes thousands of times a day and few reports need its history. What is the best default?
opts: Type 2 on the main dimension
Type 4 or a snapshot, keeping the main dimension small
Type 6 for everything
check.why: Type 2 on a fast column inflates the dimension and slows every join. Separating history keeps joins cheap.

work: Measure row growth per column in your Type 2 dimensions and flag the fast ones.
Compare daily snapshots against merge logic for a dimension with few history consumers.

m01.title: Why everyone's numbers match

beats.say: Why do two teams ask for trips by city last week and get different answers?
Imagine a receipt book. Each line is one trip, and you write down one rule: one line per trip, nothing else. That rule is called the grain. It means what one row stands for.

Now add shared lookup cards: one for city, one for date, one for customer. Every team reads the same card, so a city means the same thing everywhere. Those cards are dimensions. The receipts are facts.
Same receipts, same cards, same answer. That is the whole point: anyone can slice by anything and still agree.

show.sub: Slice by anything and still agree

check.q: What does declaring the grain of a fact table tell you?
opts: Which database stores it
What exactly one row represents
How many columns it has
check.why: Grain is the definition of one row, such as one trip. Without it, counts and joins become ambiguous.

work: Write the grain of your three busiest tables as one sentence each.
Find a metric two teams calculate differently and trace which dimension they disagree on.

m01.title: Why a star runs fast

beats.say: How can a star schema be fast when it needs joins?

show.sub: Star schema in a columnar warehouse

beats.say: The dimensions are small. Say the city table has two hundred rows. The engine copies it to every worker, so the giant fact table with a billion rows never has to move across the network. Moving data like that is called a shuffle, and it is slow.

The fact is narrow: just keys and numbers. Columnar storage reads only the three columns a query needs, not all forty. And a filter like city equals Lisbon becomes a filter on city keys, so whole files can be skipped.
Third normal form needs many more joins between big tables, and those shuffle. A single wide table skips joins, but must be rebuilt whenever a dimension changes.

show.title: Compared
items: Third normal form: many big joins, shuffles
Star: few joins, small side broadcast
Wide table: no joins, costly rebuilds

check.q: Why does a star schema avoid shuffling the large fact table?
opts: Facts are stored in memory
Small dimensions are broadcast to every worker
Dimensions are joined before loading the fact
check.why: Dimensions are small enough to copy to each worker, so the big fact stays where it is.

work: Check a query plan for a broadcast join on your dimension tables.
Confirm your fact tables are partitioned or clustered on keys that filters hit.

m01.title: Revenue doubled after a join

beats.say: You join orders to shipments on customer, and revenue suddenly doubles. Why?

show.sub: Orders joined to shipments on customer

beats.say: Both tables have many rows per customer. Customer seven has two orders and two shipments. The join pairs every order with every shipment, giving four rows, so each order amount is counted twice. This is a fan trap.
The fix: never join two facts directly. Either total each fact up to the shared grain first, then join. Or drill across: query each fact on its own by the shared dimensions, and combine the results.
Writing down each fact's grain makes this visible in review before it hits a dashboard.

check.q: Two fact tables each have many rows per customer. What is the safe way to combine them?
opts: Join them directly on customer
Aggregate each to customer grain, then join or drill across
Add DISTINCT to the join
check.why: Aggregating to a shared grain first removes the row multiplication. DISTINCT can hide duplicates but also drop legitimate repeated values.

work: Add a test comparing total revenue before and after each join in key models.
Document the grain in each fact table's description.

m01.title: A fact with no dimension row

beats.say: A trip arrives for a driver who is not in your driver table yet. Do you drop it?

No. Dropping the row makes your trip counts wrong, and blocking the load makes everyone wait. Instead, insert a placeholder driver row with the real driver id and a fresh surrogate key, flagged as inferred.

The fact points at that placeholder, so counts stay right. When the real driver record lands, you update that same row. You do not add a new history version, because the placeholder was never a real past state.
Add a test that tracks how many inferred members you have. A rising number means a source is running late.

show.sub: A rising count means a late source

check.q: When the real attributes for an inferred driver arrive, what should happen?
opts: Add a new SCD2 version
Update the placeholder row in place
Delete the fact rows and reload
check.why: The placeholder was never a true historical state, so it is completed in place and facts keep pointing at the same key.

work: Check whether your fact load joins with inner joins that silently drop rows.
Add an inferred flag column and a daily count alert.

m01.title: Point-in-time joins for history

beats.say: A driver changes city in March. How does an old trip still show the old city?

show.sub: History in a slowly changing dimension

beats.say: The driver id alone no longer names one row, because it now has two versions. So each version gets its own surrogate key, which identifies exactly one version.
Option one: the fact stores the surrogate key chosen at load time. Option two: join on driver id plus time. The trip time must be at or after valid from, and strictly before valid to.
That half open range means a trip at the exact boundary instant matches one version, not two. But overlaps or gaps in the ranges break it, so test for both.

show.title: Test the dimension
items: Half open: from inclusive, to exclusive

check.q: Why use a half open range for valid_from and valid_to?
opts: It makes the query faster
A boundary instant matches exactly one version
It removes the need for surrogate keys
check.why: With from inclusive and to exclusive, a timestamp equal to the boundary belongs only to the new version.

work: Write a test that finds overlapping or gapped SCD2 ranges per natural key.
Decide per fact whether to store the surrogate key at load time or join by time.

m01.title: When not to use it

beats.say: When would you not build a dimensional model?

Not for raw landing of many changing sources. Keep those close to source, or use Data Vault, which is better as an auditable integration layer underneath. Not for event logs or machine learning features that are naturally wide or nested.

Everywhere else it wins. Against third normal form, you get far fewer joins and business names. Against one big table, dimensions are reused and history lives in one place. For one hot dashboard, build the wide table from the star.

show.title: Why the star wins
items: Versus one big table: reuse, one home for history
Hot dashboard: derive a wide table from the star

beats.say: The real cost is ownership. Domain teams own facts, but shared dimensions like customer and date need one owner and a change process, because every fact depends on them.

check.q: A team needs one very fast dashboard. What fits best?
opts: Replace the star with third normal form
Build a wide table derived from the star
Query raw landing tables directly
check.why: A derived wide table gives speed for the one dashboard while the star stays the shared, reusable model.

work: Name an owner and a change process for each conformed dimension.
List which datasets should stay raw or Vault style rather than modelled as stars.

m01.title: Splitting dimensions that explode

beats.say: A customer dimension has sixty columns and some change daily. What happens to history?
Every change copies the full row, so history explodes. Ten million customers with one score changing daily adds over three and a half billion rows a year.
Split the fast changing columns into a small mini dimension, such as score bands. The fact points at both, and the big customer table stays stable.
You rarely move off the model. You add around it: aggregates for speed, a semantic layer for shared metrics, and a lakehouse table format underneath.

show.title: Add around it
items: Aggregates or wide tables for speed

check.q: A dimension has one attribute that changes daily. What is the best response?
opts: Version the whole row with SCD2 every day
Move that attribute to a mini-dimension
Drop history for the whole dimension
check.why: A mini-dimension holds the fast-changing values in a few rows, so the large dimension does not multiply.

work: Find dimensions with the most SCD2 versions per key and check which columns drive them.
Pick one slow dashboard and test an aggregate or wide table built from the star.

m02.title: A fact is a receipt line

beats.say: What is the one table every company ends up with the most rows in? It's the record of things that happened.

show.sub: the biggest table in the company

beats.say: Think of a shop receipt. Each line says who bought, what they bought, where, when, and how they paid. Then come the numbers: how many, and how much. That receipt line is a fact row. A fact is just one thing that happened, written down once.

chip.text: One thing that happened, written once

beats.say: Not every number can be added up. Fares add up fine. But a percentage, like cancellation rate, does not. Ten percent on a quiet Monday and thirty percent on a busy Tuesday is not twenty percent overall. So keep the counts, and work out the percentage last.

check.q: Why should a table keep cancelled trips and total trips instead of only a cancellation percentage?
opts: Percentages take more storage
You can add the counts first and divide last
Counts are easier to type
Percentages cannot be negative
check.why: Counts add up correctly across days or cities, so you compute the true percentage after adding. Percentages from different groups cannot simply be averaged.

work: List the percentage columns in one of your tables and check that the counts behind them are stored.
Write one sentence that says what a single row in your biggest table means.

m02.title: Grain and three kinds of measure

beats.say: A city has 100 trips over two days. How do you report the cancellation rate without getting it wrong?

First, declare the grain: one row per trip. Each row holds keys for rider, driver, city, date and payment method, plus measures like fare and distance. Fare and distance are additive, so you can sum them across any dimension.
Open trips at six p.m. are semi-additive. Add them across drivers, but not across days; take the last value or an average. Ratios are non-additive, so store cancelled trips and total trips instead.

show.title: Three kinds of measure
items: Semi-additive: sum across drivers, not days
Non-additive: ratios, store numerator and denominator

beats.say: Monday had 2 of 10 cancelled, twenty percent. Tuesday: 40 of 90, forty-four percent. Averaging the rates gives thirty-two. The true rate is 42 of 100, forty-two percent.

check.q: Monday has 2 cancelled of 10 trips. Tuesday has 40 of 90. What is the correct two-day rate?
opts: 32 percent, the average of 20 and 44
42 percent, 42 cancelled of 100
44 percent, the larger rate
22 percent
check.why: Add numerators and denominators first: 42 over 100. Averaging the daily rates ignores that Tuesday has far more trips.

work: Write the grain of your main fact table as one sentence starting with 'One row per'.
Tag each measure as additive, semi-additive or non-additive in your docs.

m02.title: Why the revenue is too high

beats.say: Your revenue dashboard is ten percent too high, yet every query looks correct. Why?

Often the grain is mixed. Say each trip row is repeated once per payment split. A trip paid with two cards appears twice, so its fare is counted twice. Declare one grain per table, and test that the trip key is unique.

chip.text: Test: trip key must be unique

beats.say: Balances are another trap. Adding a balance across days gives a number that means nothing. Take the end of day value instead. Averaging daily averages is also wrong, because a quiet day then counts as much as a busy one.

show.title: Aggregation traps
items: Use end of day value or an average

beats.say: Last, retries. A replayed event loads twice and inflates counts. Dedupe on a stable trip id, so a rerun gives the same answer.

check.q: A fact table at trip grain has two rows for trips paid with two cards, each carrying the full fare. What happens to SUM of fare?
opts: It is correct
It double counts those trips
It drops those trips
It only errors on joins
check.why: The fare repeats on each row, so the sum counts it once per payment split. Keep one grain per table, or put payments in their own fact.

work: Add a uniqueness test on the declared grain key of every fact table.
Make loads idempotent by deduping on a stable business id.
Audit dashboards for sums of balances or averages of averages.

m02.title: Atomic facts, rollups, and cost

beats.say: Should you store only daily totals, since the raw fact table is huge? Usually no.

Keep the atomic fact, one row per trip. A finer grain can answer any question later. A coarser grain can never be split back apart. The cost is volume: a billion rows a day means every scan and shuffle is expensive.

So add rollups on top for dashboards. Sums and counts merge cleanly, which is why you store numerators and denominators. Distinct counts do not merge, so use sketches such as HyperLogLog, accepting a small error.
Partition the raw fact by date so queries read only the days they need. Choose the grain by the questions you must answer, not by what is easy to load.

show.title: Design rules
items: Choose grain by the questions asked
Dashboards read rollups, not raw rows

check.q: Why keep an atomic fact table even when dashboards only need daily totals?
opts: Daily totals cannot be stored
A finer grain can be rolled up, but a coarse one cannot be split
Atomic tables are always cheaper
Sketches require raw rows
check.why: You can always aggregate fine data upward. Once data is stored coarsely, the detail is lost, so new questions cannot be answered.

work: Estimate daily row count and bytes of your largest fact and check it is date partitioned.
Build a rollup for the top dashboard and compare scan cost against the raw table.
Use sketches for distinct counts in rollups and document the error.

m02.title: Press twice, count once

beats.say: What if pressing the same button twice could double your money? In data, that happens all the time.

show.sub: the same event, counted two times

beats.say: Imagine a mail room. A courier is not sure a parcel arrived, so he delivers it again. Now you have two identical parcels. Fixing this means deciding what counts as one parcel, then keeping just one.
Rerunning should be like setting a thermostat to twenty degrees. Do it ten times, still twenty. Not like pressing a plus button, which climbs each time.

show.title: Safe to repeat
items: Thermostat: set to 20, ten times, still 20
Plus button: ten presses, ten more

beats.say: Late postcards are the last trick. File each by the date it was written, not the day it arrived, and glance back at the last few days of mail each morning.

check.q: A courier delivers the same parcel twice. What is the right fix?
opts: Count both, since both arrived
Decide what identifies one parcel and keep a single copy
Stop couriers from ever retrying
check.why: Retries are normal and protect against loss, so you define what counts as one item and keep one per identity.

work: Write down, in one sentence, what one row in your main table means.
Ask which of your jobs would double rows if run twice.

m02.title: Dedupe, overwrite, trail

beats.say: A producer retried, and now your fact table has twenty-five extra rows. How do you remove them safely?

First, declare the grain, say one row per trip. Then number rows within each trip id, ordered by event time and then id, so ties always break the same way. Keep number one. One thousand rows with twenty-five repeats becomes nine hundred seventy-five.
Next, make the load rerunnable. Overwrite the partition for October twenty-first, or merge on the trip id. A plain insert would double the day on every retry.

show.title: Idempotent load
show.text:
INSERT OVERWRITE fact PARTITION (trip_date = '2026-10-21')
SELECT ... FROM deduped;
show.note: Run it once or five times, same result

beats.say: Finally, partition by event date and reprocess the last three days each run, so rows from offline phones land in the right day.

chip.text: Late rows land on event date

check.q: Why order by event time and then id inside ROW_NUMBER?
opts: It makes the query faster
So ties break the same way on every run
It removes late rows
check.why: Without a tiebreaker, equal timestamps let the engine pick any copy, so results can change between runs.

work: Replace any plain INSERT daily load with a partition overwrite or MERGE.
Add a ROW_NUMBER dedupe on the declared grain key with a stable tiebreaker.

m02.title: Why totals drift overnight

beats.say: Your dedupe passes today and gives different totals tomorrow. Why?
Usually ties. If two copies share the same timestamp and you order only by time, the database may pick either one. Add the id as a final tiebreaker, so the same row wins every run.
Idempotency has traps too. Delete then insert without a transaction lets readers see an empty day. A merge fed duplicates can fail or pick randomly, so dedupe the source first.

show.title: Idempotency traps
items: Delete then insert outside a transaction: readers see an empty day
MERGE with duplicate source keys: error or random match
Dedupe the source before you merge

beats.say: Late data has a limit. If phones can be a week offline but you reprocess three days, older rows are silently missed. Keep event time and ingested time, so you can measure real lateness and size the window.

check.q: Phones can be offline up to 7 days, but you reprocess a trailing 3 days. What happens to a row that is 5 days late?
opts: It is picked up automatically
It is silently missed
The load fails loudly
check.why: The window never revisits that partition, so the row is lost without any error. Measure lateness with event and ingested timestamps.

work: Check every dedupe ORDER BY ends in a unique id.
Compute the lateness distribution from ingested minus event time and compare it to your window.

m02.title: What correctness costs

beats.say: Reprocessing three days every night triples your compute. Is that the right price?

Partition overwrite is cheap and simple, and it is safe to rerun. Merge touches only changed rows, which wins when a partition is huge but corrections are tiny. But merge costs more per row and needs a trustworthy key.

show.title: Overwrite or merge
items: Overwrite: simple, cheap per row, rewrites whole partition
Merge: touches only changes, costs more per row
Pick merge when partitions are huge and fixes are tiny

beats.say: Size the window from measured lateness, say ninety-nine percent arriving within two days. Chase the final one percent with a weekly backfill, not a bigger nightly window.
For restatements, overwrite when consumers want current truth. For finance, append adjustment rows so the audit trail survives. Either way, publish which days changed.

show.title: Restatement policy
items: Overwrite affected partitions for current truth
Append adjustment rows for finance audit trails

check.q: Finance needs an audit trail when a source corrects last month. Which policy fits?
opts: Overwrite the partitions silently
Append adjustment rows and publish affected days
Delete the month and reload
check.why: Adjustments keep the original and the correction visible, so past reports can be reproduced and explained.

work: Pick and document a restate or adjust policy per fact table.
Set the trailing window from measured lateness and schedule a weekly backfill for the tail.

m02.title: Four ways to remember what happened

beats.say: Why does a shop keep receipts, a nightly stock count, and a parcel tracker? Because each one answers a different kind of question.
A receipt is written once per sale and never changed. That is a transaction fact. A nightly stock count writes one line per shelf per night, even if nothing sold. That is a periodic snapshot.

chip.text: Periodic snapshot: a row even when nothing happened

beats.say: A parcel tracker is one line per parcel. You fill in ordered, shipped, delivered as it moves. That is an accumulating snapshot. And a guest list just records who was present, with no amounts at all. That is factless.

check.q: A shelf is counted every night, even on nights with no sales. Which fact type is that?
opts: Transaction
Periodic snapshot
Accumulating snapshot
Factless
check.why: One row per entity per period, whether or not anything happened, is the definition of a periodic snapshot.

work: List the tables you own and label each as one of the four types.
Find one report that sums history to get a balance and ask if a snapshot would be simpler.

m02.title: Transactions and periodic snapshots

beats.say: How do you get a driver's wallet balance on the fifteenth, without adding up years of payments?

A transaction fact has one row per event, like each completed trip. Rows are only added, never updated. It answers how many trips happened yesterday. But a balance needs a running sum over all history.

chip.text: Good for counts. Balances need a full running sum.

beats.say: A periodic snapshot stores one row per driver per day. With ten thousand drivers, that is ten thousand rows daily, activity or not. Now the balance on the fifteenth is a single lookup.

chip.text: Balance on the 15th is one lookup

check.q: You need each driver's balance on any past date quickly. Which design fits best?
opts: Transaction fact with a running sum
Periodic snapshot of balances
Factless fact
Accumulating snapshot
check.why: A daily snapshot stores the balance directly, so no scan of all history is needed.

work: Pick one balance-like metric and check how it is computed today.
Estimate rows per day as entities times periods before building a snapshot.

m02.title: Accumulating and factless facts

beats.say: Where do trips stall between request and pickup? One row per event makes that surprisingly hard to see.

An accumulating snapshot keeps one row per trip. It has columns for requested, assigned, picked up and completed times. As each milestone happens, you update the same row. Subtract two timestamps and you see the delay.

chip.text: Assigned to pickup: 7 minutes. That is the stall.

beats.say: Sometimes the event itself is the fact. A factless table has no measures. One row says a driver was online in a zone in an hour. Compare it with requests to find zones with drivers but no demand.

chip.text: Rows with no measure still answer questions

check.q: You want the average minutes between assigned and picked up. Which type fits?
opts: Transaction
Periodic snapshot
Accumulating snapshot
Factless
check.why: It keeps all milestone timestamps on one row per trip, so the gap is a simple subtraction.

work: Pick a process with stages and list its milestone columns.
Find a question about absence and check if a factless table could answer it.

m02.title: The missing zero rows bug

beats.say: A driver had no trips on Tuesday. Does your daily balance table have a Tuesday row?
If you build a periodic snapshot from activity, it will not. Quiet days vanish, so averages are wrong and charts show gaps. The balance did not become nothing. It stayed the same.
The fix is a date spine. That is a table listing every day. Cross it with every driver, then left join the activity. Quiet days get a row, with the balance carried forward or a zero.

check.q: A daily snapshot is built by grouping activity by driver and day. What goes wrong?
opts: Duplicate rows appear
Days with no activity have no row
Timestamps are overwritten
Measures become null on active days
check.why: Grouping only returns days that had activity, so zero-activity days are missing. A date spine fixes it.

work: Add a test that every entity has a row for every period.
Rebuild one snapshot from a date spine and compare row counts.

m02.title: Loading accumulating snapshots safely

beats.say: Why is an accumulating snapshot the awkward one to load?
Its rows are revisited. Each milestone is an update, not an insert. So the pipeline must be a merge keyed on trip id, or a rerun creates duplicate trips.
Milestones not yet reached stay empty, so queries must treat nulls as still in progress, not as errors. Late events can arrive out of order, so never let an older event overwrite a newer one.

show.title: Gotchas
items: Late events arrive out of order

beats.say: Factless tables have a trap too. They record what happened, so absence needs a coverage table to compare against.

show.sub: Compare against what could have happened

check.q: A load job for an accumulating snapshot is rerun after a failure. What protects you from duplicate trips?
opts: Append the rows again
A merge keyed on trip id
Drop null milestones
Add a date spine
check.why: Rows are updated as milestones arrive, so loading by key makes reruns idempotent.

work: Make your accumulating load a keyed merge and test a double run.
Guard each milestone update with an event time check.

m02.title: Choosing fact types wisely

beats.say: Do you really need all four fact types for every process?
Start with transactions. They are the cheapest, append only, and the source of truth. Derive the other types from them when a question demands it.

Snapshots trade storage for fast reads. Ten thousand drivers over three years is about eleven million rows. Cheap now, but with millions of entities it grows fast. Snapshot only what is queried often, like balances.
Use accumulating snapshots only for short, bounded processes. For long or looping flows, a transaction table of status changes is safer.

show.title: Rule of thumb
items: Long or looping flow: status change events

check.q: Support tickets can reopen many times over months. Which is the safest primary model?
opts: Accumulating snapshot with fixed milestones
Transaction table of status changes
Factless table only
Periodic snapshot only
check.why: Looping, long-lived flows break the fixed milestone columns. Status change events capture every step and can feed derived views.

work: Keep transactions as the base layer and build snapshots as derived tables.
Estimate snapshot storage as entities times periods before approving it.

m02.title: The notebook with no eraser

beats.say: What if your money records had no eraser at all?
Picture a notebook written in pen. Lunch, minus twelve dollars. Refund, plus twelve. Nothing is ever crossed out. Each change is a new line at the bottom.
Made a mistake? Do not erase it. Write a new line that cancels it. The wrong line stays, and so does the fix, so anyone can see what happened.
Your balance is simply every line added up. Want the balance as of last Tuesday? Add only the lines up to Tuesday. This is called a ledger.

check.q: You booked a refund of 12 by mistake. In a ledger, what do you do?
opts: Delete the refund line
Edit the refund to zero
Add a new line of minus 12 that cancels it
Start a new notebook
check.why: A ledger is append only. You cancel a wrong entry with a new reversing entry, so the original and the fix both stay visible.

work: Find one money table at work that gets updated in place and note what history it loses.
Ask your finance team how they correct a wrong entry today.

m02.title: Hold, settle, dispute: a ledger in four rows

beats.say: A customer's card hold was five hundred dollars, but the final charge was four eighty. How do you record that without editing anything?
You append entries. Day one: hold, minus five hundred. Next morning: hold release, plus five hundred, then settle, minus four eighty. Each row has a transaction id, a type, an amount and a timestamp.
Balance is the sum of amount, filtered by timestamp. Sum everything up to day one at noon: minus five hundred. Up to day two: minus four eighty.
Weeks later a dispute arrives. Append plus four eighty. History stays untouched, and the balance is right again.

check.q: Entries for t42 are hold -500, release +500, settle -480. What is the balance after settle?
check.why: Sum the amounts: -500 plus 500 minus 480 equals -480. The release cancels the hold, so only the settle remains.

work: Model one payment flow as a list of typed entries with signed amounts.
Write an as-of balance query using SUM with a timestamp filter and test it on a past date.

m02.title: Why nobody reads the raw log

beats.say: If the log is the truth, why does nobody query it for the current balance?

show.sub: so why not read it directly?

beats.say: Because current state is a fold: read every event for that account and add them up. For an account with ten million entries, that is slow on every read.

So teams keep a current-state table, with one writer, updated from the log. They add periodic snapshots, like end of day balances, so an as-of query starts from the nearest snapshot and folds only the rest.
Gotchas: a replayed message must not post twice, so give every entry a unique key. And a late event has an event time earlier than its load time, so decide which clock your as-of balance uses.

show.title: Two classic traps
items: Replays double-post: give every entry a unique key
Late events: choose event time or load time for as-of

check.q: A payment message is delivered twice by the queue. What protects the ledger from double posting?
opts: A snapshot
A unique entry key that rejects the duplicate
A bigger current-state table
Sorting by timestamp
check.why: Appending is not idempotent by itself. A unique key per entry makes a replay a no-op instead of a second posting.

work: Add a unique idempotency key to every ledger entry and enforce it.
Document whether as-of reports use event time or load time.
Reconcile the current-state table against a full fold on a schedule.

m02.title: When a ledger is worth its cost

beats.say: Should every table in your warehouse be an event sourced ledger?

show.sub: or only where it pays off

beats.say: No. Use it where audit, as-of answers and reprocessing pay for themselves: money, inventory, regulated state. You pay in storage, a fold on every read, and a second table to maintain.

show.title: Worth it, at a price
items: Use for money, inventory, regulated state
Cost: a fold on every read
Cost: a second table to maintain

beats.say: For a customer's address, nobody needs that. A simple slowly changing dimension, or an updated row with change data capture, is cheaper and easier to query.
At scale, partition the log by account and date, snapshot daily, and reconcile the current table against a full fold nightly. If they disagree, the log wins.

check.q: Which table is the best fit for a full event sourced ledger?
opts: Customer marketing preferences
Payment balances needing audit and as-of reports
Product description text
Website page colours
check.why: Ledgers earn their cost where audit trails, as-of answers and safe reprocessing matter, as with money. Low-stakes attributes are cheaper with simpler history patterns.

work: List your tables and mark which truly need audit and as-of answers.
Schedule a nightly job that compares current state to a full fold.
Use slowly changing dimensions for low-stakes attributes instead of a ledger.

m02.title: The receipt and the filing cabinet

beats.say: Picture a shop receipt that only says customer number 4471. To learn the name, you walk to a filing cabinet. Would you write the name on the receipt instead?

If you write it on, reading is fast. No walking. But every receipt is bigger. And if the customer changes their name next year, the old receipts still show the old one. Sometimes that is exactly what you want.

chip.text: Fast to read, bigger to store

beats.say: In data, the pile of receipts is the fact table. The filing cabinet is a dimension. Copying a detail onto every receipt is called denormalising. It trades space for speed, and freezes the value at that moment.

chip.text: Denormalising: copy details onto the fact

check.q: What does copying a customer's name onto every receipt in a fact table give you?
opts: Faster reads, but more storage and a frozen value
Smaller storage and automatic corrections
Nothing, it is the same as a dimension
check.why: Copying avoids the lookup, so reads are faster. The cost is extra space, and old rows keep the value they had when written.

work: Pick one fact table you use and list which descriptive columns it already copies in.
Ask yourself for each one: do I want the old value kept, or the newest value everywhere?

m02.title: Doing the volume arithmetic

beats.say: Fifty million trips a day. How big is a fact table after a year, and what does one extra column cost?

Fifty million times 365 is about 18 billion rows a year. Add a 20 byte city name to each row. That is 360 gigabytes a year before compression. Repeated text compresses well, so the real bill is smaller, but it is never zero.
Now the other side. Joining 18 billion rows to a large dimension means a shuffle, where data is moved across machines so matching keys meet. That costs time and money on every query.
So you pay storage once to save compute many times. Copy a column when most queries need it. Leave it out when it is rarely used.

show.title: The rule of thumb
items: Copy it when most queries need it
Copy it when the join is huge
Leave it out when it is rarely used

check.q: 50 million trips a day, and you add a 20 byte string to the fact. Roughly how much raw extra storage per year?
opts: About 36 GB
About 360 GB
About 3.6 TB
check.why: 50 million times 365 is about 18 billion rows. Times 20 bytes is about 360 GB before compression.

work: Write the rows per year and bytes per row for your biggest fact before adding any column.
Compare that storage cost with the cost of the join you would avoid.

m02.title: Frozen values and the rewrite trap

beats.say: A rider upgrades to gold today. What tier should last month's trips show?
If the tier was copied into the fact at trip time, those trips keep the old tier. That is the value at event time. You get history without keeping versions in the dimension.

The catch is corrections. Say a city name was misspelled. In a dimension, you fix one row. In a wide fact, every copy is wrong, so you rewrite billions of rows. Miss some, and the fact disagrees with the dimension.
So copy values that are frozen by nature, like the tier at trip time. Keep anything you may need to correct everywhere in the dimension, and keep the key in the fact either way.

show.title: What to copy
items: Copy: values true at event time
Keep in dimension: anything you will correct
Always keep the key in the fact

check.q: A city name typo must be fixed everywhere. Where is that easiest?
opts: In a dimension, by fixing one row
In every fact row that copied the city
In both places at once, equally easy
check.why: A dimension holds one row to fix. Copies in a fact must all be rewritten, and any missed copy disagrees with the dimension.

work: Mark each copied column in your facts as frozen at event time or correctable.
Move the correctable ones back to the dimension, or plan a backfill job for them.

m02.title: Narrow core, wide serving layer

beats.say: Should the fact table be wide, or should you build a wide table on top of it?

show.text: Wide fact, or wide layer on top?

beats.say: Usually the second. Keep the core fact narrow, with keys and measures, as the source of truth. Then publish a wide view or table for dashboards and language models, which struggle with joins. You rebuild it when a dimension is corrected.

chip.text: Rebuild the layer, not the truth

beats.say: Know the cost levers. Columnar storage compresses repeated text well, so a city column often costs far less than 360 gigabytes. A small dimension can be broadcast to every machine, avoiding the shuffle. Only huge dimensions truly force denormalising.

show.title: Cost levers
items: Broadcast small dimensions to skip the shuffle

beats.say: Choose by measuring. Test the join cost and the rewrite cost, then pick the cheaper pain.

show.sub: Measure both, pick the cheaper pain

check.q: Dashboards and LLM tools struggle with joins, but dimensions get corrected often. What is the best design?
opts: Copy every attribute into the core fact
Keep the core fact narrow and publish a rebuildable wide layer
Force users to write the joins themselves
check.why: A narrow core stays the source of truth and is cheap to correct. The wide layer serves easy queries and can be rebuilt when dimensions change.

work: Propose a narrow core plus wide serving table for your most-queried fact.
Benchmark one query with the join and one on the wide table, and record both costs.

m02.title: One sheet per month

beats.say: Why would you cram a whole month into a single row?
Imagine a teacher tracking attendance. One way is a separate slip of paper for every student, every day. Thirty slips for Maya in one month. Finding her attendance means hunting through a huge pile.

The smarter way is one sheet per student per month, with thirty-one little boxes, one for each day. The position of the box tells you the day. Now Maya's whole month is one sheet you pick up in one go.
Data teams do exactly this with big tables. It is called a reduced fact. The trade is that a sheet is harder to read at a glance, so you still keep the daily slips for everyday questions.

show.title: Reduced fact
items: One row per person per month
Daily values sit in a list
Harder to read, so keep daily slips too

check.q: In the attendance analogy, what tells you which day a box on the monthly sheet belongs to?
opts: A date written in each box
The position of the box on the sheet
The color of the ink
check.why: A reduced fact stores no date per value. The position in the list is the day, so box k means day k.

work: Find one table at work where you always sum many small rows per person over a long window.
Ask yourself whether people would still need the daily detail, and plan to keep it.

m02.title: Reduced fact mechanics

beats.say: How do you answer trips per day over ninety days, for every rider, without reading millions of rows?
A daily fact has one row per rider per day. Ninety days means ninety rows per rider, and grouping them forces a shuffle, which is moving rows across machines so matching riders meet.

A reduced fact keeps one row per rider per month. The daily trips sit in an array, like two, zero, one, zero, zero, three. Item k is day k. October for rider seven drops from up to thirty-one rows to one. Ninety days is then about three rows per rider.
Each rider is already one row, so the sum happens locally with almost no shuffle. To read days, you unnest the array with ordinality to get the day number. A job appends each new day's value.

check.q: Why does a reduced fact need almost no shuffle for per-rider aggregates?
opts: Arrays are compressed on disk
Each rider's month is already a single row, so nothing must move to meet
The query engine caches all riders in memory
check.why: A shuffle exists to bring rows of the same key together. With the days packed in one row, the data is already together.

work: Pick your most expensive long-window per-entity query and count rows scanned per entity.
Prototype a monthly array table and compare scanned bytes and shuffle size against the daily fact.

m02.title: Where reduced facts bite

beats.say: What breaks when a late event arrives for a reduced fact?
The array is one value in one row, so you cannot just patch a day. You must read the month's array, change position k, and rewrite the whole row. Late data means rewriting that month.

Position is the only thing that says which day. So the layout is fixed to the calendar. Every array must start on the month start, and a missing day must hold zero, not be skipped, or every later day shifts by one.
Casual analysts will struggle with arrays, so keep the daily fact and expose a daily view on top. Also, a rerun that pushes onto the end would add the day twice, so set the value by position instead.

show.title: Guardrails
items: Keep the daily fact and a daily view
Set values by position, not push
Align every array to the month start

check.q: A job reruns after a failure and appends yesterday's value to the end of each array. What goes wrong?
opts: The day is counted twice and later positions shift
Nothing, appends are always safe
The table loses its partitioning
check.why: Position is the date. A duplicate push inserts an extra item, so the array no longer lines up with the calendar. Set by position to stay idempotent.

work: Write the array update as set position k to value, so reruns give the same result.
Add a test that every array length equals the days in its month.

m02.title: When to choose reduced facts

beats.say: When is a reduced fact the wrong choice?

Use it for expensive long-window metrics, like ninety-day trips per rider, where the daily scan and shuffle cost dominates. Cost drops because you scan roughly thirty times fewer rows and skip most shuffles.

Do not make it your only fact. Ad hoc slicing by day, by hour, or by other dimensions gets painful, and heavy late data forces constant rewrites. Sparse entities also waste space, because an array of thirty-one zeros stores nothing useful.

show.title: Avoid when
items: Ad hoc slicing by many dimensions

beats.say: Alternatives: a plain daily fact with good partitioning and pre-aggregated weekly rollups is simpler and handles late data easily. Choose reduced facts only when measured query cost justifies the extra pipeline, and keep the daily table as the source of truth.

show.title: Decision path
items: Keep daily as source of truth

check.q: Which situation best justifies adding a reduced fact?
opts: A rarely run report over one day of data
A costly ninety-day per-rider metric that runs constantly and rarely sees late data
A table where analysts slice by hour and by many dimensions
check.why: Reduced facts pay off for repeated long-window per-entity queries. They hurt for ad hoc slicing and frequent late data.

work: Measure cost per query before building any reduced table, and write down the target saving.
Keep the daily fact as the source of truth and derive the reduced fact from it.

m02.title: A row of 28 light switches

beats.say: How do you remember whether someone showed up on each of the last 28 days, using almost no space?
Picture a row of 28 light switches, one per day. Switch on means the person visited that day. Instead of writing a list of dates, you just glance at the row.
Each night, slide the whole row one step along and set the newest switch. The oldest one falls off the end. Computers store that row as a single small number.
Was she here this week? Look at the last seven switches. Count the lit ones for the month.

show.title: Quick questions
items: Here today? Check the newest switch
Here this week? Any of the last 7 on
Days this month? Count the lit ones

check.q: In the switch analogy, what happens to the oldest day each night?
opts: It is copied to a backup list
It falls off the end of the row
It becomes the newest switch
check.why: The row slides by one day, so the oldest day drops off and a new switch for today is added.

work: Pick one activity metric you compute from raw events and ask whether a fixed window of yes or no flags would answer it.
Explain to a non-technical colleague how a 28-day activity flag can fit in one number.

m02.title: One integer, three activity metrics

beats.say: How can one 32-bit number answer daily, weekly and monthly active users?

show.sub: DAU, WAU, MAU in one scan

beats.say: Bit zero means active today. Bit one means yesterday, and so on up to bit twenty-seven. A user active today and three days ago has bits zero and three set, which is the number nine.

show.title: Bit k = active k days ago

beats.say: Each night, shift the number left by one, add today's flag, and mask to twenty-eight bits. That is one cheap arithmetic step per user instead of rewriting a list of dates.

Active today: bits and one is not zero. Active in last seven: bits and one hundred twenty-seven is not zero. Active days in twenty-eight: count the set bits after masking. A billion users at four bytes is four gigabytes.

show.title: Reading the bits
show.text:
L1  = bits & 1 != 0
L7  = bits & 127 != 0
L28 = bit_count(bits & (2^28 - 1))

check.q: A user has bits equal to 9 (binary 1001). Which is true?
opts: Active today and 3 days ago
Active yesterday and 4 days ago
Active 9 days ago only
check.why: Bit 0 is today and bit 3 is three days ago. 8 plus 1 equals 9.

work: Write the nightly update as one SQL expression using shift, or, and a mask.
Compute L1, L7 and L28 from a bitmask column and check them against your list-based numbers.

m02.title: Where the bitmask breaks

beats.say: Your bitmask says a user is inactive, but they were actually active. What went wrong?

Late events are the usual cause. The shift happens once a night, so a late event for two days ago needs you to set that old bit by hand, or rebuild from raw data. Backfills must replay days in order, because shifting twice corrupts the history.
Watch the width. A thirty-two bit integer shifted left past its limit overflows, so always mask. Thirty-two days is the ceiling; use sixty-four bits for longer windows.
Also, a bit only says active or not. You lose event counts, and the day boundary is baked in, so a timezone change means a rebuild.

show.title: What the bit hides
items: Day boundary and timezone are fixed in
Changing the definition means a rebuild

check.q: Why must a backfill replay days in order?
opts: Because each run shifts the bits, so wrong order corrupts history
Because bit_count only works on sorted data
Because masks expire after one day
check.why: The update shifts the previous state, so running days twice or out of order moves bits to the wrong positions.

work: Make the nightly job idempotent: rebuild a day's state from the prior day's partition, never from the current one.
Decide and document how late events are handled and for how many days.

m02.title: Bitmask or something else?

beats.say: Is a bitmask always the right way to track activity at scale?
It shines for fixed windows: DAU, WAU, MAU, retention and streaks. Retention is just an AND between two days' bits. Scans touch one narrow column, so they are fast.
Storage is not the real win. A billion users as date arrays is maybe tens of gigabytes, still affordable. The win is compute and simplicity, with no array unnesting.

Skip it when you need arbitrary date ranges, counts per day, or windows beyond sixty-four days. Use a daily partitioned active table. For approximate unique counts across dimensions, consider HyperLogLog sketches.

show.title: Choose instead
items: Per-day counts: keep a numeric fact

check.q: Which need is a poor fit for a 28-bit activity mask?
opts: Monthly active users
Seven-day retention
Total purchases per user per day
check.why: A bit only records active or not. Per-day counts need a numeric fact such as a daily aggregate table.

work: List the activity questions your dashboards ask and check each is a fixed window.
Keep a daily partitioned table alongside the bitmask for audits and ad hoc ranges.

m03.title: A restaurant kitchen for your data

beats.say: Would a restaurant serve diners straight from the delivery truck? Of course not. Data works the same way.

Raw data is the crates at the loading dock. Everything exactly as it arrived, muddy carrots and all. Only the kitchen staff go there. Next, the pantry. Things are washed, labelled and sorted, so duplicates and mistakes are gone.
Then the menu: ready-made dishes that analysts and dashboards can pick quickly. Last is the waiter's tray, the serving stage. Apps and AI assistants get exactly what they ask for, fast.

chip.text: Each reader gets a different shape

beats.say: Each stage has a different reader, so each one uses a different shape.

check.q: Why do we keep several stages instead of one set of tables?
opts: Each stage serves a different reader with a different need
Databases cannot hold more than one table
It makes the data smaller each time
check.why: The stages exist because engineers, analysts and apps need different shapes, freshness and trust. It is not about storage limits or size.

work: Name the main reader of each of your datasets in one line.
Find one place where people read raw data directly and ask why.

m03.title: Raw to serving, step by step

beats.say: Why not one set of tables for everyone? Because a data engineer, an analyst and an app need very different things.
Bronze keeps events exactly as received, append only. If an order changes three times, you store three rows. Nothing is lost, so you can always replay.
Silver cleans up. It removes duplicates, fixes types, and keeps one row per customer or order. History is kept with start and end dates, called slowly changing dimensions type two.

show.title: Silver
items: Start and end dates for history

beats.say: Gold reshapes data for questions: a star schema, or one wide table with every column pre-joined. An analyst runs one scan instead of five joins.
Serving copies the answers into a fast store, like a key-value store, that replies in milliseconds to apps and models.

check.q: An order changes status three times. What does bronze store?
opts: Only the latest status
All three changes as separate rows
Nothing until the order is final
check.why: Bronze is append only and as received, so every change is kept. Silver is where you reduce to the latest row and keep history deliberately.

work: Check whether your raw layer is append only and replayable.
List which tables hold history with start and end dates.

m03.title: Where stage models go wrong

beats.say: Where do most pipelines go wrong? They model too early.
If you clean data on the way into bronze and the rule has a bug, the original is gone. You can't replay. So bronze stays raw, even when that feels messy.
In silver, ask what changes most. If sources change often, a Data Vault absorbs new columns without rebuilding. If business rules change, keep those rules out of silver.

show.title: Silver: what changes most?
items: Rules change: rules live in gold
Questions change: star or wide tables

beats.say: In gold, wide tables are fast but rigid. Change a definition and you rebuild billions of rows. And if two teams compute revenue in two places, the dashboards disagree.

show.title: Gold gotchas
items: Definition change means a big rebuild
Revenue defined twice means two answers

beats.say: In serving, the classic trap is skew: the model trains on batch values but reads different ones online.

check.q: Sources change columns every few weeks and you must audit lineage. Which silver model fits best?
opts: A single wide table
Data Vault
Dropping history to save space
check.why: A Data Vault separates keys, relationships and attributes, so new source columns are added without rebuilding the core, and every row traces back to its source.

work: Test replaying one day of bronze through your pipeline.
Search for metrics defined in more than one place and merge them.

m03.title: Earn every layer

beats.say: Should every dataset pass through all four stages? Usually not.
Each stage is another copy and another job. Ten terabytes copied four times is forty terabytes to store, plus compute to keep them in sync, plus more things to break.
So earn each layer. One source and a small team? Go raw to a star schema, skip Data Vault. Many volatile sources and audit demands? Data Vault in silver pays off.
Rather than a wide table per team, define metrics once in a semantic layer, so BI and AI agents share one revenue number.
Add a serving store only when the latency target, say under fifty milliseconds, can't be met by the warehouse.

check.q: A small team has one source and only dashboard users. What is the best default?
opts: Raw, Data Vault, wide table, feature store, key-value store
Raw to a star schema with a semantic layer for metrics
Skip raw and transform on ingest
check.why: With one source and BI readers, extra layers add copies and cost with no benefit. Keep raw for replay, then a star schema and shared metrics.

work: Cost each layer: storage, compute and people time.
Remove or merge any layer whose reader you cannot name.
Set a latency target before adding a serving store.

m03.title: Data is a kitchen, not a truck

beats.say: Why doesn't a restaurant cook straight from the delivery truck? Because data works the same way.
Raw data is the delivery. You keep every box exactly as it arrived, with a label saying who sent it and when. If a dish goes wrong, you can check the original.
Next, the prep kitchen washes, sorts and labels everything. One clean tub per ingredient. Then the chefs build menu dishes from it, made the same way every time.
Finally each customer is served differently. A waiter gets a quick order slip. A recipe book answers questions. Each format fits who is asking.

check.q: In the kitchen analogy, why keep the raw delivery boxes untouched?
opts: So you can go back and check or redo a dish if something went wrong
Because customers eat directly from the boxes
To make serving faster
Because boxes are cheaper than tubs
check.why: Untouched raw data lets you replay and audit. If a cleaning rule was wrong, you can rebuild from the original.

work: Sketch your own pipeline as raw, cleaned, business and serving, and name what lives in each.
Ask which of your tables still holds the original data exactly as it arrived.

m03.title: Raw, silver and gold: pick the model

beats.say: Where should a duplicate order be removed: when it arrives, or later?
Raw keeps an append-only log. Each row gets an envelope: source, ingested time, schema version and the payload. Ten million events in, ten million stored. Nothing is dropped, so you can replay.

Silver turns that into clean entities. Customers, orders, payments, typed and deduplicated, with history kept as slowly changing dimension type two. If many sources feed the same customer, Data Vault keeps them apart cleanly.

Gold is built for questions. A star schema, one fact table with dimensions around it, serves most analysis. A wide one big table speeds up the hottest dashboard. Daily aggregates store repeated sums once.

check.q: Which model fits the raw (bronze) stage best?
opts: Star schema
Append-only log with an envelope
One big table
Key-value store
check.why: Raw must lose nothing and allow replay, so an append-only log with source, ingest time, schema version and payload fits. Stars and big tables are for answering questions later.

work: Check that your raw tables record source, ingest time and schema version.
List which gold tables are stars and which are one big tables, and why.

m03.title: Four consumers, four serving models

beats.say: Same data, four consumers. Why not give them all the warehouse?

show.sub: Each consumer needs a different shape

beats.say: An app needs an answer in milliseconds. So load a key value store like Redis or DynamoDB, keyed by customer id. One key, one lookup, no scanning.
Machine learning gets a feature store. The offline side builds training sets as of each past moment. The online side serves the latest values. Same definitions both ways.
Analysts and language models get a semantic layer, where revenue and its joins are defined once. AI search gets a vector table: chunk text, embedding, metadata, source id and version.

show.title: BI, LLMs and AI search
items: Semantic layer: metrics, dimensions and joins defined once
Vector table: chunk, embedding, metadata, source id, version
Both sit on top of trusted gold data

check.q: What does a feature store's offline side do that a plain latest-value table cannot?
opts: Serves results in milliseconds
Builds training rows using values as they were at each past moment
Stores raw events
Replaces the semantic layer
check.why: Point-in-time correct training sets need historical values as of each label time. A latest-value table would leak the future.

work: Name the consumer of each serving table you own and its latency need.
Check whether training and production compute each feature from the same definition.

m03.title: Fixing data too early, defining it too soon

beats.say: What is the most expensive mistake in a lakehouse? Fixing data too early.

show.text: Fix it too early, lose it forever

beats.say: Clean or deduplicate on the way into bronze, and a bad rule destroys the evidence. You cannot replay what you never stored. Keep raw untouched, and fix in silver.

chip.text: Mistakes can no longer be replayed

beats.say: Put metric definitions in silver and every team inherits them, including the wrong ones. Silver should say what happened, not what revenue means.
Gold has its own trap: one table per dashboard. Soon finance reports revenue with refunds, and sales reports it without. Two numbers, one meeting, no trust. Define revenue once in shared gold models.

check.q: Why is deduplicating while loading bronze an anti-pattern?
opts: It makes loading slower
A wrong rule permanently loses data you could have replayed
Bronze cannot hold duplicates
It breaks the star schema
check.why: Raw is your safety net. If you drop or merge rows before storing them, a mistaken rule cannot be corrected by replaying.

work: Audit ingestion jobs for filters or dedup steps that run before raw is stored.
Find metrics defined in more than one dashboard table and consolidate them.

m03.title: Serving traps: leakage, guessing and orphans

beats.say: Why does a model score ninety percent in training and fail in production?

show.sub: Where did the gap come from?

beats.say: Often the features were computed differently. Training used a nightly SQL job; production used app code. Or training used data from after the prediction moment, which is leakage. A point-in-time correct feature store joins only values known at that time.
Language models have the same problem. Let one write SQL on raw tables and it guesses joins, and guesses revenue. A semantic layer limits it to approved metrics.
Vectors need care too. Without metadata and source version, you cannot filter by tenant or re-embed when a document changes.

show.title: A vector row needs more than a vector
items: Metadata: tenant, type, date for filtering
Source id: trace back to the document
Version: re-embed when the source changes

check.q: A feature uses an account balance that was updated after the label date. What is this problem called?
opts: Skew in the online store
Data leakage from missing point-in-time correctness
Schema drift
Cold start
check.why: Using values not known at prediction time leaks the future into training. Point-in-time joins prevent it.

work: Check whether training features and online features come from one shared definition.
Make sure every vector row stores source id, version and filterable metadata.

m03.title: Not every layer earns its keep

beats.say: Do you need every layer and every model? Usually not.
