show.sub: Choose by need, not by checklist

beats.say: Data Vault pays off with many sources and constant change. With three sources, plain third normal form is cheaper, and the extra hubs and links just add joins.

show.title: Data Vault: only at *scale of sources*

beats.say: One big table is fast to query but duplicates dimensions. Change a customer region and you rewrite billions of rows. Keep it for the hottest questions only, built from the star.
Serving stores cost money and add sync lag. Add Redis, a feature store or a vector index only when the latency need is proven. Otherwise a warehouse with a semantic layer is enough.

show.title: Add serving stores when proven
items: Each store adds cost and a sync pipeline
Start with warehouse plus semantic layer
Add Redis, features or vectors on measured need

check.q: A team has three stable sources and only dashboard users. Which design is the best fit?
opts: Data Vault silver, Redis, and a vector index
Normalised silver, star schema gold, and a semantic layer
One big table per dashboard
Raw only, queried directly
check.why: With few stable sources and BI users, 3NF plus stars and a semantic layer meets the need with the least cost. The others add stores and joins with no proven benefit.

work: For each extra store or model in your platform, write the measured need that justifies it.
Review any one big table: can it be rebuilt from the star in one job?

m03.title: Taste it before you serve it

beats.say: Would a restaurant serve a dish without tasting it first?
A cook prepares the dish in the back kitchen. Nobody in the dining room can see it yet. That back kitchen is called staging, a private place to work.
Then a checker tastes it. Is it hot? Is it the right dish? Is the portion full? Only if it passes does the waiter carry it out.
Data works the same way. Write privately, check it, then publish. Customers never get a half cooked table.

check.q: In the restaurant analogy, what does the back kitchen stand for?
opts: A staging place where new data is built unseen
The final dashboard
The customer's report
A backup of old data
check.why: Staging is a private area where data is written and checked before anyone consumes it.

work: List which of your tables feed money or executive reports.
Ask where a failed load leaves its half-written data today.

m03.title: Write, audit, publish in three steps

beats.say: How do you load a million rows and never show a customer a broken table?
Step one, write. The job lands today's data on a staging branch, not the live table. Readers still see yesterday's version.

Step two, audit. Run checks on the branch. Is the order id unique and never null? Does every customer key exist in the customer dimension? Is the row count near the usual two million, give or take ten percent? Is the latest event under an hour old?

show.title: Step two: audit the branch
items: Rows within 2M plus or minus 10 percent

beats.say: Step three, publish. If every check passes, merge or fast forward the branch, one cheap metadata swap. If one fails, the branch is dropped and the live table stays untouched.

check.q: An audit on the staging branch fails. What happens to the live table?
opts: It keeps yesterday's data unchanged
It gets partial new rows
It is deleted and rebuilt
It switches to the branch anyway
check.why: Publish only happens after all checks pass, so a failure leaves the live table as it was.

work: Pick one pipeline and write its five audit checks with thresholds.
Check whether your table format supports branches or an atomic swap.

m03.title: Why passing checks can still lie

beats.say: Your checks passed, so why is the revenue dashboard still wrong?

show.sub: Gates only catch what you wrote down

beats.say: Because checks only catch what you wrote down. Row counts can look normal while half the amounts are zero. So add validity rules, like money never negative, and reconcile totals against the source system to the cent.
Referential integrity has a trap too. A late arriving dimension row makes foreign keys fail. Map those to an unknown member instead of blocking the whole load, and fix them later.
Decide severity. Block on broken keys and money. Only warn on small freshness drift. And remember the publish must be atomic, or readers see half of it.

check.q: Row counts are normal but half the amounts are zero. Which check would catch it?
opts: Uniqueness of the key
Reconciliation with the source
A not null check on keys
Freshness of the latest event
check.why: Reconciling totals with the source exposes missing money that count, key and freshness checks all miss.

work: Add a source reconciliation check to your most important money table.
Define which checks block a publish and which only warn.

m03.title: Where gates pay off and where they don't

beats.say: Should every table get a full audit gate, and should the data team own all of it?

No. Gates cost compute and delay delivery. Audits scan data, so on a huge table check partitions that changed, not everything. Spend strict gates on money and executive tables, light ones on exploratory data.

Better still, shift left with data contracts. The producing team promises schema, meaning and freshness, and changes go through review. That stops breakage at the source, instead of at two in the morning downstream.
WAP needs branch support, like Iceberg or Delta. Without it, use a staging table and a swap. Choose by how costly a bad publish is.

show.title: Choosing the mechanism
items: Match rigor to cost of a bad publish

check.q: What is the main benefit of data contracts compared with downstream audits alone?
opts: They make audits unnecessary
They prevent breaking changes at the producer before they spread
They speed up table scans
They replace reconciliation
check.why: Contracts move agreement upstream so schema changes are reviewed, while downstream audits remain a safety net.

work: Tier your tables and set gate strictness per tier.
Propose a contract with your top event producer covering schema and freshness.

m03.title: Pantry, meal tray, menu board

beats.say: Why would anyone store the same sales numbers three different ways? Picture a restaurant kitchen.
A star schema is a pantry. Receipts sit in the middle. Small labeled shelves surround them: customers, products, cities. You can cook any dish, but you fetch from several shelves each time.

chip.text: Flexible, but you fetch from shelves

beats.say: One big table is a ready meal tray. Everything is already on one plate, so serving is instant. The catch is that it is one fixed meal.

chip.text: Fast to serve, one fixed view

beats.say: Aggregates are the menu board. Totals per city per day, counted once, so nobody recounts every receipt. Copy the board from the receipts, never type it by hand, or it drifts.

check.q: Which analogy best fits an aggregate table?
opts: A pantry with labeled shelves
A menu board of totals copied from the receipts
A ready meal tray holding every detail
A single receipt
check.why: An aggregate stores precomputed summaries at a coarser grain, such as city by day, derived from the base records.

work: List the three dashboards your team opens most and note which shape each one reads today.
Ask who owns each summary table and whether it is generated from the base fact.

m03.title: Star, wide table, aggregate: the mechanics

beats.say: A dashboard wants yesterday's trips by city. Should it read fifty million rows, or three hundred?
In a star, one fact row is one trip, holding keys and numbers like fare. Keys point to small dimension tables: rider, city, date. Every question joins the fact to the dimensions it needs.

A one big table does that join once, ahead of time. Fare, city name and rider tier sit side by side in one wide row. Columnar engines read only the columns asked for, so width is cheap and the query needs no join.
An aggregate goes further. Group trips by city and day, and fifty million rows shrink to about three hundred. Dashboards that repeat the same summary all morning read that instead.

check.q: Why is a wide table cheap to scan on a columnar engine?
opts: It stores fewer rows than the fact
Only the requested columns are read, so extra columns cost little
It never needs to be rebuilt
It compresses rows into one file
check.why: Columnar storage reads just the columns a query touches, so width adds little scan cost while removing the join.

work: Write down the grain of your main fact in one sentence.
Pick one repeated dashboard query and estimate rows scanned with and without an aggregate.

m03.title: Physical layout of a lakehouse fact

beats.say: Why can the same table take two seconds or two minutes? Often it is the physical layout, not the model.

Partition the big fact by event date. A query for yesterday then opens one folder and skips the rest. Inside it, cluster or sort by the most common filter, such as city, so matching rows sit together.

chip.text: Skip what you do not need

beats.say: Aim for files of about 128 megabytes to one gigabyte. Ten thousand tiny files mean ten thousand opens and listings, and that slows every query.
Finally, use nested types. A trip can carry an array of stops inside one row, so you avoid yet another join.

show.title: Nested types
items: An array holds many stops in one trip row

check.q: A lakehouse fact has millions of 100 KB files. What is the main problem?
opts: Too many columns
Per-file open and listing overhead slows queries
Partitioning by date is impossible
Dimensions cannot join
check.why: Small files multiply metadata and open costs. Compact into files of roughly 128 MB to 1 GB.

work: Check the median file size of your largest fact and schedule compaction if it is tiny.
Confirm the table is partitioned by event date and sorted by the top filter column.

m03.title: Fan-out and the frozen view

beats.say: Your one big table shows revenue double what finance reports. What went wrong?
Fan-out. You joined trips to payments, and one trip has two payments. Now the trip row appears twice, and its fare is counted twice. Joining along any one-to-many path multiplies rows.
Prevent it by checking row counts after every join against the fact's grain. Aggregate the many side first, or nest it as an array.

show.title: Guard the grain
items: Assert rows out equal rows in
Or nest it as an array

beats.say: Second trap: a rider's city is corrected in the dimension. The wide table still holds the old value, so you must rebuild affected partitions. And remember, it freezes one view of the data.

check.q: After joining trips to payments, summed fares are too high. Most likely cause?
opts: Missing partition
One-to-many join duplicated trip rows
Files too large
Wrong sort key
check.why: A trip with several payments repeats on each payment row, so its fare is summed more than once.

work: Add a row-count assertion after each join in your wide-table build.
Document which dimension corrections trigger a rebuild and how far back.

m03.title: Drifting totals and as-of joins

beats.say: Two dashboards show different totals for the same city and day. Why?

show.text: Same city, same day, two totals

beats.say: Someone defined an aggregate separately from the base fact. One excludes cancelled trips, the other does not. The fix is to generate every aggregate from the fact with one shared query, never hand-maintain it.

Star schemas have their own gotcha. When a rider's tier changes, history is kept as dated versions of the dimension row. Analysts must join where the trip date falls between a version's start and end. That is an as-of join. Forget it, and old trips take today's tier.

show.title: As-of join
show.text: join dim_rider r on t.rider_id = r.rider_id and t.trip_date between r.valid_from and r.valid_to
show.note: Match the version live on the trip date

check.q: Why do analysts need an as-of join on a history-tracking dimension?
opts: To speed up partition pruning
To match each fact to the dimension version valid on the event date
To avoid fan-out from payments
To compress the dimension
check.why: With several versions per rider, a plain key join would match all of them or the latest, giving wrong history.

work: Replace any hand-written summary tables with ones generated from the base fact.
Provide a ready-made as-of view so analysts never write that join themselves.

m03.title: Choosing among star, OBT and aggregates

beats.say: Should you just flatten everything into one big table and delete the star?
No. Keep the star as the flexible core. It serves many questions, and shared conformed dimensions mean every team uses the same definition of city or rider.

Then generate the wide table and aggregates from it for the hottest dashboards and text-to-SQL, where a model writing joins often gets them wrong. You pay storage and rebuild compute to save query cost and mistakes.

show.title: What you trade
items: Pay: extra storage and rebuild compute
Save: query cost and join errors
Win: simple tables for BI and text-to-SQL

beats.say: Skip the wide table when questions change daily or dimensions are corrected often. For entity history and states, use cumulative tables, and accept sequential backfills.

show.title: When not to
items: Questions change daily: stay on the star
Entity history: cumulative tables, slow sequential backfills

check.q: Best architecture for many teams plus a few very hot dashboards?
opts: Only one big table
Star core, with generated wide tables and aggregates for hot paths
Only hand-built aggregates
Raw files queried directly
check.why: The star keeps flexibility and shared definitions. Generated derivatives speed hot paths without letting definitions drift.

work: Identify the three hottest dashboards and build generated wide tables only for them.
Track rebuild cost per derived table so you can retire ones that no longer pay off.
Test text-to-SQL accuracy on the star versus the wide table before choosing.

m03.title: Why a model must not peek at the future

beats.say: Imagine sitting an exam when someone slipped you the answers. You would score perfectly. Then you would fail the real one. Why does this matter for data?

show.sub: Models can cheat without anyone noticing

beats.say: A model that predicts whether a trip will be cancelled can only use what was known when the rider asked. If we attach today's rider statistics to an old trip, the model has peeked at the future.

A feature store fixes this. A feature is just a fact the model uses, like cancellations in the last thirty days. The store remembers each fact with a timestamp, so every old trip gets what was known then, not what is known now.

check.q: Why does a model trained with today's rider statistics on old trips fail in production?
opts: It used facts that were not known at request time
The statistics were too old
The model was too small
check.why: Using future information inflates offline scores. In production those facts do not exist yet, so performance drops.

work: Ask your ML teams what timestamp each training feature is joined on.
List features that are recomputed as of today rather than stored with a date.

m03.title: One dictionary for every number

beats.say: Three people ask for revenue last week and get three different numbers. How can that happen?

One analyst leaves out refunds. Another counts unfinished trips. Each wrote their own formula. A semantic layer is a shared dictionary. It defines revenue once, in code, along with the ways you can slice it, such as by city.
Now dashboards, notebooks and AI assistants all ask for revenue by city, and the layer writes the same query every time. For an AI, it is choosing from a menu instead of guessing how tables join.

check.q: What is the main benefit of defining revenue in a semantic layer?
opts: Queries run faster on raw tables
Every tool gets the same definition and the same number
It removes the need for a warehouse
check.why: The layer centralises the formula, dimensions and joins, so every consumer, including AI agents, gets consistent results.

work: Pick your three most disputed metrics and write down who defines each.
Move one metric definition into a shared, version-controlled file.

m03.title: As-of joins and the online store

beats.say: A rider has five cancellations on Monday and twelve on Friday. Which number does a Tuesday trip get for training?
Five. The feature store keeps every value with a timestamp. For each training row, an as-of join picks the latest value at or before the trip's request time. Never after.
For live traffic, an online store keeps only the newest value per rider in a key-value database. A lookup takes a few milliseconds.
Both paths come from one feature definition, so what the model learned on is what it sees in production.

check.q: A trip is requested Tuesday. Feature values exist for Monday and Friday. Which does an as-of join use?
opts: Friday, the latest value
Monday, the latest value at or before the request
The average of both
check.why: As-of joins take the most recent value not later than the event time, preventing future leakage.

work: Check that your feature tables store a valid-from timestamp.
Test one training set by confirming no feature timestamp is later than its event time.

m03.title: Building a vector table for retrieval

beats.say: How does an AI assistant find the one paragraph, among a thousand runbooks, that answers your question?

show.text: One paragraph in a thousand documents

beats.say: You split each document into chunks of a few hundred words. Each chunk becomes an embedding, a list of numbers that captures its meaning. Similar meanings sit close together, so search means finding the nearest numbers.
Store beside each chunk its text and metadata: source, owner, date, access level and version. Then you can filter, such as only payments runbooks this person may see.
Add a content hash. When a document is edited, only chunks whose hash changed get re-embedded, which saves cost.

check.q: What is the content hash on a chunk used for?
opts: Ranking results by relevance
Encrypting the text
Detecting which chunks changed so only those are re-embedded
check.why: Comparing hashes shows what changed, so you avoid paying to re-embed unchanged chunks.

work: Add source, owner, access level, version and hash columns to your chunk table.
Measure how much embedding spend a hash check would save on one nightly refresh.

m03.title: Why a great offline model flops live

beats.say: Your model scored ninety-five percent offline and flopped live. What do you check first?

Leakage. Typical causes are joining on when a record was processed instead of when the event happened, or using late-arriving data that was not available at request time. An as-of join on the wrong timestamp still leaks.

show.title: Leakage suspects
items: Processing time used as event time

beats.say: Next, training-serving skew. If training computes a feature in batch and serving recomputes it in app code, small differences creep in. One shared definition prevents that.
Also watch freshness. An online value that stopped updating hours ago quietly serves stale data. Set a time to live and alert on its age.

check.q: Training computes a feature in a batch job. Serving recomputes it separately in application code. What risk is this?
opts: Training-serving skew
Index fragmentation
Schema evolution
check.why: Two implementations drift apart, so the model sees different values live than it learned on.

work: Audit which features have two separate implementations.
Add an age alert on online store values.

m03.title: Stale chunks, leaked chunks

beats.say: You updated a policy, but the assistant still quotes the old one. Why?
Stale chunks. If you embed the new text without deleting the old version, both stay in the index. Use the document version, and delete or filter out anything not current.
Second, access. If a restricted chunk is retrieved before permissions are checked, the model can reveal it. Filter by access level inside the search, not after.

show.title: Access control
items: Never trust the prompt to hide data

beats.say: Third, embeddings from different models are not comparable. Change the model and you must re-embed everything, so record the model name on every row.

show.sub: Store the model name per row

check.q: Where should access-level filtering happen in retrieval?
opts: After the model writes its answer
Inside the search query, before results reach the model
In the user's prompt instructions
check.why: Filtering at query time guarantees restricted chunks never reach the model; later or prompt-based controls can fail.

work: Check that every chunk row carries version, access level and embedding model name.
Test that old document versions are removed after an update.

m03.title: Do you really need a feature store?

beats.say: Should every team that trains a model adopt a feature store?
No. If you only score in batch, a warehouse table with a valid-from timestamp and an as-of join gives point-in-time correctness without running extra systems.
An online store earns its cost when you need millisecond lookups and share features across many models. Then you pay for streaming pipelines, a key-value store and backfills.
Rule of thumb: start with as-of joins in the warehouse, and add the online store when latency demands it.

check.q: A team only scores customers once a night. What is the sensible choice?
opts: Warehouse feature tables with as-of joins
A full streaming online store
Skip timestamps entirely
check.why: Batch scoring needs correctness, not millisecond serving. Warehouse as-of joins give that without extra infrastructure.

work: List models needing under 100 ms feature lookups; only those justify an online store.
Estimate the running cost of streaming and backfills before buying a platform.

m03.title: Choosing semantic layers and vector stores

beats.say: Where do you put metric logic, and where do you put vectors?
A semantic layer beats wide tables when many tools and AI agents need consistent answers. But it adds a service, and complex ad hoc analysis still needs raw SQL. Do not force everything through it.

show.title: Semantic layer
items: Win: one definition for all tools

beats.say: For vectors, a few million chunks fit in Postgres with a vector extension, beside your metadata and permissions, with simple filters and transactions. Past tens of millions, or under heavy query load, consider a dedicated vector database.
Choose by scale, filter needs and who owns operations, not by hype.

check.q: You have two million chunks, strict per-user permissions and a small team. What is a sound default?
opts: A dedicated vector database cluster
Postgres with a vector extension, keeping metadata beside the embeddings
Flat files read by the model
check.why: At this scale Postgres handles vectors well, and keeping permissions and metadata in one place simplifies filtering and operations.

work: Count chunks and peak queries per second before choosing a vector store.
Write down which metrics truly need cross-tool consistency and put only those in the layer.

m03.title: Blank page: where do you start?

beats.say: Someone says: design the data for a taxi app. You have a blank page and forty-five minutes. Where do you even start?

show.sub: Design the data for a taxi app

beats.say: Not with boxes. Start with questions. What does the boss need to know? Revenue per city, trips per driver, late pickups. Write down five. That list is your target, like a shopping list before you enter the shop.

Next, list what happens: trips, payments, ratings. Then list who is involved: rider, driver, city. Finally say in one sentence what one row means. One row is one completed trip. That sentence is called the grain, and everything else hangs on it.
Then say your reasons out loud as you go. Interviewers score your thinking, not your drawing.

check.q: What is the grain of a fact table?
opts: The list of columns it has
One sentence saying what a single row represents
The size of the table in gigabytes
The tool used to load it
check.why: The grain says what one row means, such as one completed trip. Measures and dimensions are only valid once that is fixed.

work: Before your next design review, write down the five questions the model must answer.
Write the grain of each table as one sentence in its description.

m03.title: Dimensions and facts around the grain

beats.say: You have the grain: one row per completed trip. What goes around it?

show.text: Grain: one row per completed trip

beats.say: Dimensions describe the who and where. Rider, driver, city, date. For each attribute that changes, pick a history rule. A driver's phone number? Overwrite it, that is type one. A driver's city? Keep every version with dates, that is type two, because Finance reports by city at trip time. Rider and driver are the same person table, used in two roles.

Now the fact table. Transaction type, one row per trip. Measures: fare, distance, tip. Those add up across anything, so they are additive. Driver rating average does not add, so store the sum and the count. Keep the trip id on the row itself, a degenerate id, with no table of its own.

check.q: Average driver rating per trip is stored. How should you keep it so it can be rolled up by city?
opts: Store the average and sum it
Store the rating sum and rating count
Store it only in the dimension
Round it to a whole number
check.why: Averages are not additive. With sum and count you can add both across any grouping and divide at the end.

work: Review one fact table and label each measure additive, semi-additive or non-additive.
List which dimension attributes truly need history before choosing SCD2.

m03.title: Prove it, then scale it

beats.say: How do you prove a model works before the clock runs out?

Take two of your five questions and write the query. One easy: fare by city by day, a join and a group by. One needs history: revenue by the driver's city at trip time. That is an as-of join. Match each trip to the dimension row where trip time falls between valid-from and valid-to.

Then scale and evolve. Partition trips by date, say about two million rows a day. Late events? Reload the affected day. Duplicates? Dedupe on trip id. A new source or attribute? Add a column or dimension, not a rebuild. And say which layer each table lives in.

show.title: Scale and evolve
items: New attribute: add, do not rebuild
Name the layer of each table

check.q: A report needs revenue by the driver's city at the moment of the trip. What do you need?
opts: Join to the current driver row
An as-of join to an SCD2 dimension on trip time
A bigger fact table
A type one dimension
check.why: Only versioned history lets you recover the city that was true at trip time, and the as-of join picks that version.

work: Write one as-of join on your own data and check each trip matches exactly one row.
Write down how late and duplicate events are handled for your busiest fact.

m03.title: Why strong candidates still fail

beats.say: Why do strong candidates still fail this round?

Mistake one: skipping the grain. Mix one row per trip with one row per payment, and a join doubles revenue. Mistake two: type two on everything. A rider's email changing creates millions of useless rows. Mistake three: a sloppy as-of join. Use valid-from less than or equal to trip time, and trip time less than valid-to, or boundary trips match twice.
Also watch ratios and balances. Averages and account balances cannot be summed across time, so store the parts. And never go silent. A diagram with no spoken trade-off scores low.

check.q: A fact joins to a dimension and total revenue doubles. What is the most likely cause?
opts: The warehouse is too small
The dimension has overlapping or duplicate rows for the key
Revenue is non-additive
The table is partitioned
check.why: Duplicate or overlapping dimension versions make one fact row match twice, inflating sums.

work: Add a test that each fact key matches exactly one dimension row.
Audit your SCD2 tables for attributes that never need history.

m03.title: Spending 45 minutes like a budget

beats.say: Forty-five minutes, one design. How do you decide what to leave out?
Spend time like money. About five minutes clarifying, ten on grain and dimensions, ten on facts, ten proving with queries, and ten on scale. Hold the rest back for questions.

Then name the alternative. If one team just needs dashboards, a wide one big table is cheaper to query but harder to change. If many sources keep arriving, a Data Vault raw layer absorbs change, with star schemas on top for serving. A semantic layer defines revenue once.
And say when you would not model at all. Tiny data, one question, a single report? A view is enough.

check.q: Many new source systems keep arriving, and a team also needs fast dashboards. What is a sound choice?
opts: One big table loaded directly from every source
A Data Vault integration layer with star schemas for serving
No modelling, query raw files
A single SCD1 dimension
check.why: A vault absorbs source change without rework, while stars give simple fast reads for dashboards.

work: Practise a mock round with a timer and the five stage budget.
For one project, write down why you chose its layers and what you would use if scale doubled.

m03.title: Crates and prep kitchen: raw and cleaned

beats.say: Why keep a messy copy of your data and a clean copy too?
Think of a restaurant. Crates arrive from suppliers and go in the storeroom untouched, with the delivery date on each one. That is the raw layer: data exactly as received, only ever added to.
Then the prep kitchen washes, trims and weighs everything into standard portions. That is the cleaned layer: no duplicates, the same units, one clock.
If a recipe goes wrong, you go back to the crates and prep again. Throw the crates away, and you can never prove what arrived.

show.title: Why keep the crates
items: Redo the cleaning when a rule was wrong
Prove what the source really sent

check.q: A cleaning rule turns out to be wrong. What lets you fix it fully?
opts: Edit the cleaned tables by hand
Reprocess from the untouched raw layer
Ask the source to resend everything
check.why: Raw is kept exactly as received and never edited, so you can rerun cleaning with a corrected rule and rebuild the cleaned layer.

work: Check whether your pipeline overwrites or keeps the original landed files.
Ask where you would go to prove what a source sent last March.

m03.title: Hubs, links and sticky notes: Data Vault

beats.say: How does a bank keep every fact from ten systems about one customer, and never lose any?
Picture a library card catalogue. Each person gets one index card showing only their ID number. That card is a hub: just the business key, nothing else.
A link is a string between two cards: this rider took a trip with that driver.

Details go on sticky notes pinned to a card, each stamped with a date and its source. Those are satellites. Nothing is erased; new notes are just added. A new system just means a new note, and no card changes.

check.q: A new system starts describing your riders. In a vault, what do you add?
opts: A new column on the hub
A new satellite attached to the existing hub
A new copy of every table
check.why: Satellites hold descriptive attributes per source, so a new source is a new satellite and existing tables stay untouched.

work: Sketch one business entity of yours as a hub with two satellites.
List which systems describe the same customer in your company.

m03.title: How raw and cleaned layers work

beats.say: A source sends the same order twice and renames a column overnight. What happens to your tables?
Raw lands it append-only, in a folder per ingestion date, wrapped in an envelope with the source name and arrival time. Say five million rows a day, written once and never edited.
With Iceberg or Delta, schema evolution lets you add, rename or widen a column without rewriting old files. Time travel lets you read yesterday's version.

show.title: Table formats help raw
items: Time travel: read an older snapshot

beats.say: Cleaned then removes the double order, casts strings to dates and decimals, converts times to UTC, and maps each source's customer key to one shared key. It keeps history with type two slowly changing rows, or snapshots.

check.q: Why is schema-on-read acceptable in the raw layer?
opts: Raw data is never queried
Raw only stores what arrived, and strict checks happen when cleaning
Schemas are not possible there
check.why: Raw's job is to capture faithfully. Enforcing types and rules is the cleaned layer's job, so source changes don't break ingestion.

work: Check raw tables are partitioned by ingestion date with source and arrival time recorded.
Write down your dedup key for each cleaned table.

m03.title: Hubs, links, satellites in motion

beats.say: How can three kinds of table model a whole business?
A hub holds the business key, like rider id, plus a hash of it called the hash key, a load timestamp and the source. One row per key, ever.
A link stores each trip: the rider hash key, the driver hash key and the trip id.

Satellites carry the attributes. One from the app database holds name and city. Another from the ratings service holds rating. Each row has a hash diff, a fingerprint of its columns. If the fingerprint changes, insert a new row. If not, skip it.
Because keys are hashed from the business key, tables load in parallel with no lookups.

check.q: What is the job of hash_diff in a satellite?
opts: Join the satellite to the hub
Detect whether the attributes changed, so a new row is inserted only when needed
Encrypt the attributes
check.why: hash_diff fingerprints the descriptive columns. Comparing it to the latest row tells the loader whether anything changed.

work: Draw hub, link and satellites for one of your entities, with the hash key columns.
Decide which columns go in which satellite by source and change rate.

m03.title: Vault gotchas interviewers probe

beats.say: Why does nobody query a data vault directly?

Even asking for a rider's city and latest rating means a hub, two satellites, and picking the newest row per key in each. Many joins. So teams build point-in-time tables and then star schemas or wide tables on top.

Next, the hash. If one loader trims spaces or uppercases keys and another does not, the same rider gets two hash keys, and your history silently splits. Null handling in hash diff causes the same trouble.

show.title: Hashing traps
items: Standardise case, trim and nulls before hashing
One hash rule for every loader
Pick a stable business key, not a source surrogate id

beats.say: Finally, load timestamp is when you received data, not when it happened. Late arrivals and satellites split too finely, or lumped too widely, make rows explode or hide change.

show.title: Time and design traps
items: load_ts is arrival time, not event time
Split satellites by source and change rate
Too many tiny satellites means more joins

check.q: Two loaders hash the same rider id, one trimmed and one not. What happens?
opts: Nothing, hashes are equal
The rider gets two hub rows and history splits
The load fails loudly
check.why: Different input strings give different hashes, so the same entity appears as two keys, silently breaking joins and history.

work: Write one shared hashing function and test it on whitespace, case and nulls.
Add point-in-time tables before exposing vault data to analysts.

m03.title: Vault, Kimball or one big table?

beats.say: When is a data vault the wrong answer?
With two or three sources and a small team, a vault adds tables, modelling effort and a second layer you must still turn into marts. Going from cleaned straight to a Kimball star ships weeks sooner.

Choose a vault when many systems describe the same entities, sources change often, and auditors need insert-only history, as in banks and insurers. A new source then costs one satellite, not a redesign.

For lakehouse analytics, medallion layers feeding one big table is simpler and fast to query. The strong answer: Kimball for clear reporting, vault for the enterprise core, one big table for lakehouse serving, and a marts layer on top of any of them.

check.q: A startup has three sources and four analysts. Which is the best default?
opts: Full Data Vault with marts on top
Cleaned layer feeding a Kimball star or wide tables
Query raw files directly forever
check.why: With few sources and little audit pressure, the vault's extra layer and effort are not repaid. A dimensional model on cleaned data delivers value faster.

work: Count your sources per core entity and your audit needs before proposing a vault.
Prepare a one-minute answer comparing vault, Kimball and one big table.

p01.title: Guess the cost before you run

beats.say: Would you drive across a city without glancing at how far it is? Code has a distance too, and you can estimate it before you run anything.
Picture finding one name in a phone book. Reading every page from the front is slow. Jumping straight to the right page using the index is fast. Programmers call that difference cost, or Big-O.
So before you run, ask: how many times do I touch each item? Once, or once for every other item? Saying that out loud takes five seconds and catches slow code early.

show.text: Touch each item once, or once per other item?

check.q: What does saying the Big-O before running your code help you catch?
opts: Typing mistakes in variable names
Code that will get very slow as the data grows
Whether the output is formatted nicely
check.why: Big-O describes how work grows with the amount of data, so it warns you about slow approaches before you spend time running them.

work: Before running any loop at work, say aloud how many times each item is touched.
Look for a loop inside a loop over the same data, and ask if a lookup table could replace the inner one.

p01.title: List versus set on a million events

beats.say: You have one million events and must drop duplicates. Why does one version finish in a second while another runs for hours?

show.text: 1,000,000 events. Same job. Seconds or hours?

beats.say: Version one keeps a list of seen ids. Every check scans that list, about half a million comparisons on average. Times a million events, that is roughly five hundred billion steps.
Version two keeps a set. A set turns the id into a number, called a hash, and jumps straight to that slot. One check is about one step, so a million events cost about a million steps.
That is n squared against n. Say it before you run, and you pick the set the first time.

show.title: Dedupe with a set

check.q: Why is checking membership in a set faster than in a list?
opts: A set sorts its items first
A set hashes the value and jumps straight to its slot
A set stores fewer items
check.why: Hashing lets a set go directly to where the value would live, so a check is about one step. A list must compare against items one by one.

work: Replace any 'if x in some_list' inside a loop with a set built once before the loop.
Write the Big-O in a comment above each solution before you run it.

p01.title: Read the expected and got line

beats.say: A test fails. Do you start changing code right away? That is the slowest move you can make.

The failure prints two values: what was expected, and what your code got. That pair is the whole clue. Expected three rows but got four? You kept a duplicate. Got an empty list? Your filter was too strict.
Reading code works the same way. Before you run, say what each line prints. Then run it and compare. A mismatch points to exactly where your mental model is wrong.

show.title: Predict, run, compare
items: A mismatch shows your wrong assumption

check.q: A test says expected 3 rows, got 4. What is the best first step?
opts: Rewrite the whole function
Compare the extra row with the expected ones to see why it slipped through
Rerun the test until it passes
check.why: The expected and got difference localizes the bug. Inspecting the extra row tells you which rule failed, so you fix one thing instead of guessing.

work: On every failing test, copy the expected and got lines into your notes before editing.
Predict the output of a snippet in code review before running it.

p01.title: Why a set of dicts crashes

beats.say: You try to dedupe events by putting each event dictionary into a set. Python raises an error. Why?

show.title: TypeError
show.text:
seen = set()
seen.add({'id': 1})
# TypeError: unhashable type: dict

beats.say: A set finds items by hash, a number computed from the contents. A dictionary can change after it is stored, so its hash could change and the set would lose it. Python refuses.
Fix it by hashing a stable key instead: the event id, or a tuple of the fields that define a duplicate. A dictionary keyed by id also keeps first-seen order and lets you choose which duplicate wins.

show.title: Safer dedupe
items: Key on the id or a tuple of fields
Tuples hash, lists and dicts do not
A dict keyed by id keeps order and picks the winner

check.q: Why can a tuple of strings go in a set but a list cannot?
opts: Tuples are shorter
A tuple cannot change, so its hash stays stable
Lists are always too large
check.why: Hashable objects must keep the same hash for life. Tuples of immutable values qualify, while lists can change and so are refused.

work: Define in writing which fields make two events duplicates before coding the key.
Decide whether first or last duplicate should win, and test it.

p01.title: When the set is the wrong answer

beats.say: The set solves dedupe in linear time. So why not use it everywhere?

show.text: Fast is not the same as fits

beats.say: A set holds every id in memory. In Python, one hundred million ids can take eight gigabytes or more. At a billion events the job simply dies. Then you sort and compare neighbours, or let PySpark shuffle rows by key across machines.

show.title: Approx memory for ids in a Python set

beats.say: A Bloom filter uses far less memory but sometimes wrongly says seen, so it is fine for caching and bad for billing. And for ten thousand rows, simple code wins. Match the tool to the scale and to the cost of being wrong.

show.title: Choose by scale and risk
items: Approximate filters only if errors are cheap

check.q: You must dedupe five billion payment events exactly. What fits best?
opts: A Python set on one machine
A Bloom filter
A distributed dedupe that shuffles by key
check.why: The ids will not fit in one machine's memory, and a Bloom filter gives false positives that would drop real payments. A shuffle by key is exact and scales out.

work: Estimate memory as rows times roughly 80 bytes before choosing an in-memory set.
Record the scale at which your dedupe approach must change.

p01.title: A name is a tag, not a box

beats.say: Is a Python variable a box that holds a value? Actually, no.

show.sub: A variable is a name tag

beats.say: Picture a name tag stuck on an object. When you write b equals a, you do not copy the list. You just stick a second tag on the same list.
Now add a four through b. Look through a, and the four is there too. One list, two names. That is the classic bug where your data changes by itself.
Want a separate list? Ask for a copy. Then you get a brand new list, and the new tag points only at that.

check.q: You write b = a where a is a list, then b.append(4). What does a show?
opts: The original list, unchanged
The list with 4 added
An error, because b is a copy
check.why: b = a only adds a second name to the same list object. Appending through b changes that one list, so a sees it too.

work: Next time data changes unexpectedly, ask how many names point at that object.
When you need an independent list, write a.copy() on purpose instead of b = a.

p01.title: Mutable, immutable, equal, same

beats.say: What really happens when you write x plus equals one?
An int cannot change. So Python builds a new int, say six from five, and moves the name x onto it. Any other name on the old five stays put.
Lists are different. They change in place. Append on a list mutates the one object, so every name pointing at it sees the change. Lists, dicts and sets are mutable. Ints, strings and tuples are not.

show.title: Mutable or not
items: Mutable: list, dict, set, your own objects
Immutable: int, float, str, tuple, frozenset
Mutating changes the one shared object

beats.say: Two checks exist. Double equals asks if values are equal. Is asks if it is the same object. Two lists holding one and two are equal, but not the same.

check.q: a = [1, 2] and b = [1, 2] are built separately. What are a == b and a is b?
opts: True and True
True and False
False and False
check.why: The values are equal, so == is True. They are two different list objects, so is is False.

work: Before mutating an argument, check whether its type is mutable.
Use == to compare values and keep is for checking None.

p01.title: Shallow copies share the insides

beats.say: You copied a list of dicts, changed the copy, and the original changed too. Why?
List of a, a dot copy, and a slice all make a shallow copy. The outer list is new, but the dicts inside are shared. Two lists, same three dict objects.
So setting copy at zero, fare, to nine changes the original row as well. Deepcopy fixes this by copying everything, but it is slow on big data.
Functions bite the same way. Pass a list in, append inside, and the caller's list grows. Return a new list instead. And use is only for None, never to compare values.

show.title: Gotchas
items: Appending to an argument changes the caller's list
Return a new list instead of mutating
Use is only for None checks

check.q: You make c = a.copy() where a is a list of dicts, then set c[0]["fare"] = 9. What happens to a[0]["fare"]?
opts: It stays unchanged
It becomes 9
It raises an error
check.why: copy() is shallow: the outer list is new but both lists hold the same dict objects, so editing a dict through the copy changes the original.

work: Review functions that append to or edit a passed-in list, and return a new one instead.
Use copy.deepcopy only where nested data is truly edited, and measure its cost.

p01.title: Share by default, copy at the edge

beats.say: Should you deepcopy your data to be safe? Usually not.
Sharing is the cheap default: a name costs one pointer. A deep copy of a million row list doubles memory and walks every item. At scale that hurts.
Pick by who owns the data. Copy at the boundary, once, if a function must change input. Otherwise build and return a new object, so nothing is surprising.

show.title: Ownership rule
items: Function copies once if it must edit

beats.say: For safety without cost, use immutable types like tuples and frozensets for shared data. Then nobody can change it, and sharing is safe. Copy only the part you edit.

show.title: Safer sharing
items: Tuples and frozensets for shared data
Copy only the part you edit

check.q: A function receives a large list and must not alter the caller's data. What is the best approach?
opts: Deepcopy it on every call, always
Build and return a new list, copying only if it must edit
Use is to check the list first
check.why: Returning a new object avoids side effects without paying for a full deep copy. Copy once at the boundary only when mutation is needed.

work: Set a team rule: functions do not mutate their arguments unless documented.
Store shared reference data as tuples or frozensets.
Profile before adding deepcopy to a hot path.

p01.title: Lockers and sealed envelopes

beats.say: Why can you open locker five instantly, but adding a locker at the front is painful?

show.sub: lists and tuples in plain terms

beats.say: A Python list is like a row of numbered lockers. You can open locker five instantly, without walking past lockers one to four. Adding one at the far end is easy. Adding one at the front means everyone shifts down one place.

show.title: A list is a row of *lockers*

beats.say: A tuple is a sealed envelope. Latitude and longitude go in, and nobody can change them afterwards. Because it never changes, it can be used as a label to file things under.

show.title: A tuple is sealed
items: Safe to use as a label for filing

beats.say: So use a list for a collection that grows. Use a tuple for one small record with a fixed shape.

check.q: You store a map point as latitude and longitude, and want to file trip counts under each point. What fits best?
opts: A list for each point
A tuple for each point
Neither can work
check.why: A tuple cannot change, so it is safe as a filing label. A list can change, so it cannot be one.

work: Pick one place in your code that uses a list for a fixed pair or triple, and ask whether a tuple fits better.
Explain lists versus tuples to a colleague using the lockers and envelope picture.

p01.title: Why the end is fast and the front is slow

beats.say: Why is appending to a list instant, but inserting at the front slow?

show.text: Append: fast. Insert at front: slow.

beats.say: A list is an array of references, sitting side by side in memory. To read slot seven, Python computes the address and jumps there. That is constant time, whatever the size.
Append writes into spare room at the end. When the room runs out, Python copies everything to a bigger array. That is rare, so the average stays constant. We call it amortised.

show.title: Amortised O(1)
items: Average cost per append stays flat

beats.say: Insert at zero is different. With one million items, every one shifts one place. That is a million moves, for a single insert. Same for a membership check: it scans from the start.

show.title: Work for one operation, one million items

check.q: Why is xs.insert(0, v) O(n) on a list?
opts: Python must sort the list afterwards
Every existing item shifts one slot to make room
The list is copied to a bigger array every time
check.why: Items sit side by side, so opening slot zero means moving all n items one place along.

work: Search your code for pop(0) or insert(0, ...) inside loops.
Time append versus insert(0) on a million items to see the gap yourself.

p01.title: Unpacking: pairs without indexes

beats.say: How does Python loop over index and item, without you ever writing an index?
The enumerate function hands back pairs. Each pair is a tuple: the position and the item. Unpacking splits the pair straight into two names.

show.title: Index and item
show.text:
for i, trip in enumerate(trips):
    print(i, trip)

beats.say: Dictionary items work the same way. Each pass gives a key and a value pair, and you name both in the loop. For a city count, that is city and n.

show.title: Key and value
show.text:
for city, n in counts.items():
    print(city, n)

beats.say: Star unpacking grabs the rest. Given one, two, three, first becomes one, and rest becomes the list two, three. Swapping, returning two values, and reading a coordinate all use the same trick.

check.q: After first, *rest = [1, 2, 3], what is rest?
check.why: Star unpacking collects all remaining items into a new list, so rest is the list two, three.

work: Replace range(len(xs)) loops with enumerate in one module.
Return two values from a helper as a tuple and unpack them at the call site.

p01.title: Hidden costs and gotchas

beats.say: Why can one innocent slice quietly double your memory?
Slicing copies. Take the first million items of a big list, and Python builds a new million-slot list. Not the objects, only the references, but still real time and memory.

Appends over-allocate, so growth adds a little extra each time, and a resize briefly needs both old and new arrays in memory. Pop from the front, or run the in check on a long list inside a loop, and you get quadratic slowdowns.

show.title: Where it bites
items: Resize briefly holds old and new arrays
pop(0) in a loop is quadratic
in on a long list inside a loop is quadratic

beats.say: Tuples are shallow. A tuple holding a list is frozen, but that inner list can still change, so it cannot be a dict key. Sort is stable: equal items keep their original order.

show.title: Edge cases
items: Tuple freezes slots, not what they point to
Tuple containing a list is not hashable
sort is stable, so equal items keep order

check.q: What happens if you use the tuple (1, [2, 3]) as a dict key?
opts: It works, since tuples are immutable
It raises an error, because the inner list is not hashable
It works but the list is copied
check.why: A tuple's hash depends on its contents. A list inside cannot be hashed, so the whole tuple cannot be a key.

work: Look for large slices in hot paths and use iterators or index ranges instead.
Test whether any dict keys contain nested lists, and convert them to tuples.

p01.title: When a list is the wrong choice

beats.say: When is a Python list the wrong tool, even though it works?

show.text: Works is not the same as right
show.sub: match the structure to the access pattern

beats.say: Used as a queue, pop at the front is linear. Use a deque, which removes from either end in constant time. Used for lookups, the in check is linear. Build a set or dict once, and each check becomes constant.

For millions of numbers, a list stores a pointer to each boxed object, so it costs perhaps thirty-two bytes per float. A NumPy array or the array module stores raw eight-byte values, and is far smaller and faster.
For records, prefer a named tuple or a dataclass over a bare tuple once fields pass three. Names beat positions when someone reads your code in a year.

show.title: Records
items: Bare tuple: two or three obvious fields
Dataclass: when you need behaviour or defaults

check.q: A job checks whether each of 5 million IDs is in a 1 million item list. What is the best fix?
opts: Sort the list before every check
Load the IDs into a set once, then check against it
Use a tuple instead of a list
check.why: A list check scans, so this is about n times m work. A set check is constant time on average, so the job drops to roughly 5 million cheap lookups.

work: Review code using lists as queues or lookup tables and switch to deque or set.
For big numeric columns, measure memory with a list versus a NumPy array before choosing.
Set a team convention for when a bare tuple should become a named tuple or dataclass.

p01.title: The coat check that never searches

beats.say: How can a coat check find your coat among a thousand, without looking at every hook?
You hand over a ticket. The number on it says exactly which hook to walk to. No searching. Python calls that number a hash, and the hook is a slot.

chip.text: Ticket points straight to the hook

beats.say: A dict is a coat check that keeps a value on each hook, like Pune with one hundred twenty. A set is the same, but you only ask whether a coat is there.
So asking is quick whether you hold ten coats or ten million. A list is like walking the whole row, checking every hook.

check.q: In the coat check analogy, why is finding a coat fast?
opts: The ticket number points straight to one hook
The staff check hooks in alphabetical order
Coats are sorted by size
The rack is small
check.why: A hash works like the ticket number: it points directly to a slot, so nothing is scanned.

work: Name one place in your code where you search a list again and again.
Say aloud what a hash and a slot are, in your own words.

p01.title: One hash, one jump, one compare

beats.say: How does Python find Pune in a dict of a million cities without scanning any of them?
It runs a hash function on the key, which turns the text into a big number. That number, reduced to fit the table size, picks a slot. Pune lands in slot five.
Python jumps to slot five, checks the stored key equals Pune, and returns the value. One hash, one jump, one compare. That is constant time on average.
Set intersection costs the two sizes added together, not multiplied. Looping over a whole dict touches every entry, so that part is linear.

check.q: You check x in seen inside a loop over 100000 items. What makes the loop fast?
opts: seen is a list kept sorted
seen is a set, so each check is one hash and jump
The loop runs in C
Python caches the loop
check.why: A set lookup hashes x and jumps to a slot, so the whole loop is linear. A list makes each check a scan, giving n squared.

work: Time a membership loop with a list and with a set, using 100000 items.
Replace one list lookup in your code with a set or dict built once.

p01.title: Hashing gotchas interviewers probe

beats.say: Why can a tuple be a dict key, but a list cannot?
A key's hash must never change, or the dict would look in the wrong slot and lose it. Lists can change, so Python refuses them. A tuple holding a list fails too.
Two different keys can land in the same slot. That is a collision. Python probes another slot and compares keys. Many collisions push lookups toward linear, so constant time is only average.
Two more traps. Adding or deleting keys while looping raises an error, so loop over a copy. And dicts keep insertion order since Python three seven, but sets do not.

show.title: More traps
items: Do not resize a dict while looping over it
Loop over list of keys to be safe

check.q: Why does Python reject a list as a dict key?
opts: Lists are too large
Lists have no length
A list can change, so its hash could change and the entry would be lost
Lists are slower to compare
check.why: Keys must keep the same hash for life. A mutable list could change, so the dict could not find it again.

work: Try using a list as a key and read the error message.
Fix any loop that deletes from a dict while iterating it by looping over list of its keys.

p01.title: When a hash table is the wrong tool

beats.say: When is a Python dict the wrong tool for a billion keys?

Hash tables trade memory for speed. They keep spare empty slots, plus an object for every key and value, so a million small entries can cost many tens of megabytes. A numpy array or sorted column is far smaller.

show.title: Memory for a million integer pairs

beats.say: Everything lives in one process's memory. Beyond that, use a key value store like Redis, a database index, or a sorted file with binary search. For approximate membership on huge data, a Bloom filter needs only a few bits per item.
Inside a pipeline step, though, dict and set are ideal for dedup, joins and lookups. Build the set once, then probe it. Never test membership against a list in a loop.

check.q: You must test membership for 2 billion IDs against a reference of 500 million IDs on one small machine. What is the best first thought?
opts: Put them all in a Python set
Keep the reference in a list
Use a disk-based store or a Bloom filter, because a set will not fit in memory
Loop twice
check.why: A Python set spends memory on spare slots and objects, so 500 million entries will not fit. An external store or a Bloom filter trades space for speed or accuracy.

work: Measure memory of your largest dict with sys.getsizeof and a sample, then scale it up.
Write down the size limit where you would move a lookup to Redis or a database.

p01.title: Big-O as a guest list

beats.say: Your friend hands you a guest list. How long does it take to find one name? It depends on how the list is built.
Big-O is a way to say how the work grows when the list grows. Forget the stopwatch. Just ask: if the list gets ten times longer, what happens to my effort?

A coat check with numbered hooks takes one step, however big the crowd. Flipping through a dictionary, halving the pages each time, barely grows. Reading every name grows with the list. Comparing every guest with every other guest explodes.

show.title: Four kinds of growth
items: Read every name: grows with the list

beats.say: So Big-O is a warning label. It tells you which jobs stay calm when the crowd gets big, and which ones quietly melt your laptop.

check.q: Your list grows from 1,000 to 10,000 names. Which job grows the most?
opts: Grabbing a coat from a numbered hook
Reading every name once
Comparing every guest with every other guest
Flipping a dictionary to the right page
check.why: Comparing everyone with everyone grows with the square of the list: ten times more names means about a hundred times more work. The others grow far less.

work: Next time something is slow, ask what happens to the runtime if the data grows ten times.
Spot any place where you look through a whole list once for every item in another list.

p01.title: The five classes with real numbers

beats.say: How many steps does a job take on one hundred thousand rows? It depends on one thing: the shape of your loops.
A dict lookup is one step. Binary search is about seventeen. One pass is a hundred thousand. Sorting is about one point seven million. A loop inside a loop is ten billion.
To count, walk the code from the inside out and multiply nested loops. We loop over trips, n times. Inside, checking an id in a list scans m items. So the cost is n times m.

show.title: Count from the inside out
show.note: n times, times m per check when ids is a list

beats.say: Swap the list for a set, and each check becomes one step. Now the whole loop is just n.

check.q: You loop over n trips and, inside, test membership in a list of m ids. What is the time cost?
opts: O(n)
O(n + m)
O(n·m)
O(log n)
check.why: Each of the n iterations may scan all m items of the list, so the costs multiply. A set makes each check O(1) and the total O(n).

work: Annotate one slow loop at work with its cost per line, working from the inside out.
Replace one list membership test in a hot loop with a set and time it.

p01.title: Hidden costs and fine print

beats.say: Why can a loop that is supposedly linear still crawl?
Big-O hides constants. Two passes and ten passes are both O of n, yet one takes five times longer. And with a small n, a fancy method can lose to a plain one.

Hidden costs sit in innocent lines. The in check on a list scans every item. Inserting at the front of a list shifts every item along. Adding strings in a loop copies the growing string each time, which becomes n squared.

show.title: Innocent lines, hidden cost
items: x in list: scans every item, O(n)
list.insert at front: shifts everything, O(n)
string plus string in a loop: O(n²)
Fix: set, deque, or join once

beats.say: Even the fast ones have fine print. A set lookup is one step on average, because hashing spreads items out. Append is one step amortized: sometimes it copies everything, but rarely enough that the average stays flat.

check.q: A loop builds a big report by doing text = text + line for 200,000 lines. What is the likely problem?
opts: Each add copies the growing string, so the total is about O(n²)
Appending to a string is always O(1)
The loop is O(log n)
Strings cannot be added in a loop
check.why: Strings are immutable, so every add copies everything built so far. Collect the pieces in a list and join once to get O(n).

work: Search your code for string building or insert-at-front inside loops.
Remember that O(1) for sets and appends is average or amortized, and say so in interviews.

p01.title: Trading time for memory

beats.say: Your set made the join O of n. So why did the job crash with out of memory?
Because speed was bought with space. Ten million ids in a Python set can take over a gigabyte. Time and space trade against each other, so always state both.

When memory is the limit, choose differently. Sort both sides and merge in one pass with almost no extra memory. Stream the file line by line, which is constant space. Or push the join into the warehouse, which does this for you.

show.title: When RAM is the limit
items: Sort both sides, then merge in one pass
Stream line by line: O(1) space
Push the join to the warehouse
Choose by n and memory, not habit

beats.say: And when n is a few thousand, skip all this. Clear code beats clever code. Optimise where n is large or growing, and say the trade-off out loud.

show.sub: optimise where n is large or growing

check.q: You must join two files, each far larger than memory. Which approach fits best?
opts: Load one file into a set and scan the other
Sort both and merge in one streaming pass, or use the warehouse
Use nested loops to avoid extra memory
Load both files into lists
check.why: Sorting and merging uses little memory and is O(n log n) time. Hash sets and lists need memory proportional to the data, which is the very thing you lack.

work: For your biggest job, write down time and space cost and check it against the machine's memory.
Ask whether a streaming or sort-merge version would remove a memory risk before scaling data up.

p01.title: Four helpers, in everyday terms

beats.say: What if four tiny tools could each replace ten lines of boring code?
A Counter is a tally sheet. You read through a list of words, and it makes a mark next to each one. At the end, you can see how many times every word showed up.

A defaultdict is a mail room with bins. A letter arrives for Boston, and if there is no Boston bin yet, one appears on its own. A deque is a short line of people. New ones join the back, and the oldest leave from the front.
A namedtuple is a form with labeled boxes, so you say fare, not slot two. Each tool saves you from writing dull bookkeeping by hand.

show.title: Labeled boxes
items: Reads like the form it is

check.q: Which everyday picture best matches a defaultdict of lists?
opts: A mail room where a new bin appears when a letter needs one
A stopwatch that counts seconds
A locked safe with one slot
check.why: A defaultdict creates a missing entry, here an empty list, the first time you ask for it, just like a new bin.

work: Find a loop in your code that counts things by hand and note it.
Find a loop that groups rows by a key and note it.
Say each of the four types in one sentence using a picture.

p01.title: How the four helpers work

beats.say: How do you count a million trips per city without writing a single if statement?

With a plain dictionary you check whether the key exists, create it if not, then add. Counter does that check for you. Counter of words gives a count per word, and most common three returns the top three pairs.

show.title: Counter
show.note: Same idea as GROUP BY with COUNT

beats.say: With defaultdict of list, ask for a missing city and it creates an empty list. Then you append the trip. That is grouping rows, like a SQL group by.
A deque with max length three keeps only the newest three items. Append a fourth and the first drops off. Both ends cost constant time, so it is a cheap sliding window.

check.q: What does deque with maxlen equal to 3 do when you append a fourth item?
opts: Raises an error
Drops the oldest item and keeps the newest three
Drops the newest item
check.why: A bounded deque discards from the opposite end, so it always holds the newest three, a sliding window.

work: Replace one manual count loop with Counter and compare the line count.
Replace one if key not in d grouping loop with defaultdict of list.
Use deque with maxlen for a rolling average of the last N values.

p01.title: Gotchas inside the collections types

beats.say: Why is removing from the front of a list slow, but fast on a deque?

show.sub: O(n) on a list, O(1) on a deque

beats.say: A list is a row of slots in memory. Remove the first, and every other item shifts left by one. With a million items, that is a million moves for every pop. A deque links blocks together, so popleft just moves a pointer.
Gotcha with defaultdict: just reading a missing key creates it. Look up a mistyped city and you silently add an empty list. Use the in operator, or get, when you only want to look.

show.title: Reading inserts!
show.text:
d = defaultdict(list)
d["Bostn"]        # adds empty list
"Bostn" in d      # True now
d.get("Paris")    # safe, adds nothing
show.note: Lookup changes the dict

beats.say: Also, a deque is slow in the middle, and a namedtuple cannot be changed after creation. A Counter returns zero for a missing key, without adding it.

show.title: More edges
items: Counter missing key gives 0, not inserted

check.q: After d = defaultdict(list), you run x = d["paris"] on a key never set. What happens?
opts: KeyError is raised
None is returned and d is unchanged
An empty list is returned and the key is now in d
check.why: defaultdict calls its factory on a missing key and stores the result, so a plain read grows the dict.

work: Search for list.pop(0) used as a queue and switch to deque popleft.
Use in or get for existence checks on a defaultdict.
Remember namedtuple is read-only when you need to update a field.

p01.title: When to outgrow the collections types

beats.say: When should you stop using Counter and defaultdict?

show.sub: all keys live in one process

beats.say: When the data outgrows one machine's memory. A Counter or defaultdict holds every key in RAM. Ten million distinct keys can cost over a gigabyte. Past that, push the group by into SQL or Spark, which spill to disk and run in parallel.
Prefer aggregating over storing. A defaultdict of lists keeps every row. A Counter or running sum keeps one number per key. Same answer, far less memory.

show.title: Memory held for 1 million rows, 1,000 keys

beats.say: A deque is a bounded buffer inside one process only. If the window must survive a crash or span workers, use a durable queue like Kafka. For records that need types, choose a dataclass or typed NamedTuple.

show.title: Choose instead
items: Durable or shared window: Kafka or a queue service
Huge group by: SQL or Spark

check.q: You must group 2 billion rows by user. What is the best choice?
opts: defaultdict of lists in one Python process
A distributed group by in SQL or Spark
A deque with a large maxlen
check.why: Two billion rows will not fit in one process's memory. A distributed engine partitions the work and spills to disk.

work: Estimate distinct keys and bytes per key before using a Counter on big data.
Replace stored lists with running aggregates where only totals are needed.
Move windows that must survive restarts into a durable queue or stream.

p01.title: Rewriting the letter

beats.say: Why would adding one word to a sentence ever mean rewriting the whole page?

show.text: One word added. Whole page rewritten?

beats.say: Picture a printed letter. A string in Python is like that: once written, it cannot be changed. To add a word, you must print a whole new copy.

chip.text: Every addition means a full copy

beats.say: Do that ten thousand times and you copy the letter ten thousand times. Better: jot each word on a sticky note, then write the letter once. That is a list, then join.

chip.text: Collect in a list, join once

beats.say: Files work the same way. Reading a giant log is like reading a book one page at a time, not carrying the whole library home. Go line by line.

check.q: Why is collecting parts in a list and joining once better than adding to a string in a loop?
opts: Lists store text more compactly
Each addition to a string makes a new full copy, while join writes the result once
Join sorts the parts first
Strings cannot hold more than a few thousand characters
check.why: Strings cannot change, so every addition copies all the text so far. Join builds the final string in a single pass.

work: Search your code for plus equals on strings inside loops and swap them for a list and join.
Check where logs or large files are read in one go and switch them to a line by line loop.

p01.title: Fifty billion copies

beats.say: Why is building a string with plus equals in a loop so slow?

Strings cannot change. Each plus equals allocates a new string and copies the old text plus the new piece. Add one hundred thousand pieces of ten characters, and the copies grow longer every pass. That adds up to about fifty billion characters copied.
Join does it differently. It adds up the total length first, one million characters, allocates once, and copies each piece once. One million copies instead of fifty billion.
Files follow the same logic. A for loop over a file reads a buffered chunk and hands you one line at a time, so memory stays flat.

show.title: A buffer feeds *one line* at a time

check.q: You join 100,000 pieces of 10 characters. Roughly how many characters does join copy in total?
opts: About 50 billion
About 1 million
About 100 thousand
About 10 trillion
check.why: Join works out the total length of one million characters, allocates once, and copies each piece one time. The plus equals loop is the one that copies tens of billions.

work: Time a plus equals loop against list and join on 100,000 pieces and note the gap.
Use split with maxsplit when only the first few fields matter, so the message stays whole.

p01.title: Where the shortcuts break

beats.say: Your loop with plus equals ran fast on your laptop. So why does it crawl in production?

show.text: Fast on a laptop, slow in production

beats.say: CPython sometimes grows a string in place when nothing else points to it. That trick is an implementation detail. It fails when another reference exists, and other Python runtimes do not do it. Never rely on it.

File gotchas. Each line keeps its newline, so strip it. Split on commas breaks on quoted fields like a quoted name containing a comma; use the csv module. Set the encoding, or the machine default decides. Use split with maxsplit two to keep a message intact.

show.title: Line parsing gotchas
items: Each line keeps its newline: strip it
Split on commas breaks on quoted fields: use csv

beats.say: Calling read on a twenty gigabyte log pulls all twenty gigabytes into memory and can kill the job. The with block closes the file even on error.

check.q: Why is relying on CPython's in place string growth for plus equals risky?
opts: It only works for strings shorter than 100 characters
It is an implementation detail that fails with extra references or other runtimes
It changes the string's contents
It is slower than join in every case
check.why: The speedup depends on there being a single reference and on CPython. Code that leans on it can silently become quadratic elsewhere.

work: Replace manual comma splitting with the csv module wherever fields may be quoted.
Pass encoding explicitly on every open call.
Strip the trailing newline from each line before parsing.

p01.title: Streaming is not the whole answer

beats.say: Line by line keeps memory flat. Does that make it the right way to process twenty gigabytes?

Not always. Memory is safe, but one Python loop uses one core, so a big file takes a long time. Split the data into many files and run workers in parallel, or hand it to an engine like DuckDB or Spark.

chip.text: Scale across cores, not just memory

beats.say: Text logs are also costly: every field is parsed from characters each time. For data you read often, convert once to a columnar format like Parquet, which is smaller and skips unneeded columns.
Keep it simple for small jobs. Read a config file whole. Build output with join. Stream only when size is unbounded.

show.title: Pick by size
items: Unbounded input: stream line by line
Repeated analytics: columnar format and an engine

check.q: A nightly job streams a 20 GB log line by line and takes hours, though memory is fine. What is the best next step?
opts: Use read to load the whole file
Add plus equals to build the output
Split the input and process in parallel, or use a columnar engine
Shorten the lines
check.why: Streaming solves memory but a single Python loop is limited to one core. Parallel workers or an engine over columnar data attack the real bottleneck.

work: Measure the time and memory of your largest file job before choosing streaming or an engine.
Convert logs that are queried repeatedly into Parquet.
Document the size limit above which a read-whole approach is not allowed.

p01.title: Python is the expediter

beats.say: Who in a restaurant never cooks, yet keeps every dish coming out on time?

show.sub: Yet every dish arrives on time

beats.say: The expediter. They call the grill, check the plate, send it out, and redo it if something burns. Python plays that role in a data platform.

The heavy cooking, like crunching billions of rows, happens in big engines such as Spark or the warehouse. Python tells them when to start, calls outside services, retries failures, and checks the results.
So keep Python as the expediter. If you carry every ingredient by hand through Python lists, the kitchen jams.

check.q: What is Python's best role in a data platform?
opts: Doing all heavy row processing itself
Scheduling, calling and checking the engines
Replacing the warehouse
Storing the data
check.why: Python is the glue that orchestrates and verifies. The heavy data work belongs in Spark, DuckDB or the warehouse.

work: List your pipelines and mark which steps only orchestrate and which move heavy data.
Move any row-by-row data crunching in a DAG task into SQL or Spark.

p01.title: Why loops are slow, vectors are fast

beats.say: Why can NumPy add a million numbers in about a millisecond, while a plain Python loop takes dozens?
In a Python loop, every number is a full object on the heap, holding a type, a reference count and a value. Each plus means checking types, creating a new object, and updating counts.
NumPy stores raw machine numbers side by side in one block. A compiled loop in C runs straight over it, with the CPU cache and SIMD instructions handling batches at once.
Same algorithm, about a hundred times less work per element. So vectorise, or push the work down to Spark or SQL.

show.sub: Same algorithm, far less work per element

check.q: Why is a NumPy sum so much faster than a Python loop?
opts: Python cannot add numbers
It runs a compiled loop over raw contiguous values with no per-element objects
It uses more threads
It skips some numbers
check.why: Avoiding per-element objects and interpreter overhead, and using cache and SIMD, cuts the work per element enormously.

work: Find loops over large columns in your code and replace them with pandas, Polars or NumPy operations.
Profile before rewriting, so you fix the real hot path.

p01.title: Lists versus arrays in memory

beats.say: Why does a list of a million integers eat around thirty-six megabytes, when an array holds them in eight?
A list stores a million pointers, eight bytes each. Each pointer leads to a separate integer object of about twenty-eight bytes. That is roughly thirty-six bytes per value.
An array, or a NumPy array, stores the raw eight-byte values side by side. Smaller, and the CPU cache reads it in order, which is faster.
One trap: Python shares small integers from minus five to two fifty-six, so tiny tests can hide the difference. Test with realistic sizes.

check.q: Why does a list of ints use far more memory than an array of ints?
opts: Lists compress badly
Each list slot is a pointer to a separate int object
Arrays are stored on disk
Lists store strings
check.why: A list holds pointers plus separate int objects, about 36 bytes per value, while an array holds raw 8-byte values.

work: Use array or NumPy for large numeric data instead of lists.
Measure memory with realistic data sizes, not toy samples.

p01.title: What a PySpark UDF really costs

beats.say: Why can a single Python function make a fast Spark job crawl?

Spark runs on the JVM. For a plain Python UDF, rows are serialised out of the JVM, sent over a socket to a Python worker, unpickled, and your function runs once per row. Results travel back the same way.
Worse, the optimizer cannot see inside your function, so it cannot push filters past it.
A pandas UDF sends whole column batches in Arrow format, and runs vectorised. Fastest is a built-in from pyspark dot sql dot functions, which never leaves the JVM.

check.q: Why are pandas (Arrow) UDFs faster than plain Python UDFs?
opts: They run inside the JVM
They ship column batches in Arrow and run vectorised instead of row by row
