They skip serialisation entirely
They use the GPU
check.why: Arrow batches avoid per-row conversion and let your code run vectorised, though data still crosses to Python workers.

work: Replace UDFs with pyspark.sql.functions built-ins where possible.
Where Python is unavoidable, switch to a pandas UDF.
Check query plans to confirm filters still push down.

p01.title: What the GIL blocks and what it doesn't

beats.say: You add eight threads to a Python script, and it gets no faster. Why?
The global interpreter lock lets only one thread run Python bytecode at a time in a process. For CPU-bound work, threads just take turns.

show.title: One *lock*, one thread at a time

beats.say: But the lock is released while a thread waits on a network call, disk, or database, and inside C libraries like NumPy. So threads do speed up an ingestion script calling many APIs.
For heavy computation, use processes, a vectorised library, or the engine. Python 3.13 offers an optional free-threaded build, but treat it as new.

check.q: Which job benefits most from adding threads in CPython?
opts: Hashing in pure Python loops
Calling 200 slow APIs
Computing a pure Python sum
Sorting a list in Python
check.why: Threads waiting on network I/O release the GIL, so many waits overlap. Pure Python CPU work stays serialised.

work: Use a thread pool for API ingestion and processes for CPU-bound steps.
Before parallelising, label each step I/O-bound or CPU-bound.

p01.title: When Python should step aside

beats.say: When should a Python job not be Python at all?
Three cases. A transformation the warehouse can do in SQL belongs in dbt, where it is tested and costed. A hot loop over millions of rows should be vectorised or pushed to Spark or SQL.

show.title: Step aside when
items: Warehouse can do it in SQL: use dbt
Hot loop over millions of rows: vectorise or push down

beats.say: And a low-latency stream processor with large state belongs on the JVM, in Flink or Kafka Streams.
When a job's cost or latency is dominated by Python itself, rewrite the hot path in SQL, Spark built-ins or a vectorised library first. Reach for another language last.

check.q: A Python task's runtime is dominated by a row-by-row loop. What do you try first?
opts: Rewrite the whole pipeline in Java
Vectorise it or push it down to SQL or Spark
Add more threads
Buy a bigger machine
check.why: Moving the hot path to vectorised or engine-side code usually fixes it without changing language.

work: Audit Python transformations the warehouse could run as tested dbt models.
Profile your slowest task before choosing a rewrite.

p01.title: Who owns the Python base

beats.say: A hundred pipelines, a hundred different Python versions. What goes wrong?
Works on my machine. Dependency drift breaks jobs at night, and nobody can reproduce the bug.
So the platform team owns the base: one pinned Python version, a shared package template, a lockfile, and a base container image.
Pipeline teams own their code and pay for its runtime and memory. Data stays in Spark, DuckDB or the warehouse, never in big Python lists, or memory blows up.
That split gives repeatable builds and cheap upgrades.

check.q: What should a platform team standardise for Python?
opts: Every team's business logic
Python version, package template, lockfile and base image
Only the editor
Nothing; teams choose freely
check.why: A shared base prevents dependency drift and makes builds reproducible, while teams keep ownership of their own code.

work: Pin one Python version and a lockfile for every pipeline repo.
Publish a base container image and a project template.

p02.title: A function is a recipe card

beats.say: What if you could hand a friend a recipe card, instead of a cooked meal?
In Python, a function is that recipe card. Writing its name alone, with no brackets, just holds the card. Adding brackets means cook it right now.
So you can keep cards in a labelled drawer. That drawer is a dictionary. Ask for the card marked fare, and you get the steps for turning text into a number.
You can even hand a card to a sorter and say, order the pile using this rule. Functions are things you pass around, not only things you run.

check.q: In Python, what is the difference between writing to_upper and writing to_upper with brackets?
opts: Nothing, they mean the same
The name alone holds the function; brackets run it now
The name alone runs it; brackets store it
check.why: The bare name is the function object itself, like holding the recipe card. Brackets call it and give you the result, like cooking the meal.

work: Find one place in your code where an if-chain picks a behaviour, and sketch it as a dict of functions.
Say out loud the difference between f and f with brackets in a few lines you wrote.

p02.title: Passing and looking up functions

beats.say: How can Python call a function you only looked up from a dictionary?
The def statement builds a function object and binds a name to it. Then f equals to_upper copies the reference, not the code. Both names point to one object. Calling f on pune returns PUNE.
Now a dictionary. Rules maps city to str dot title, and fare to float. Looking up fare gives float. Add brackets with the text twelve point five, and you get the number 12.5.

show.title: Dict of functions
show.note: lookup first, then call

beats.say: A function that takes or returns a function is called higher-order. Sorted with a key, map and filter are examples. An agent loop does the same: look up the tool by name, then call it with the arguments.

check.q: After f = to_upper, what does f point to?
opts: A copy of the function's code
The same function object as to_upper
The string returned by to_upper
check.why: Assignment copies the reference. Both names refer to one function object, and nothing is called until you add brackets.

work: Write a small dict that maps column names to cleaning functions, then apply it in a loop.
Check that every sorted, map or filter call in your code passes a function without brackets.

p02.title: Three traps with function values

beats.say: Why does one pair of brackets break your sort?
Write key equals to_upper with brackets, and Python calls the function first, with no argument, and passes its result along. You get a TypeError. Without brackets, sorted calls it once for each item.

show.title: Trap one
show.text:
sorted(xs, key=to_upper())   # TypeError
sorted(xs, key=to_upper)     # correct
show.note: pass the function, do not call it

beats.say: Second trap: lambdas made in a loop. Each one remembers the variable, not its value at that moment. After three loops, all three see the last value. Fix it with a default argument that freezes the value.

show.title: Trap two: late binding
show.text:
fs = [lambda: i for i in range(3)]
[f() for f in fs]   # [2, 2, 2]
fs = [lambda i=i: i for i in range(3)]  # [0, 1, 2]
show.note: closures capture variables, not values

beats.say: Third, dispatch tables. If a model asks for a tool name that is not in the dictionary, you get a KeyError. Use get, check the name, and never call anything the model names without an allow list.

check.q: You build three lambdas in a for loop that each return i. Why do they all return the last value?
opts: Lambdas can only return the last number
Each lambda looks up i when it runs, not when it was made
The loop deletes the earlier lambdas
check.why: Closures capture the variable, not a snapshot of its value. By the time you call them, i holds its final value. A default argument i=i freezes the value.

work: Search your code for lambdas created inside loops and add default arguments where needed.
Make every dispatch dict lookup use get with a clear error for unknown names.

p02.title: When a Python function is the wrong value

beats.say: When is passing a Python function the wrong choice?

In PySpark, F dot upper is a built-in that Spark optimises inside the engine. Wrap your own Python function as a UDF, and every row travels to a Python worker and back. That is often several times slower. Prefer built-ins.
For dispatch, a dictionary beats a long if chain. Adding a tool is one line, and tests can swap in fakes. But once functions share state or need setup and cleanup, move to a class.

show.title: Dict or class?
items: Dict: one line per new tool
Dict: easy to swap in fakes for tests
Class: setup and cleanup in one place

beats.say: In agents, the dictionary is also your security boundary. Only registered functions can ever run. Keep the registry explicit, validate every argument, and log each call.

check.q: You need to upper-case a column in a large Spark job. What should you choose first?
opts: A Python UDF, because it is flexible
The built-in F.upper, so Spark can optimise it
A loop over collected rows in Python
check.why: Built-ins run inside the engine and are optimised. A Python UDF moves every row between the engine and Python workers, which costs time at scale.

work: Audit your Spark jobs for UDFs that have a built-in equivalent and replace them.
Turn any agent tool list into an explicit registry with argument validation and call logging.

p02.title: A sorting tray for your data

beats.say: Imagine a pile of a thousand trip receipts. How do you grab just the fares from completed trips, in one sweep?
A comprehension is that sweep. You tell Python three things: what to keep from each receipt, which pile to look through, and which receipts to skip.
It is like a mail sorter. Letters go in, a rule rejects some, and what comes out lands in a new tray. The tray can be a list, a lookup table, or a set of unique items.
Read it like a sentence: take the fare, from each trip, where status is completed.

show.text: Take the fare, from each trip, where completed
show.sub: It reads left to right like SQL

check.q: What does a comprehension do?
opts: Builds a new collection from a pile by keeping, transforming and skipping items
Deletes items from the original pile
Sorts the pile in place
check.why: It reads items from an iterable, optionally filters them, and produces a new collection. The original is untouched.

work: Find one loop in your code that builds a list with append and read it aloud as a sentence.
Say what it keeps, where it looks, and what it skips.

p02.title: Four shapes, one line

beats.say: One line can build a list, a dictionary, a set, or just a total. How?
Square brackets build a list. Take fare from each trip where status is completed. Out of ten thousand trips, maybe seven thousand fares come back.

show.title: List
show.text: fares = [t["fare"] for t in trips if t["status"] == "completed"]
show.note: 10,000 trips in, about 7,000 fares out

beats.say: Curly braces with a colon build a dictionary, keyed by trip id. Curly braces without a colon build a set, so the cities come out with no duplicates.

show.title: Dict and set
show.text:
by_id = {t["id"]: t for t in trips}
cities = {t["city"] for t in trips}
show.note: Colon means dict. No colon means set.

beats.say: Round brackets make a generator. Wrapped in sum, it adds fares one at a time and never builds a ten thousand item list in memory. Read it like SQL: select, from, where.

check.q: You only need the total of all fares. Which is best?
opts: sum of a list comprehension
sum of a generator expression
a set comprehension then sum
check.why: A generator feeds sum one value at a time, so no full list is built. A set would also drop duplicate fares and give a wrong total.

work: Replace one sum over a list comprehension with a generator expression.
Build a dictionary keyed by id to replace a repeated search through a list.

p02.title: Where comprehensions bite

beats.say: What goes wrong when a comprehension gets clever?
Two for clauses are fine, like looping rows then columns. Three, and nobody can tell which loop is inner. Past that, write a plain loop.
Never use one for side effects. A list of print calls builds a throwaway list of None values, wasting memory and hiding intent. Use a for loop.

show.title: Anti-pattern
show.note: Builds a list of None just to run print

beats.say: Also, a generator can be read only once. Sum it, then try again, and you get zero. And a dictionary comprehension silently keeps the last trip when two share an id.

check.q: Two trips share the same id. What does a dict comprehension keyed by id do?
opts: Raises a KeyError
Keeps the first trip
Keeps the last trip silently
check.why: Each assignment overwrites the previous key, so the later trip wins with no warning. Check for duplicates if ids must be unique.

work: Search your code for comprehensions with side effects and turn them into loops.
Add a uniqueness check before building any dictionary keyed by id.

p02.title: When to reach for something else

beats.say: When is a comprehension the wrong tool at scale?

show.text: Fast code can still be the wrong code

beats.say: It runs in memory on one machine. A list of fifty million fares may need gigabytes of RAM. Use a generator, or stream in chunks, so memory stays flat.
The speed gain over append is modest, often a third. The real cost is Python itself. Filtering a billion rows belongs in SQL or a dataframe engine, not a Python loop.
Rule for reviews: if it needs a comment, write the loop. Readable code is cheaper than a clever line at three in the morning.

show.text: Needs a comment? Write the loop.

check.q: You must filter a billion rows from a warehouse table. What is the best choice?
opts: A list comprehension after fetching all rows
A generator over all fetched rows
A WHERE clause in the warehouse query
check.why: Filtering where the data lives avoids moving a billion rows into Python. Comprehensions are for small or already-loaded data.

work: In reviews, flag comprehensions that need a comment and ask for a loop.
Push filters into SQL before data reaches Python.

p02.title: The notepad bolted to the counter

beats.say: Why would a function remember things from the last time you used it? Odd, right?
Think of a function as an order form at a coffee shop. Some boxes you must fill in, like your name. Other boxes come pre-filled, like medium size. You can change them, or leave them as they are.

Now the trap. Imagine the pre-filled box says, use this notepad. Not a fresh notepad each time. One notepad, bolted to the counter. Every customer writes on it, so the second customer sees the first customer's order.
The fix is simple. Pre-fill the box with nothing. Then, if it is empty, hand the customer a brand new notepad.

show.title: The fix
items: If empty, make a fresh notepad

check.q: In the coffee shop story, what causes the second customer to see the first customer's order?
opts: The customer forgot to write their name
The pre-filled box points to one notepad shared by all
The shop has too many customers
The notepad is too small
check.why: The default is created once and reused, so every call that skips the box uses the same notepad.

work: Scan your helper functions for defaults that are empty lists or dictionaries.
Explain the shared notepad idea to a teammate in one sentence.

p02.title: Defaults are built once

beats.say: You call add row with one, then with two. Why does the second call return one and two?

show.title: The surprise
show.text:
def add_row(row, batch=[]):
    batch.append(row)
    return batch

add_row(1)  # [1]
add_row(2)  # [1, 2]

beats.say: Because Python builds default values once, at the moment the function is defined, not on each call. The empty list is created a single time and stored on the function. Every call that skips that argument gets that same list.
So append in call one changes it, and call two sees the change. The list now holds one, then one and two, and keeps growing for the life of the process.
The fix is the none idiom. Default to none, which is safe because it never changes. Inside, if batch is none, make a new empty list. Now every call gets its own.

show.title: The None idiom

check.q: When is the default value in a Python function signature evaluated?
opts: On every call
Once, when the function is defined
Only on the first call
When the function returns
check.why: Python evaluates defaults at definition time and stores them, so a mutable default is one shared object.

work: Rewrite one mutable default in your code with the None idiom.
Run the broken add_row twice in a REPL and watch the list grow.

p02.title: Frozen defaults and falsy traps

beats.say: Your pipeline stamps every row with a default timestamp, yet every row shows the same time from this morning. Why?

show.title: Same stamp on every row

beats.say: Same cause. A default like now is evaluated once, at definition. It is frozen when the module loads. Use none, and call now inside the function.

show.title: Fix: call it inside

beats.say: Watch the none check. If you write if not batch, a caller who passes their own empty list gets silently replaced, and their list stays empty. Write batch is none instead.
Also, star args arrives as a tuple, and double star kwargs as a dict. Put a bare star before flags, so overwrite must be named. Then load path comma true cannot happen.

show.title: Argument kinds
items: double star kwargs is a dict

check.q: Why is "if not batch: batch = []" a worse guard than "if batch is None"?
opts: It is slower
It replaces a caller's own empty list, so their list never fills
It raises a TypeError
It only works with tuples
check.why: An empty list is falsy, so not batch swaps it for a new list and the caller's object is never updated.

work: Search for datetime.now() or uuid calls used as default values.
Turn boolean flags in public functions into keyword-only arguments.

p02.title: Hidden state is an architecture risk

beats.say: A job passes in tests, then fails in production only after a worker has run for days. Could a default argument be why?

show.text: Passes in tests, fails after days

beats.say: Yes. A shared default is hidden global state. In a long-lived worker, it leaks rows between tasks, so output depends on what ran before. It also breaks tests, which pass alone but fail in a different order.
Catch it early. Turn on the lint rule for mutable defaults, such as B zero zero six in Ruff. Prefer tuples for fixed defaults, and default factory in data classes.

Also, avoid kwargs sprawl. Ten loose options hide typos and bypass review. Use a typed config object instead. Keep keyword-only flags in public functions, since adding one never breaks existing callers.

show.title: API design
items: New keyword-only args stay backward compatible

check.q: Which choice best prevents shared-state bugs and option sprawl across a large codebase?
opts: Code review comments only
A lint rule for mutable defaults plus typed config objects
Using global variables instead
Passing everything through kwargs
check.why: Automated linting catches the trap consistently, and typed config objects make options explicit and reviewable.

work: Enable the mutable-default lint rule in CI and fix the findings.
Replace a long kwargs signature in a shared library with a typed config object.
Add a test that calls a function twice and checks the results are independent.

p02.title: A function with a pocket

beats.say: How can a function remember a value after the function that created it has finished?

show.sub: even after its creator is gone

beats.say: Picture a manager training a new barista. She tucks a sticky note into the barista's apron: always add two sugars. Then the manager leaves for good. The barista still has the note and keeps following it.

Python does this with a function defined inside another function. The inner one carries a pocket of the outer one's values, even after the outer one returns. That pocket is called a closure. Make a multiplier with two, and it will double anything you give it.
To find a name, Python searches nearest first: inside the function, then the outer function, then the file, then the built-in names. The nearest match wins.

check.q: What is a closure?
opts: A function that cannot be called twice
A function that keeps the outer function's values after the outer one has returned
A function that closes a file automatically
check.why: A closure is an inner function plus the enclosing values it uses, kept alive after the outer function finishes.

work: Find a small helper in your pipeline code that is built inside another function and name what it remembers.
Explain the four lookup places to a teammate, nearest first.

p02.title: How a closure remembers

beats.say: What does double of twenty-one actually do to know that k is two?

Calling make multiplier with two creates a local variable k equal to two. Normally k would vanish when the call ends. But the inner function mul uses k, so Python stores k in a small cell and attaches it to mul.
Now double twenty-one runs mul. Python looks for x: found locally, it's twenty-one. It looks for k: not local, so it checks the enclosing scope, finds the cell, reads two. Result: forty-two.
Each call to make multiplier builds a fresh cell. So double and triple, made separately, each hold their own k and never interfere.

check.q: After make_multiplier(2) returns, where does the value 2 live?
opts: In a global variable
In a cell attached to the inner function
It is gone and recomputed each call
check.why: Because the inner function uses k, Python keeps it in a cell tied to that function, so it outlives the outer call.

work: In a REPL, inspect double.__closure__ and read the cell contents.
Build two closures from the same factory and confirm they hold separate values.

p02.title: Nonlocal and the loop trap

beats.say: Why does a counter that simply adds one to n crash with UnboundLocalError?

Reading an outer variable is fine. But the moment you assign to a name inside a function, Python decides at compile time that the name is local. So n plus equals one tries to read a local n that has no value yet, and fails.
The fix is nonlocal n, which tells Python to rebind the enclosing variable. Each counter from make counter then keeps its own running total, starting at zero.

show.text:
def make_counter():
    n = 0
    def nxt():
        nonlocal n
        n += 1
        return n
    return nxt

beats.say: A second trap: closures capture the variable, not its value. Build three functions in a loop that each return i, and all three return two, the final value, because they share one cell. Fix it by passing i as a default argument.

show.text:
fs = [lambda: i for i in range(3)]
[f() for f in fs]   # [2, 2, 2]

fs = [lambda i=i: i for i in range(3)]
[f() for f in fs]   # [0, 1, 2]

check.q: Three lambdas built in a loop each return i, and all return the last value. Why?
opts: Each lambda copied i at creation
They all share one captured variable i, read when called
Lambdas cannot use loop variables
check.why: Closures capture the variable itself, not a snapshot. By call time the loop has finished, so every lambda sees the final i.

work: Search your code for lambdas or inner functions created in loops and check for late binding.
Add nonlocal only where you truly rebind, and not for reads or in-place mutation.

p02.title: Closure or class?

beats.say: When should a data engineer pick a closure, and when a class?
Closures shine for small configured behaviour: a retry policy, a rate limiter, a connection factory. One function, a few captured settings, no boilerplate.

show.title: Good closure fits
items: Rate limiter with a set pace

beats.say: But the captured state is hidden. You can't easily inspect it, and an unlocked nonlocal counter is not thread safe, since plus equals one is not atomic. If several methods need shared state, or you need to test and reset it, use a class.

chip.text: Use a lock or a class

beats.say: Distributed engines add a limit. Spark serializes your function and its captured values and ships them to every worker. Capture a large lookup table and each task carries a copy. A counter you change on a worker never updates the driver's copy. Use broadcast variables or accumulators instead.

chip.text: Broadcast big data, don't capture it

check.q: A Spark job captures a 2 GB dictionary in a mapped function. What is the best fix?
opts: Make the function a closure with nonlocal
Broadcast the dictionary so each worker gets one shared copy
Increase the number of tasks
check.why: Captured values are serialized into every task. A broadcast variable sends the data once per worker instead of once per task.

work: Review functions passed to Spark or multiprocessing for large captured objects.
Replace closure state with a class when it needs locking, testing or reset.
Use accumulators, not nonlocal counters, to count across workers.

p02.title: A label on every book

beats.say: How does a librarian shelve books by author, then by title, without comparing whole books every time? She puts a small label on each one.
In Python, that label is called a key. You hand sorted a tiny function. It looks at each item and returns the one thing to compare, like a city name or a price.
Need two rules? Make the label a pair. City first. If two cities match, fare breaks the tie. That pair is called a tuple, a small fixed list of values.

chip.text: Ties fall to the next value

beats.say: Your original pile stays untouched. Sorted hands you a fresh, ordered copy.

check.q: What does a key function do in sorted?
opts: Turns each item into the value used for comparing
Deletes items that do not match
Sorts the list in place and returns None
check.why: The key maps each item to the value Python compares. It does not filter, and sorted returns a new list rather than changing the old one.

work: Find one place where you sort records and name the key out loud in plain words.
Replace a hand-written comparison with a simple key function.

p02.title: One key, three rules

beats.say: How do you sort trips by city, then highest fare first, then lowest id? With one key function.
The key returns a tuple: city, minus fare, id. Python compares tuples one slot at a time. Only when cities tie does it look at fare. Only when fares tie does it look at id.
Why minus fare? Sorting always runs low to high. Negating a number flips it. A fare of 40 becomes minus 40, which sorts before minus 10. So the highest fare comes first.
This trick works only for numbers. Strings cannot be negated, so they need a different approach.

check.q: In key=lambda t: (t["city"], -t["fare"]), when is fare looked at?
opts: Always, before city
Only when two cities are equal
Never, because it is negative
check.why: Tuples compare slot by slot, so the second value only matters when the first values tie.

work: Write a multi-field sort as a single tuple key.
Negate numeric fields to reverse just one direction.

p02.title: The None bug and stability

beats.say: Why does xs equals xs dot sort leave you with None?

show.title: Classic bug
show.text: xs = xs.sort()   # xs is now None

beats.say: List dot sort changes the list in place and returns nothing. So you just overwrote your list with None. Use sorted when you want a new list back. Use sort when you want to save memory.
Now a trap: city A to Z, but name Z to A. You cannot negate a string. Use stability instead. Equal items keep their original order.
So sort by the secondary key first, name reversed. Then sort by the primary, city. Cities that tie stay in name order, because the second sort never shuffles equals.

check.q: To sort by city A to Z then name Z to A using two sorts, what is the order?
opts: City first, then name
Name reversed first, then city
Either order gives the same result
check.why: The last sort is the primary key. Stability keeps the earlier name order inside each city.

work: Search your code for assignments of the form x = x.sort().
Add a comment on any two-pass sort explaining why the order matters.

p02.title: When a lambda is not enough

beats.say: Is a lambda the right key for a hundred million rows? Probably not.
Python calls the key once per item, so a slow lambda costs you once per row. Itemgetter does plain field access in C, which is faster. It also takes several fields and returns a tuple.
Two passes using stability cost two full sorts. A tuple key with a negated number costs one. Prefer one pass when you can.
At real scale, sorting in memory breaks, because Python holds the whole list at once. Push the ordering into the database or a Spark job, where it can spill to disk and run in parallel.

check.q: Which choice best fits sorting a table too big for memory?
opts: Use sorted with itemgetter
Sort twice with stability
Push the order by to the database or Spark
check.why: Python sorted needs the whole list in memory. A database or Spark can spill to disk and parallelize.

work: Swap simple field lambdas for itemgetter on hot paths and measure.
Prefer a single tuple key over two sorts when fields are numeric.
Set a row-count threshold above which sorting moves to SQL or Spark.

p02.title: A case for your function

beats.say: How do you add a feature to a tool without opening it up and changing it?

show.text: Add a feature without opening the tool?

beats.say: Think of a phone case. The phone inside is untouched, but now it survives drops. A decorator is a case for a function. It wraps the original and adds behaviour around it.
Say you want to know how long a job takes. Instead of editing the job, you wrap it. The wrapper starts a stopwatch, runs the job, then reports the time.
You write the wrapper once. Then you put it on any function with a single line above it, the at sign and a name.

check.q: What does a decorator do to the function it is placed on?
opts: Deletes it and replaces it with new logic
Wraps it, adding behaviour around the original
Makes it run faster automatically
check.why: A decorator surrounds the original function with extra behaviour, like a case on a phone, without editing the function itself.

work: Find a place where you copy and paste the same timing or logging lines, and note it as a decorator candidate.
Explain the phone case analogy to a teammate in one sentence.

p02.title: What the at sign really does

beats.say: What does the at sign above a function actually do?
Nothing magic. At timed above def f is just f equals timed of f. Python defines f, passes it to timed, and rebinds the name f to whatever comes back.

show.title: Shorthand
show.text:
@timed
def f(x): ...

# same as
f = timed(f)

beats.say: That returned thing is a wrapper. It accepts any arguments using star args and star star kwargs, starts a clock, calls the original, and prints the elapsed time, even if the original raises an error, thanks to a finally block.

Now a decorator with settings, like retry three. That needs three layers. Retry of three runs first and returns the real decorator. That decorator takes the function and returns the wrapper. The wrapper runs on every call.

check.q: What is the plain-Python equivalent of putting @timed above def f?
opts: timed = f(timed)
f = timed(f)
f = timed()
check.why: The decorator is called with the function, and the name f is rebound to the returned wrapper.

work: Rewrite one decorated function in your codebase without the at sign, using f = deco(f), to see the mechanics.
Write a retry decorator with three layers and trace which layer runs when.

p02.title: Why everything is called wrapper

beats.say: Why does every task in your Airflow screen say wrapper?

show.text: Why is every task named wrapper?

beats.say: Because a decorator replaces your function with the wrapper, so the name and docstring of the original are lost. Logs, tracebacks and task names all show wrapper. The fix is functools wraps on the inner function, which copies the name and docstring across.
Other gotchas. Forget to return the result, and every call quietly gives back None. Forget star args, and the wrapper breaks on any function with different parameters.

Timing with a finally block still reports when the function fails, and the error still reaches the caller. Also, decoration runs once at import time, but the wrapper runs on every call. Mixing those up causes surprising bugs.

check.q: What does functools.wraps fix?
opts: It makes the wrapper run faster
It copies the original name and docstring onto the wrapper
It lets the wrapper skip returning a value
check.why: Without it the decorated function reports itself as wrapper in logs, tracebacks and task names; wraps preserves the original metadata.

work: Check every custom decorator in your repo for functools.wraps.
Add a test that asserts the decorated function keeps its name and returns its result.

p02.title: When not to reach for a decorator

beats.say: When is a decorator the wrong tool?

show.text: When is a decorator the wrong tool?

beats.say: They are great for cross-cutting concerns: timing, retries, logging, caching. One line, applied everywhere, fixed in one place. That is why Airflow task and dag, pytest fixture and agent tool all use them.

But they hide behaviour. A retry decorator on a function that charges a card can charge twice unless the function is idempotent, meaning safe to repeat. Stacked decorators run in order, and the order changes meaning: retry outside timing measures all attempts.
Heavy logic or state in a decorator is hard to test. Prefer plain code, or an explicit helper, when the behaviour is specific to one function. Keep decorators small, and always use wraps.

show.title: Rule of thumb
items: Specific logic stays in plain code

check.q: Why is stacking order of decorators important?
opts: Python rejects the wrong order
Each layer wraps the next, so order changes what each one sees, such as what retry covers when timing
Only the top decorator ever runs
check.why: Decorators nest. A retry outside a timer times all attempts together; inside, it times each attempt separately.

work: Audit retry decorators and confirm the wrapped functions are idempotent.
Document the intended order wherever you stack more than one decorator.
Move function-specific logic out of decorators into plain, testable code.

p02.title: The calculator and the messy helper

beats.say: What if a function could quietly wreck your data, and never show an error?
A pure function is like a calculator. You type in numbers, you get an answer, and nothing else in the room changes. Same input, same answer, every time.
An impure function is like a helper who answers your question, but also rearranges your desk while doing it. Run it twice and the desk ends up in a different state.
In a data pipeline, that matters. If a step crashes, you rerun it. With a calculator step, rerunning is harmless. With the messy helper, you get doubled or damaged data.

show.title: Why reruns matter
items: Impure step: rerun can double or damage data

check.q: Why is a calculator-style step safer in a pipeline that gets rerun?
opts: It runs faster
Running it again changes nothing outside it
It uses less memory
check.why: A pure step only returns an answer from its inputs. Rerunning it cannot leave behind extra changes, so retries are safe.

work: Pick one transformation step in your pipeline and ask: does it change anything besides its return value?
Write down which steps would cause damage if they ran twice.

p02.title: Two questions that make a step safe

beats.say: How can you tell if a cleaning step is safe to rerun?
Ask two questions. Does the answer depend only on the inputs? Does it change anything outside itself? That means globals, the caller's data, files, or network calls.
Take clean, which strips spaces and title-cases a city. The pure version builds a new dictionary and leaves the original row alone. The bad version overwrites the city in the caller's row.

show.title: clean versus clean_bad
show.note: First returns a new dict. Second mutates the caller's.

beats.say: Pure steps give three wins. Rerun them safely. Test them with a two-line assert. And run them in parallel, because Spark can ship the function to many machines. Keep reading and writing at the edges, logic in the middle.

check.q: Which function is pure?
opts: One that sets row city in place and returns row
One that returns a new dict with a cleaned city
One that cleans the city and writes the row to a file
check.why: Only the second depends solely on its input and changes nothing outside. The others mutate the argument or perform I/O.

work: Refactor one in-place cleaning function so it returns a new dict.
Add a two-line assert test for it with a sample row.
List where your pipeline does I/O and move it to the first and last steps.

p02.title: Pure on the surface, impure underneath

beats.say: Is a function pure just because it copies the dictionary?
Not always. Copying with double-star only copies the top level. If the row holds a list, both dictionaries share that same list. Append to it, and you've changed the caller's data.
Hidden inputs also break purity. Calling the current time, a random number, or a global setting means the same row gives different answers on different runs. Pass them in as arguments instead.

show.title: Hidden inputs
items: Fix: pass them in as arguments

beats.say: Spark may retry a failed task, so your function can run twice on the same row. A hidden counter or API call inside it then happens twice.

check.q: A Spark task fails and is retried. Your function increments a global counter. What happens?
opts: The counter is incremented only once
The counter may be incremented more than once for the same row
Spark blocks the retry
check.why: Retries rerun your function on the same data. Side effects such as counters or API calls then repeat, which is why impure steps are unsafe.

work: Search your transforms for datetime now, random, and global variables, and pass them in as parameters.
Check rows with nested lists or dicts for shallow copy mutation, and use a deep copy or rebuild the nested value.

p02.title: Pure core, impure shell

beats.say: Should every function in your pipeline be pure?
No, but push impurity to the edges. Keep reading and writing in a thin shell, and the transformation logic in a pure core. Then retries, backfills, and tests all become cheap.
Purity has a cost. Copying a million-row batch row by row wastes memory and time. Prefer vectorised column operations, which also never mutate the source.

show.title: Cost of purity
items: Python loops are slow at scale

beats.say: Some steps must touch the world, like enrichment from an API. Don't call it per row inside a transform. Load the lookup as a table and join, and make the final write idempotent with an upsert on a key.

check.q: You need reference data from an API for each row. What is the best design?
opts: Call the API inside the transform for every row
Fetch the data once as a table, join it in a pure step, write with an upsert
Store the response in a global dict as you go
check.why: Fetching at the edge keeps the transform pure and retry-safe. An upsert on a key makes the final write idempotent.

work: Draw your pipeline and mark each step as I/O or pure, then move logic out of I/O steps.
Replace per-row API calls with a lookup table join.
Make sinks idempotent with upserts on a natural key.

p03.title: A loop is a conveyor belt

beats.say: How does a loop know where it is, and when to stop? Picture a sushi conveyor belt.
A list is like the whole menu printed on paper. You can read it again and again. To loop, Python asks for a belt, called an iterator. It is a helper that remembers your place.
Each time the loop asks for the next plate, the belt hands over one and moves on. When the belt is empty, it shouts stop. That signal is named StopIteration. The loop hears it and quietly ends.
Here is the catch. Plates you have eaten are gone. A file or a generator is a belt, so a second loop over it sees nothing. A list is a menu, so you can loop all day.

check.q: You loop over a file once, then loop over the same file object again. What happens in the second loop?
opts: It starts again from the first line
It does nothing, because the file is already used up
It raises an error right away
check.why: A file is its own iterator, like a belt. After one full pass it is at the end, so the second loop gets StopIteration at once and runs zero times, with no error.

work: Next time you loop twice over the same thing, ask: is it a list or a one-shot belt?
Check which of your data sources are files or generators rather than lists.

p03.title: iter and next, step by step

beats.say: What is a for loop actually doing behind your back?
First, Python calls iter on your data. That returns an iterator, an object that tracks its position. Then it calls next again and again. Each call returns one value, like ten, then twenty.
When values run out, next raises StopIteration. The loop catches it and breaks out. No error reaches you.
Try it by hand with iter of a list holding ten and twenty. Next gives ten. Next gives twenty. The third next raises StopIteration. Two items, three calls.

show.title: By hand
show.text:
it = iter([10, 20])
next(it)  # 10
next(it)  # 20
next(it)  # StopIteration

beats.say: Iter on a list makes a fresh iterator each time, so lists loop many times. Iter on a file returns the file itself, so it is spent after one pass.

chip.text: Iterator is spent after one pass

check.q: For it = iter([10, 20]), what does the third call to next(it) do?
opts: Returns None
Returns 10 again
Raises StopIteration
check.why: After two values the iterator is exhausted. The next call raises StopIteration, which is the signal a for loop uses to end.

work: Open a Python shell and step through iter and next on a list, then on a generator.
Read a loop you wrote and write out the iter and next calls it implies.

p03.title: The silent empty second pass

beats.say: Why does your second pass over a file give you nothing, with no error?

A file or generator is its own iterator. Calling iter on it returns itself, with the same position. After the first loop, that position is the end. The second loop gets StopIteration on the very first next, so it runs zero times, silently.
This bites in pipelines. Say you count rows, then loop again to write them. The count works, the write sees zero rows, and your output file is empty. No crash, no warning.

Fixes: rebuild the generator or reopen the file for each pass, do everything in one pass, or load into a list if it fits in memory. Also, calling next by hand on an empty iterator raises StopIteration, so pass a default.

show.title: Safe patterns
items: Rebuild or reopen for each pass
Do all work in one pass
Use a list if it fits in memory

check.q: A generator is looped once to count rows, then looped again to write them. The output file is empty. Why?
opts: The generator was exhausted by the first loop
Writing to files is lazy and was skipped
The count loop corrupted the data
check.why: A generator is its own iterator and is consumed by the first pass. The second loop gets StopIteration immediately and writes nothing, without raising an error.

work: Add a test that asserts row counts after each stage, so empty second passes are caught.
Grep your code for generators or file objects used in more than one loop.

p03.title: One-shot iterators: cost and trade-offs

beats.say: When should you refuse to use a list, and when is a one-shot iterator a trap?
A list of one hundred million rows at about one hundred bytes each needs ten gigabytes of memory. An iterator holds one row at a time, so memory stays flat, whatever the file size.
The price: one pass only, no length, no jumping back. Two consumers can't share one iterator without stealing each other's rows.

So design for single pass. Do filter, transform and aggregate in one chain. If several steps need the data, either read the source again, which is cheap for files and costly for APIs, or write an intermediate result to disk such as Parquet.
Use a list when data is small and reused. Use iterators when it is big or streaming.

show.title: Choose
items: Many readers: persist to disk first

check.q: Three steps each need the full output of an expensive API crawl that is too big for memory. What is the best design?
opts: Pass one generator to all three steps
Write the crawl to disk once, then let each step read it
Re-crawl the API for each step
check.why: One generator would be consumed by the first step. Re-crawling is slow and costly. Persisting once, for example as Parquet, keeps memory flat and lets each step read independently.

work: Estimate row count times row size before choosing a list for any dataset.
Document which pipeline stages are single-pass and who consumes them.
Persist expensive intermediate results when more than one consumer needs them.

p03.title: A river you can't rewind

beats.say: Ever tried to rewind a river?
A generator is like a river. Water flows past you once. You can count what went by, but then it is gone.
A list is like a bucket. You scoop the water in once. Then you can look, count, and pour it as often as you like.
Here is the trap. You count the river first, then ask for the fares, and find a dry riverbed. Nothing crashes. You just quietly get nothing.
The fix is simple. Fill a bucket if it fits. Or walk back to the spring and start the river again.

show.title: Two fixes
items: Fill a bucket: make a list if it fits
Walk back to the spring: restart from the source

check.q: You count a generator's items, then try to read them again. What do you most likely get?
opts: The same items again
An error that stops the program
Nothing, with no error
Only the first item
check.why: The generator is already used up after the first pass, so the second pass finds nothing and raises no error.

work: Look for any variable holding a generator that is used in two places.
Ask yourself whether each data source is a river or a bucket before you reuse it.

p03.title: Why the second pass is empty

beats.say: Why does the second line of this code return an empty list?

show.title: The trap
show.text:
rows = (parse(l) for l in open('trips.csv'))
n = sum(1 for _ in rows)
fares = [r['fare'] for r in rows]

beats.say: A generator keeps one pointer into its source. Each time you ask for a next item, the pointer moves forward. It never moves back.
Say trips dot csv has ten million rows. Sum over the generator walks the pointer to the end. Ten million rows are read, and the pointer now sits at the finish.
The next loop asks for a row and gets told the stream is finished straight away. No error, just an empty list.
So either call list once, if it fits in memory, or build a fresh generator from the file for the second pass.

show.title: Two ways out
items: Call list once, if it fits in memory
Build a fresh generator for each pass

check.q: After sum consumes a generator, what is the state of that generator?
opts: Reset to the first item
Exhausted, so loops end at once
Holding a copy of all rows
Raising an error on every next call
check.why: The pointer sits at the end, so any new loop finishes straight away without error or items.

work: When you need two passes, write a small function that opens the file and returns a fresh generator.
Test with a tiny file and assert the second result is not empty.

p03.title: Gotchas of one-shot iterables

beats.say: Why can len on a generator never work?
A generator does not know its size. It makes each item only when asked, so the count exists only after you have walked it all. Walking it uses it up.

Worse, a function that takes any iterable may quietly loop twice. Say it checks for empty, then processes. With a list that works. With a generator, the check eats the first row, or the second loop sees nothing.
Also beware itertools tee, which splits one stream into copies. It buffers every item one copy has read and the other has not, so memory can balloon.
Rule: loop once, or state clearly that you need two passes, or take a list.

show.title: The rule
items: Or say clearly that you need two passes

check.q: A function receives an iterable, checks whether it is empty by reading one item, then loops over it. What goes wrong with a generator?
opts: Nothing, the check is free
The check consumes the first row
It raises a type error
It copies the data to disk
check.why: Reading one item advances the pointer for good, so that row is lost to the later loop.

work: Review functions that accept an iterable and flag any that loop twice.
Document in the docstring whether a function needs one pass or many.

p03.title: Replay, store or single pass

beats.say: When is rerunning the source better than storing the data?
Materialising with list costs memory. Ten million rows of dicts can take several gigabytes. If it exceeds RAM, the job dies, so list is only safe when you know the size is bounded.
Restarting costs time. Reading the file twice doubles the input and parsing work, and a network stream or database cursor may not be replayable at all.
Better still, use one pass. Compute the count and the fares together, keeping running totals. Constant memory, one read.
If you truly need many passes, write to Parquet once, or load into DuckDB, and query it repeatedly from disk.

check.q: You need a count and a fare average from a file far larger than RAM. What is the best design?
opts: Call list on the generator
Make two generators and read the file twice
Compute both in one pass with running totals
Call len on the generator
check.why: One pass with running totals keeps memory constant and reads the data only once.

work: Rewrite two-pass jobs as one pass with accumulators where you can.
For repeated analysis of big data, land it once in Parquet and query it with DuckDB.
Check whether your source can be replayed before choosing to restart.

p03.title: Batching is carrying more per trip

beats.say: Would you carry groceries from the car to the kitchen one item at a time?
Of course not. The walk takes the same time whether you hold one tin or five bags. That walk is the fixed cost of every trip.

Databases work the same way. Every insert is a trip across the network, with waiting at both ends. Sending one thousand rows in one trip beats one thousand trips. Grouping items like this is called batching.
But a bag can get too heavy. Too big, and you strain, or drop everything. And the last bag is often half empty. Still carry it, or those items stay in the car.

show.title: Two things to watch
items: Too heavy a bag: a failure costs everything
The last half-empty bag still has to go

check.q: Why is sending 1,000 rows in one insert faster than 1,000 single inserts?
opts: Each row is smaller when grouped
You pay the fixed cost of the trip once, not 1,000 times
The database skips checking the data
check.why: Each call carries a fixed cost, such as network wait and setup. Batching shares that cost across many rows.

work: List the loops in your code that call a database or API once per row.
Pick one and ask: could it send a group of rows in one call?

p03.title: How a chunking generator works

beats.say: How do you send ten million rows to a database without loading them all, or sending them one by one?

show.sub: too many to hold, too slow one by one

beats.say: Say each insert costs five milliseconds of round trip, and the row itself takes almost nothing. One thousand single inserts cost five seconds. One insert of one thousand rows costs about five milliseconds plus a little. That is the saving.
A chunking function does it. It reads items from the source, adds each to a buffer, and when the buffer reaches the size, it yields the buffer and starts a new one.
Memory stays flat, because only one buffer exists at a time. Ten million rows at a thousand per batch means ten thousand inserts.

check.q: You load 10 million rows with a chunk size of 1,000. How many insert calls do you make, and how much data is held in memory?
opts: 10,000 calls, about 1,000 rows in memory
10 million calls, 1 row in memory
10,000 calls, all 10 million rows in memory
check.why: The generator holds one buffer at a time, so memory stays at roughly one batch while you make 10,000 calls.

work: Write a chunked helper and run it on a lazy source, such as a file reader.
Time 1,000 single inserts against one batch of 1,000 on your own database.

p03.title: Chunking gotchas that bite

beats.say: Your batch loader ran clean, but the last forty rows never arrived. What happened?
The loop only yields when the buffer is full. With 10,040 rows and a size of 1,000, the final 40 sit in the buffer when the loop ends. After the loop, you must yield whatever is left.

show.title: The easy-to-forget line

beats.say: Another trap is reusing the buffer. If you clear the list instead of making a new one, anything still holding the old batch sees it change under its feet. Make a fresh list each time.
And when a batch fails, you retry all of it. So the insert must be safe to repeat, for example an upsert by key, or you get duplicates.

show.title: Retry the whole batch
items: A failure repeats every row in the batch
Use upserts or unique keys so repeats are harmless

check.q: A chunker yields only inside the loop when len(buf) equals size. What goes wrong with 10,040 rows and size 1,000?
opts: It crashes at row 10,000
The last 40 rows are silently dropped
The first batch is too large
check.why: The final partial buffer is never full, so it is never yielded unless you add a check after the loop.

work: Add a test with a row count that is not a multiple of the batch size.
Make your batch writes idempotent, with an upsert or a unique key.

p03.title: Choosing batch size as an architect

beats.say: Is bigger always better when you batch? No, and the cost shows up in three places.

Bigger batches mean fewer round trips, but more memory, longer locks, and a bigger retry when one fails. Rows vary in size, so cap by bytes, not only row count. Start with five hundred to five thousand rows, or a few megabytes, then measure.
For files, aim near one hundred twenty-eight megabytes. Ten thousand tiny Parquet files make every query slow, because opening each file costs more than reading it.
In streams, batching adds waiting. Flush on size or on a timer, whichever comes first, so a quiet trickle is not stuck. And skip batching when you need each result immediately.

show.title: Flush rules
items: Flush when full or when the timer fires
Skip batching when each result is needed at once
Measure throughput and p99 latency before settling

check.q: A stream sends only a few events per minute into a batch of 5,000. What should you add?
opts: A bigger batch size
A time-based flush
Fewer retries
check.why: Without a timer, events wait until the batch fills, which may take hours. Flushing on size or time bounds the delay.

work: Cap batches by bytes as well as rows, then load-test a few sizes.
Add a time-based flush to any streaming writer, and compact small files on a schedule.

p03.title: The dish line that never piles up

beats.say: How do you wash a million dishes in a kitchen with room for only three?
You build an assembly line. One helper fetches a plate, one scrubs, one dries, one stacks. Each plate goes through every helper before the next plate is fetched.

show.title: One plate at a time down the *line*

beats.say: Nothing moves until the last helper asks for a plate. That request travels back down the line to the pantry. So the counter only ever holds a few plates, whether there are ten dishes or ten million.

chip.text: Only a few plates at once

beats.say: In Python, each helper is a generator. That is a function that hands out one item, then pauses until asked again. Chain small generators together, each doing one job, and you can process data far bigger than memory.

show.title: Generator pipeline
items: Generator: hands out one item, then pauses
Each stage does one small job
Memory stays flat at any size

check.q: In the dish line, when does the first helper fetch a plate?
opts: Immediately, to fill the counter
Only when the last helper asks for one
After all dishes are counted
When the counter is full
check.why: Work is pulled from the end of the line. Nothing is fetched until the last stage asks, which keeps the counter nearly empty.

work: Think of one job where you load a whole file into a list, and picture it as a line of single-item helpers instead.
Write down which of your scripts would break if the input grew ten times larger.

p03.title: Filter and load fifty million rows

beats.say: A trips file has fifty million lines. How does Python filter and load it using almost no memory?

You chain generators. Read lines yields one line. Parse turns it into a dictionary. Only completed keeps rows whose status is completed. Building this chain runs nothing. It only wires the stages together.

Work starts when the loop asks for a batch. Chunked pulls from only completed, which pulls from parse, which pulls from the reader. One row flows through every stage before the next row is read. Chunked collects one thousand rows, then write batch sends them to the database in one call.
Memory holds one line plus one batch of a thousand rows. Fifty million lines or five hundred million, the footprint is the same.

check.q: Which line makes the pipeline actually start reading the file?
opts: Calling read_lines on the file
Wrapping stages inside each other
The for loop over chunked that asks for a batch
Defining the parse function
check.why: Generators are lazy. Wiring them runs nothing. The for loop asking for the next batch pulls rows through every stage.

work: Replace a read-all-then-loop script with a chain of generators and compare peak memory.
Pick a batch size by testing database write time at 500, 1000 and 5000 rows.

p03.title: Lazy like Spark, endless like Kafka

beats.say: What do a Python generator pipeline and a Spark job have in common?

Both are lazy. Spark transformations like filter and map only build a plan. Nothing runs until an action such as count or write pulls data through it. Generators work the same way. The last stage asks, and everything upstream responds.
A Kafka consumer loop is the same shape with an endless source. It pulls a message, handles it, and pulls the next, so memory stays flat forever.
To read many files as one stream, use yield from. It hands out everything another generator produces, so a loop over a list of daily files looks like one long file to the next stage.

show.title: Many files, one stream

check.q: What does yield from do in a pipeline?
opts: Runs several generators in parallel
Hands out every item another generator produces, as one stream
Loads that generator's output into a list
Restarts the generator when it ends
check.why: It forwards each item from another generator one at a time, so many files look like one stream without building a list.

work: Write an all_lines generator that chains daily files into one stream.
Explain in one sentence which Spark calls are transformations and which are actions in a job you own.

p03.title: Why the pipeline ran dry

beats.say: You loop over the same pipeline twice, and the second loop writes nothing. Why?
A generator is single use. Each value is handed out once, then gone. After the first pass it is exhausted, and asking again gives nothing, with no error. To rerun, build a fresh pipeline.

Errors also surface late. One malformed line makes parse raise, and the exception kills the generator for good, since it cannot resume. Catch bad lines inside parse and send them to a reject file, so one bad row does not stop fifty million good ones.

Two more gotchas. Chunked must flush the last partial batch, or you lose up to nine hundred ninety nine rows. And open the file in a with block inside the reader, so it closes even if the pipeline stops early.

show.title: Two more traps
items: Open files with a with block in the reader
Debugging with list consumes the rows

check.q: A parse stage raises on line 7 million and you did not catch it. What happens?
opts: Parse skips that row and continues
The exception propagates and the generator cannot resume
The pipeline restarts from the first line
Only that batch is dropped
check.why: An uncaught exception ends the generator permanently. Handle bad rows inside the stage and route them to a reject file.

work: Add a reject file path to your parse stage and count rejected rows.
Test your chunked function with a row count that is not a multiple of the batch size.
Never call list on a live pipeline while debugging; use itertools islice to peek at a fresh copy.

p03.title: When generators stop being enough

beats.say: At what point should you stop writing generator pipelines and reach for Spark?

A generator pipeline is one thread on one machine. Pure Python parses maybe two hundred thousand rows a second, so fifty million rows take about four minutes. That is fine for a nightly job. At five billion rows it is seven hours, and you cannot split the work across machines.

show.title: Run time at 200k rows per second

beats.say: It also handles only row by row work. Sorting, joins and group bys need to see many rows at once, so a streaming pipeline cannot do them without spilling to disk. For those, pick DuckDB or Polars on one big machine, or Spark when data outgrows it.
Keep generators for simple streaming loads, and make writes idempotent so a failed batch can be retried safely. Bigger batches mean fewer round trips but more to redo on failure.

show.title: Design rules
items: Idempotent writes so retries are safe
Batch size: round trips versus redo cost

check.q: Which job is the worst fit for a plain generator pipeline?
opts: Filtering a huge CSV and loading it in batches
Sorting five billion rows and joining them to another large table
Streaming Kafka messages into a database
Combining daily files into one stream
check.why: Sorts and joins need many rows at once and benefit from parallelism, so use DuckDB, Polars or Spark instead of a single-thread streaming pipeline.

work: Measure rows per second of your slowest stage before deciding whether to scale out.
Make your batch writes idempotent, for example with upserts keyed on trip id.
Write down the row count at which your job misses its deadline; that is your trigger to move to Spark.

p03.title: A conveyor belt of parcels

beats.say: How do you look at the first five items on a belt that never ends, without unloading the whole thing?
Picture a conveyor belt of parcels. A tool called islice grabs the first five, then stops the belt. The rest is never touched, even if a billion parcels are waiting.
Chain joins two belts end to end, so they act like one long belt. It is the same idea as union all in a database.

Groupby makes piles, but only of neighbours. Three red parcels in a row make one pile. A blue one, then red again, starts a brand new red pile. So shuffled colours give many small piles. Sort first if you want one pile per colour.

chip.text: Sort first for one pile per colour

check.q: A belt of parcels has colours red, red, blue, red. How many piles does groupby make?
opts: Two, one red and one blue
Three, because the last red is not next to the first reds
Four, one per parcel
check.why: Groupby only joins neighbours with the same key. Red, red is one pile, blue is another, and the final red starts a new pile, making three.

work: Next time you need first N rows to inspect a big file, use islice instead of loading a list.
Before using groupby, ask yourself whether equal keys are guaranteed to sit next to each other.

p03.title: Lazy tools, flat memory

beats.say: A file has fifty million rows. How do you take the first five, add up running totals, and never load the file?
These tools are lazy. Islice of rows, five, pulls exactly five items from the source, then stops. Memory stays flat, and the file is read only as far as row five.
Accumulate turns one, two, three into one, three, six, a running total, one value at a time. Count starts at one and counts up forever, so always pair it with islice or a break.
Chain takes several files and yields their rows in order, one file after another. Still nothing is loaded up front.

check.q: Why must count(1) be paired with islice or a break?
opts: It is lazy and never ends on its own
It loads every number into memory first
It only works on sorted data
check.why: Count yields numbers forever, one at a time. Without something that stops the loop, it runs endlessly.

work: Replace head-of-file list slicing with islice so you do not load the file.
Use chain over a list of file readers to process many files as one stream.

p03.title: The groupby trap

beats.say: Why does groupby on city return Paris three times?

Because groupby only merges consecutive equal keys. It compares each row to the one just before it. Paris, Paris, Rome, Paris gives three groups, not two. SQL group by sees all rows at once. Groupby cannot, because it streams.
Second trap: each group is a live view of the same stream. Move to the next group and the old one is gone. Turn it into a list or consume it before moving on.

show.title: Groups are live views
items: Advancing the loop kills the old group
Use list of group, or consume it inside the loop

beats.say: The fix for true grouping is sorting first, which needs all data in memory or on disk, or a dict of counters. But the consecutive behaviour is useful for runs, like an online streak or a user session.

show.title: Choose on purpose
items: True group by: sort first, or use a dict
Runs and streaks: groupby is perfect
Sessions: consecutive events by one user

check.q: You saved groups from groupby into a list of the group objects, then looped over them afterwards. What do you most likely see?
opts: Every group is full and correct
The groups are empty or wrong, because the stream moved on
Python raises a sorting error
check.why: Each group shares the underlying iterator. Once the outer loop advances, earlier groups are exhausted. Materialise each group with list while you are still on it.

work: Add a sort or a dict whenever you mean SQL group by.
Wrap each group in list or sum it inside the loop, never after.
Use groupby on purpose for streaks and sessions.

p03.title: When itertools is not enough

beats.say: When is a lazy Python pipeline the wrong tool?

show.text: When is lazy Python not enough?

beats.say: Itertools is great for one pass over a stream on one machine. It uses almost no memory and it is simple to test. But it runs on one core, and python loops handle roughly a million rows a second at best.
Real group by across a huge dataset needs sorting or hashing, so use a database, DuckDB, or Spark, which spill to disk and run in parallel. Do not hand sort fifty gigabytes in Python.

show.title: Hand the *heavy* work to an engine

beats.say: Keep itertools for glue: sampling, batching, stitching files, and detecting runs. Once you need joins, many keys, or retries, move to an engine.

show.title: Rule of thumb
items: Itertools: sample, batch, stitch, find runs
Engine: joins, wide group by, big sorts
Switch when one core or one pass breaks

check.q: You must count orders per customer across 50 GB of unsorted files. What is the best choice?
opts: Sort in Python, then use groupby
Use an engine like DuckDB or Spark that hashes and spills
Use accumulate over the files
check.why: True group by needs hashing or sorting at scale. An engine does it in parallel and spills to disk, while Python sorting is slow, single-core and memory hungry.

work: Document which pipelines are single-pass glue and which should move to an engine.
Benchmark rows per second on a sample before committing to a pure Python design.

p03.title: A function that keeps its place

beats.say: How can a program read a file bigger than your computer's memory? Picture a friend reading you a long novel aloud.
They don't memorize the whole book first. They read one line, stop, and keep a finger on the page. Ask for the next line, and they carry on from that finger.
A generator is exactly that. It's a function that hands you one piece, then pauses, remembering where it was.
So you only ever hold one line at a time. A billion lines, or an endless stream, costs almost nothing. Compare that with copying the whole book out by hand before you start.

check.q: What makes a generator able to handle a file bigger than memory?
opts: It compresses the file
It hands out one piece at a time and pauses between them
It reads the whole file faster
check.why: A generator keeps only the current item and its place, so memory stays tiny however long the data is.

work: Think of one job that loads a whole file and ask whether one line at a time would do.
Explain generators to a teammate using the finger-on-the-page picture.

p03.title: How yield pauses and resumes

beats.say: What actually happens when you call a function that contains yield? Nothing runs at all.
The call just returns a generator object. Each next runs the body up to the next yield, hands back that value, and pauses with every local variable kept.
The first next prints opening and returns line one. The second returns line two. The file is not reopened, and nothing is reread.
Memory is the point. A list of a hundred million squares takes gigabytes. The same thing in round brackets builds nothing until consumed, so sum over it runs in constant memory.

check.q: After g = read_lines('trips.log'), which is true?
opts: The file is open and line 1 is read
Nothing has run yet; the body starts at the first next
The whole file is loaded into a list
check.why: Calling a generator function only creates the generator object. The body runs on the first next.

work: Replace a list comprehension feeding sum or max with a generator expression.
Add a print inside a small generator to see exactly when it runs.

p03.title: Generator gotchas

beats.say: Why does your generator seem to do nothing, then give you nothing the second time? Generators have sharp edges.
First, laziness. The file opens at the first next, not when you call the function. So a typo in the path only fails later, far from the line that caused it.
Second, one shot. Once exhausted, a generator raises StopIteration forever. Looping over it twice gives an empty second pass. Need two passes? Call the function again.

Third, cleanup. The closed message prints only if the loop finishes. Stop early, and the with block closes the file only when the generator is closed or garbage collected. Close it explicitly, or use try finally.

show.title: Stopping early
items: Closing message skipped if you break out
with block runs on close or garbage collection
Call close, or use try finally for cleanup

check.q: You loop over the same generator twice. What does the second loop do?
opts: Restarts from the first item
Raises a file error
Produces nothing, because it is already exhausted
check.why: A generator cannot rewind. Once finished, it yields nothing more. Call the function again for a fresh one.

work: Audit pipelines for generators consumed twice, such as len followed by a loop.
Wrap resource-holding generators in try finally or contextlib closing.

p03.title: When generators are the wrong tool

beats.say: When is a generator the wrong choice? When you need the data more than once, or need it fast.

show.sub: you pay in speed and flexibility

beats.say: Generators give constant memory, but they run one item at a time on one thread. Python overhead per item adds up. A hundred million rows through pure Python takes minutes.
Need random access, sorting, or several passes? Materialize to disk, or use a tool like DuckDB or Polars that streams in batches natively.

show.title: Choose instead
items: Several passes: write to disk, then reread
Sorting or joins: DuckDB or Polars
Parallel work: split files across workers

beats.say: If you stay with generators, yield chunks of ten thousand rows to spread the per-item cost. Remember debugging is harder, since state hides inside paused frames. Use them for one pass pipelines.

show.title: Yield batches

check.q: A job must sort 500 million rows and scan them three times. What fits best?
opts: One generator pipeline over the raw file
A list comprehension in memory
An engine like DuckDB, or an intermediate file on disk
check.why: Sorting and multiple passes need random access or reuse. A single-use generator cannot give that, so use a streaming engine or stored intermediate data.

work: Benchmark a per-row generator against a batched version on real data.
Document which pipeline stages are single pass and which need materialized data.

p04.title: Function, dict or class: the kitchen view

beats.say: Why would you build a whole restaurant just to make toast?

show.kicker: Pick the simplest tool that works

beats.say: Think of a kitchen. A recipe card is a function. Ingredients go in, a dish comes out, and nothing is remembered afterward.

A shopping list is like a dict, short for dictionary. It is just labelled facts you read: milk, two. Eggs, twelve. A dataclass is the same list on a printed form, so every field has a name and a place.

show.title: A list is a *dict*, a form is a dataclass

beats.say: A class is a cashier with a till. It remembers how much money is inside, and it refuses to give change it does not have. That memory plus the rules is what makes a class worth it.

check.q: In the kitchen picture, which thing most needs to be a class?
opts: A recipe card that turns eggs into an omelette
A cashier whose till total changes and who must refuse bad requests
A shopping list read once at the shop
check.why: A class earns its place when it holds changing state and guards rules. The recipe is a function and the list is a dict or dataclass.

work: Look at one class in your code and ask whether it holds any changing state.
Name one function that could stay a plain function.

p04.title: The five-row decision table

beats.say: You are passing the same five values to six functions. Is that a problem?
Start simple. A transformation with no state, like converting cents to dollars, is a function. Same input, same output, nothing to remember.
A record that is only read, say a trip with an id, a fare and a pickup time, is a dict. Better, a dataclass, because a typo in a field name then fails loudly instead of silently returning nothing.
Once data has rules, like fare is never negative, or state changes over time, like a rate limiter counting requests per minute, use a class. It holds the state and guards the rules in one place.
Five values times six functions is thirty places to get it wrong. Bundle them into one object and there is one place.

show.title: Bundle repeated values
items: Same five values everywhere means an object is hiding
One object means one place for rules
Thirty chances to err become one

check.q: You pass user_id, rate, window and count to six functions that update a counter. What is the best move?
opts: Convert them all to global variables
Bundle them into a class with methods
Store them in a dict and keep the six functions
check.why: Repeated values with changing state and rules want to be an object, so the rules live in one place.

work: Search your code for parameter groups repeated across several functions.
Replace one hand-passed dict of records with a dataclass.

p04.title: Where dicts and classes bite back

beats.say: Why does a dict let a fare of minus fifty slip through, while a class does not?
A dict accepts anything. A typo like fare underscore amt quietly creates a new key, and the real one stays empty. A dataclass catches the wrong name, but by default it still does not check values.
To enforce rules, validate in the constructor. For dataclasses that is a method called post init. Reject bad data at the door, so every object that exists is valid.

Two traps. Mutable state shared between instances, like one list reused as a default by every object, leaks data across them. And records that anyone can change later break your rules, so freeze them with a frozen dataclass.

show.title: Gotchas interviewers probe
items: Shared mutable default leaks data between objects
Rules checked only at creation break if fields change later
A class with no state is a function in disguise

check.q: Why can a validated dataclass still end up holding a negative fare?
opts: Dataclasses cannot hold numbers
Validation ran only at creation and the field was changed afterward
Dicts are always safer
check.why: Checking in post init protects only construction. If the field is mutable, later assignment bypasses it, so freeze it or validate in setters.

work: Add a post init check for one invariant, such as fare at least zero.
Mark read-only records as frozen dataclasses.
Grep for list or dict default arguments.

p04.title: Choosing by what changes

beats.say: When is a class the wrong answer, and when is it the only answer?

Wrong: wrapping a stateless transform in a class. It adds ceremony and hides that the logic is pure and easy to test. Also wrong at scale. A million small Python objects can eat hundreds of megabytes, where columnar data needs a fraction.
Right: several interchangeable behaviours, like sinks or LLM providers. Give each small class the same method name, such as write, and callers never change when you add a new one.

chip.text: Add a sink, change nothing else

beats.say: So choose by what changes. Pure logic, a function. Bulk records, dataframes or typed schemas. Rules with evolving state, or swappable behaviours, a class.

show.title: Choose by what changes
items: Bulk records: dataframe or typed schema
Swappable behaviours: small classes, one method name

check.q: You must support three output destinations and add more later. What fits best?
opts: One big function with an if branch per destination
A dict of settings only
Small classes sharing one method name, one per destination
check.why: Interchangeable behaviours behind a shared method let callers stay unchanged when a new destination is added.

work: Find one if-chain that picks behaviour by type and consider replacing it with classes sharing a method.
Check whether any pipeline holds millions of rows as Python objects instead of columnar data.

p04.title: A class is a blank form

beats.say: Why do programmers write a class, when a plain list of values would do?

show.sub: instead of a loose list of values

beats.say: Think of a class as a blank trip form. It says every trip needs an id, a fare, and a distance. Each time you fill one in, you get one real trip. The blank form is the class. Each filled copy is called an instance.

The form can also have rules. If someone writes a negative fare, the form refuses it straight away. It can also do small jobs for you, like working out fare per kilometre. A job that belongs to the form is called a method.
So a class keeps the data and its rules together, in one place, and every copy follows them.

check.q: In the form analogy, what is an instance?
opts: The blank form itself
One filled-in copy of the form
The rule that refuses bad values
The printed description of a trip
check.why: The class is the blank form. Each filled-in copy, such as one particular trip, is an instance.

work: Find a place in your code where a dictionary is passed around and ask which keys it must always have.
List the rules one record must obey, such as no negative fare, and see where they are checked today.

p04.title: What happens when you call Trip

beats.say: What really happens when you call Trip with seven, one hundred twenty, and eight?

Python makes an empty object, then runs the special method named init on it. Init receives the object as its first argument, called self, plus your three values. It checks the fare is not negative, then stores trip id, fare, and km on self.

Now call fare per km on that trip. Python quietly rewrites it as Trip dot fare per km, passing the trip as self. So self is not magic. It is just the trip you called the method on. With fare one twenty and eight kilometres, the answer is fifteen.
