Last, repr controls how the trip prints, so a failing test shows Trip seven, fare one twenty, instead of a useless memory address.

check.q: When you write t.fare_per_km(), what is self inside the method?
opts: The class Trip
A copy of the fare
The object t
A new empty trip
check.why: Python passes the instance the method was called on as the first argument, so self is t.

work: Add a repr to any class you own, then print a list of its objects in a test.
Write a tiny class with a check in init and test that bad values raise an error.

p04.title: Where a class still leaks

beats.say: Your class rejects a negative fare, so why can a bad trip still sneak in later?

Because init only checks at birth. Anyone can write t dot fare equals minus five afterwards, and Python allows it. The rule is guarded once, not forever. To guard it always, use a property with a setter that repeats the check.

chip.text: Use a property setter to re-check

beats.say: Another gotcha: fare per km divides by km. The code returns zero when km is zero, which avoids a crash but hides bad data. A trip of zero kilometres might deserve an error instead. Choose on purpose.

show.title: Silent zero vs loud error
items: Zero km avoids a divide-by-zero crash
But a fake 0.0 flows downstream unnoticed
Decide: default value or raise an error

beats.say: Also, if init raises, no object is returned, so you never hold a half-built trip. And two trips with identical values are still not equal, unless you define equality, because the default compares identity.

show.title: Two more gotchas
items: Init raises: no object, no half-built trip

check.q: A Trip checks fare is not negative in init. What can still happen?
opts: Nothing, the check runs on every change
Someone sets t.fare to a negative number later and Python allows it
The Trip object is created half built
Python refuses to create any second trip
check.why: Init validates only at creation. Plain attributes can be reassigned freely, so use a property setter or a frozen design to keep the rule.

work: Review classes that validate in init and ask whether attributes can be changed afterwards.
Decide for each divide-by-zero guard whether a default or an error is the honest answer.
Add a test that two trips with the same values compare as you expect.

p04.title: When not to hand-write the class

beats.say: Should every record in your pipeline be a hand-written class?

Not always. A plain class like Trip needs init, repr, and ideally equality, all boilerplate. A dataclass generates them from three lines, and a frozen one blocks later changes. Use that by default for simple records.

Scale matters too. Millions of Python objects each carry a dictionary of attributes, costing roughly a hundred bytes or more apiece. For bulk data, keep columns in Arrow, pandas, or Spark, and validate with a schema at the boundary.
Reserve hand-written classes for things with behaviour and rules, like a fare calculator, where the logic deserves a home and tests.

show.title: Choose by job
items: Behaviour and rules: a real class

check.q: You must process 50 million trip rows. What is the best default?
opts: One hand-written Trip object per row
Columnar data such as Arrow or Spark, validated by a schema
A list of dictionaries
One giant class with every method
check.why: Per-object memory and loop overhead in Python grow painfully at tens of millions of rows. Columnar structures are compact and fast, and a schema validates at the boundary.

work: Replace simple hand-written record classes with frozen dataclasses where it fits.
Check whether any job builds millions of Python objects and measure its memory.
Keep real classes for logic that needs rules, tests, and a clear home.

p04.title: The blank card Python prints for you

beats.say: How much boring writing would you do to make a simple form? Python can print the form for you.

show.sub: so you don't write it by hand

beats.say: Think of a library card. Every card has the same boxes: name, member number, expiry date. A dataclass is that blank card. You list the boxes once, and Python builds the rest: how to fill one in, how to print it, and how to check if two cards match.
Now laminate the card. Nobody can scribble over it. That is a frozen dataclass. Because it can never change, you can safely hand the same card to many people, and use it as a key in a filing index.

chip.text: Can't change, so safe to share

check.q: In the library card analogy, what does laminating the card stand for?
opts: A frozen dataclass that cannot be changed
Printing the card faster
Checking two cards match
Adding more boxes
check.why: Lamination means nobody can edit the card, which matches frozen=True. That is why it is safe to share and to use as a key.

work: Find a class in your code that only holds fields and has hand-written init and repr. Note it as a dataclass candidate.
Pick one value that should never change after creation, such as a currency amount or a config, and mark it as frozen.

p04.title: What the decorator writes for you

beats.say: You write four lines of class. How does Python hand you a constructor, a printout and an equality check for free?

show.title: Four lines in

beats.say: The decorator reads your type annotated fields, in order. From them it generates init, repr and eq. So Batch of orders prints as Batch, table equals orders, and two batches with the same fields compare equal. Without it, equality would just compare memory addresses.

Money is the classic example. Store amount as an integer in paise, so five hundred rupees is fifty thousand, never a float. Set frozen true, and assigning to amount raises an error. Frozen also makes the object hashable, so it works in sets and as a dict key. Add order true and a list of Money sorts by its fields.

show.title: Money as a value object
items: amount is an int in paise: 500 rupees is 50000
Frozen means hashable: sets and dict keys work
order=True: instances sort by their fields

check.q: Why does frozen=True let a dataclass be used as a dict key?
opts: It makes the object hashable because it can't change
It converts the object to a string
It sorts the fields
It copies the object on each lookup
check.why: A dict key needs a stable hash. Frozen fields can't change, so the hash stays valid and Python generates one.

work: Replace float money fields with an integer in the smallest unit, wrapped in a frozen Money dataclass.
Use order=True on a small value type and sort a list of them instead of writing a key function.

p04.title: Gotchas that interviewers probe

beats.say: What happens if you write rows colon list equals empty brackets in a dataclass?

Python refuses, with a ValueError, because one shared list would be the default for every instance, so every batch would append into the same rows. Use field with default factory set to list. The factory runs once per instance, giving each batch its own list.

Next gotcha: validation. The generated init does no checking, so put checks in post init, which runs right after it. Raise ValueError if table is empty. Also, frozen is shallow. A frozen object holding a list can still have that list mutated, and hashing it will fail. Type hints are not enforced either: pass a string for amount and nothing complains.

show.title: Three more caveats
items: __post_init__ runs after init: put validation there
Frozen is shallow: a list inside can still change
A frozen object with a list field can't be hashed
Type hints are not enforced at runtime

check.q: You need each Batch to start with its own empty list of rows. What is correct?
opts: rows: list = []
rows: list = field(default_factory=list)
rows: list = None, then never set it
rows: list = list
check.why: default_factory runs for every new instance, so each gets a fresh list. A literal empty list would be one shared object.

work: Search your dataclasses for list, dict or set defaults and switch them to default_factory.
Move input checks, such as non-empty names and positive amounts, into __post_init__.
Before freezing a class, check it has no mutable fields that break the immutability promise.

p04.title: Dataclass, Pydantic or dict?

beats.say: Dataclass, Pydantic, or plain dict? Which one should model your data?

show.sub: pick by where the data comes from

beats.say: Use a dataclass inside your own code, where types are already trusted. It is light, standard library, and fast. Use Pydantic at the boundary, where untrusted data enters: API payloads, tool inputs, structured model output. There it coerces types and rejects bad values, at the price of a dependency and slower construction.

Prefer frozen value objects for money, keys and config. They are safe to share across threads and cache. Skip dataclasses when an object has rich behaviour and hidden state, or when millions of rows per second matter: then use tuples, slots, or columnar tools like Arrow instead of one Python object per row.

show.title: When to choose what
items: Frozen value objects: money, keys, config
Rich behaviour or hidden state: a normal class
Millions of rows a second: tuples, slots or Arrow
Untrusted input: Pydantic at the boundary

check.q: You process 50 million rows a second in a hot loop. What is the best fit?
opts: One Pydantic model per row
One frozen dataclass per row
A columnar format such as Arrow, not one object per row
A dict per row with validation on every access
check.why: At that scale, per-row Python objects cost too much memory and time. Columnar data processes whole batches with far less overhead.

work: Draw the boundary in one service: validate with Pydantic where data enters, then pass plain dataclasses inward.
Benchmark object-per-row against a columnar approach before choosing a model for any high-volume path.

p04.title: One socket, many plugs

beats.say: Why does len work on a list, a word, and a dictionary, when they are totally different things?
Think of a power socket. Any appliance with the right plug just works, and the wall never needs to know if it is a kettle or a lamp.
Python is the wall. Special methods are the plug shapes. A class that has a length method fits the len socket. One with an add method fits the plus socket.
So you write the plug once, and everyone else uses the familiar socket. Nobody has to learn your custom method names.

check.q: What is a special method, in the socket analogy?
opts: The plug shape that lets your object fit a built-in socket like len
A faster version of a normal method
A method that only Python itself can define
check.why: Special methods are the agreed shapes Python looks for, so your object works with built-in syntax.

work: Pick one class you use daily and list which built-ins callers wish it supported.
Notice in code review where callers use a custom method name when len or in would read better.

p04.title: What len of x really does

beats.say: What really happens when you write len of x?
Python does not look inside x. It asks the type of x for a method named double underscore len, and calls it. If you wrote it, you get a number back. If not, you get a TypeError.

Take a buffer holding three readings. Define len to return three, and len of buffer gives three. Define iter, and a for loop walks the readings. Define contains, and the in operator answers yes or no.
Same idea for money. Define add, and five dollars plus ten dollars calls add and returns fifteen dollars. Define getitem, and square brackets work too.

check.q: What does Python do for the expression a + b?
opts: Calls a.__add__(b) on a's type
Copies the fields of a and b together
Calls len on both objects
check.why: Operators are translated into calls to the matching special method.

work: Add __len__ and __iter__ to a small container class and delete its custom count and items helpers.
Write a Money class with __add__ and __eq__ and test it with simple examples.

p04.title: Dunder gotchas

beats.say: You defined equals on your class, and suddenly it cannot go in a set. Why?

Because Python sets hash to none when you define equals alone. Equal objects must share a hash, and Python cannot guess yours. Define hash from the same fields you compare, or keep the object unhashable on purpose.
Another trap: add with the wrong type. Do not raise an error. Return NotImplemented, so Python tries the other side's reflected add before giving up.

show.title: Be polite with other types

beats.say: Also, truth tests fall back to len, so an empty container is false. And with only getitem, a for loop still works, counting zero, one, two, until an index error.

check.q: Your __add__ receives an unsupported type. What is best?
opts: Raise ValueError
Return NotImplemented
Return None
check.why: NotImplemented lets Python try the other operand's reflected method and then raise a clean TypeError.

work: Check every class that defines __eq__ and decide whether it needs __hash__ or should stay unhashable.
Add a test that an empty instance of your container is falsy, and that bad operand types raise TypeError.

p04.title: When dunders are a trap

beats.say: Your teammate overloads plus to mean send this message. Good design or trap?

Trap. Special methods hide cost and meaning behind familiar syntax. A len that runs a database query, or an in check that scans a million rows, looks free at the call site and is not. Keep dunders cheap and unsurprising.
Use them for value types and containers, where the meaning is obvious: money, ranges, buffers. For actions with side effects, write a named method like send or flush. The name documents the cost.

Before hand-writing everything, reach for dataclasses, which generate equals, or the collections abc Sequence, which gives contains, iteration and reversed from just getitem and len. Less code, fewer bugs.

check.q: Which use of a special method is the riskiest design?
opts: __len__ on a fixed-size buffer
__add__ on a Money value type
__len__ that issues a database query each call
check.why: Callers assume len is cheap and safe; hiding I/O behind it surprises them and hurts performance.

work: In review, flag any dunder that does I/O or has side effects and give it a named method.
Prefer dataclass or collections.abc base classes before hand-writing equality, ordering or sequence methods.

p04.title: A property is a worked-out answer

beats.say: What if you could ask a question and get a calculated answer, without ever seeing the calculation?

show.text: Looks like a fact. Is really a sum.
show.sub: Ask, and the answer is worked out for you

beats.say: Picture a taxi meter. You never ask the driver to do the sum. You just glance at the cost per kilometre, and it is worked out from the fare and the distance.
In Python, a property is that glance. The caller reads it like a plain fact, but behind it a small method runs and does the sum.

show.title: Reads like a fact, runs a *method*

beats.say: It can also guard the door. A property with no setter is read only. You can look at the value, but you cannot overwrite it.

show.title: Look, but do not *touch*
items: Writing to it raises an error
A setter can refuse nonsense values

check.q: A property has no setter. What happens when someone assigns a value to it?
opts: The value is stored silently
Python raises an AttributeError
The method runs again and ignores the value
check.why: Without a setter the property is read only, so assignment fails loudly with an AttributeError instead of quietly corrupting the object.

work: Find one method in your code that is called only to compute a value from stored fields, and note if it could be a property.
Explain a property to a teammate using the taxi meter picture.

p04.title: How a property computes on read

beats.say: How can reading trip dot fare per kilometre give 12 point 5, with no brackets?
Mark a method with the property decorator. Python then runs it whenever the name is read. A trip with fare 100 and 8 kilometres computes 100 divided by 8, rounded to two places: 12 point 5.

show.title: The decorator
show.note: Read the name, the method runs

beats.say: Nothing is stored. Change the fare to 120 and the next read gives 15, so the value can never go stale.
Try to assign to it and Python raises an attribute error, because no setter exists. Add a setter and you can check a value on assignment, while callers keep writing the same plain line.

check.q: A trip has fare 100 and 8 km. The fare is then changed to 120. What does fare_per_km return on the next read?
opts: 12.5, the value cached at creation
15.0, recomputed from the current fare
An AttributeError
check.why: A plain property stores nothing. It runs the method on each read, so it uses the current fare: 120 divided by 8 is 15.

work: Replace a stored, hand-updated derived field with a property so it cannot drift out of sync.
Add a guard for zero or missing denominators in every ratio property.

p04.title: Property traps interviewers probe

beats.say: Why can a harmless looking property crash your program with a recursion error?

show.sub: From a setter that looks innocent

beats.say: Because a setter that assigns to its own public name calls itself forever. Store the real value under an underscore name, like underscore fare, and let the property guard it.

chip.text: set fare inside set fare loops forever

beats.say: That underscore is only a convention. Python does not stop anyone reading it. Also, if the constructor assigns through the public name, the setter validates there too, so bad data is rejected at birth.

show.title: Convention and construction
items: Underscore means please do not touch
It is not enforced by Python
Assign via the public name in init to validate early

beats.say: Last, a property runs on every read. Divide by a zero distance and it crashes, so guard it. And a database call here would run on every glance, silently.

chip.text: Looks cheap, costs a call each time

check.q: A setter for fare contains the line self.fare = value after a check. What happens?
opts: It infinitely recurses, because it calls the same setter
It stores the value normally
The property becomes read only
check.why: Assigning to self.fare inside the fare setter triggers the setter again, forever. Store to a separate name such as _fare.

work: Review every setter and confirm it writes to a separate underscore attribute.
Search for properties that touch files, networks or databases and turn them into explicit methods.

p04.title: When to use properties, and when not

beats.say: Should every attribute get a getter and setter, just in case?

show.text: Getters and setters, just in case?

beats.say: No. Start with plain attributes. If you later need logic, turn one into a property, and no caller changes. That is the real payoff: you can defer the decision without breaking anyone.
Know the limits. Anything slow, like a query or an API call, belongs in an explicit method, where the name warns of the cost. For a costly value read many times, cache it once with cached property.

chip.text: Readers assume attribute access is cheap

beats.say: For validating records at a pipeline boundary, a schema library or frozen data class is cleaner than hand written setters. Use properties for small derived values, not as your validation framework.

show.title: Choose the right tool
items: Schema library or frozen data class: validate records at the boundary

check.q: Which is the best fit for a plain property?
opts: Fetching a driver's rating from the database
Fare per km computed from two stored numbers
Calling a web API for today's exchange rate
check.why: A property should be cheap and side-effect free. Dividing two stored numbers fits. Queries and API calls should be explicit methods so the cost is visible.

work: Add a review rule: no I/O or side effects inside a property.
Use cached_property or an explicit method for expensive derived values, and note when the cache could go stale.
Validate incoming pipeline records with a schema tool instead of custom setters.

p04.title: Labels on the boxes

beats.say: Ever opened a moving box with no label, and found kitchen knives inside?
A type hint is a label on the box. It says what goes in, and what comes out. Python itself never reads the label. It just runs your code anyway.
But a checker tool, like mypy, or your editor, reads every label before the code runs. Promise a number, hand over a word, and it flags the mistake, like a mover stopping at the door.
So the label does two jobs. It tells the next person what you meant. And it catches mistakes early, while they are still cheap to fix.

show.title: Two jobs
items: Documents intent for the next reader

check.q: What does Python do with type hints when it runs your code?
opts: Rejects wrong types
Ignores them; tools like mypy use them
Converts values to the hinted type
check.why: Hints are notes for people and checkers. Python does not enforce them at runtime.

work: Add hints to the signature of one function you wrote this week.
Run mypy or turn on your editor's type checking and read what it flags.

p04.title: Reading a typed signature

beats.say: What does a function signature with hints actually promise?
Take top cities. It takes a list of dicts, and an int k, defaulting to three. It returns a list of pairs, each a city name and a count. Anyone reading it knows the shape without opening the body.

show.title: Shape without the body
show.text: def top_cities(trips: list[dict], k: int = 3) -> list[tuple[str, int]]: ...
show.note: input shape, default, output shape

beats.say: Now find. It returns a Trip or None. That pipe None means it may come back empty. The checker then forces you to handle the empty case before you touch the trip, which stops the classic none has no attribute crash.

Last, Iterable and Callable. Iterable says anything you can loop over. Callable says a function taking a dict and returning a dict. Accept general types like Iterable, so lists, sets and generators all work.

show.title: Accept general, return specific
items: Iterable: anything you can loop over
Callable: a function dict in, dict out
Lists, sets, generators all fit Iterable

check.q: A function returns Trip | None. What does the checker make you do?
opts: Handle None before using the trip
Convert None to zero
Nothing, it only warns at runtime
check.why: The checker flags any use of the result that assumes it is not None, preventing attribute errors on None.

work: Mark every function that can return nothing with | None.
Change list parameters to Iterable where you only loop over them.

p04.title: When hints lie

beats.say: If Python ignores type hints, what stops a wrong one from running?

Nothing. At runtime the hints are just notes. Pass a string where an int was promised, and Python happily runs it, and may fail ten lines later with a confusing error. Only the checker, run in your editor or in the build, catches it.

Two gotchas. First, a bare list of dict says nothing about the keys inside, so a typo in a key still slips through. A typed dictionary or a class fixes that. Second, hints can lie. If the function can return None and you wrote Trip, the checker trusts you.

show.title: Two gotchas
items: list of dict hides the keys: use a typed dict or class
A hint can lie, and the checker trusts it

beats.say: So run the checker in your build, so a wrong hint fails the pull request, not production. And keep hints honest.

check.q: A function can return None but is hinted as returning Trip. What happens?
opts: Python raises an error at runtime
The checker trusts the hint and misses bugs
The hint is auto-corrected
check.why: Checkers trust declared types, so a dishonest hint hides real None bugs.

work: Add a type checker step to your CI so wrong hints fail the pull request.
Replace list of dict with a TypedDict or dataclass where keys matter.

p04.title: How strict, and where

beats.say: Should every function in your codebase be fully typed?

Mostly yes, and strictness should rise with the code's lifespan and reach. Shared libraries, pipeline interfaces, and anything other teams call deserve strict checking. A throwaway notebook does not. Adopt it gradually, module by module, and fail the build only on typed code.

Hints are not validation. They vanish at runtime, so data arriving from files or APIs still needs real checking with something like Pydantic, which enforces the types when data enters the system. Hints cover your code. Validation covers the outside world.

In AI work, hints double as contracts. Tool frameworks read your signature to tell the model what arguments a tool takes. A vague type means a vague tool, and the model guesses. Precise types are cheap, and they steer the model.

show.title: Hints as tool schemas
items: Vague type, vague tool, model guesses

check.q: Data arrives from an external API with unknown quality. What protects you?
opts: Type hints alone
Runtime validation like Pydantic at the boundary
A bigger mypy strictness setting
check.why: Hints vanish at runtime, so untrusted input needs real validation where it enters.

work: Pick strict checking for shared libraries and loosen it for scratch code.
Validate external data at the boundary, then trust the typed core.
Give agent tool functions precise hints so the generated schema is clear.

p04.title: The kitchen that never gets rebuilt

beats.say: Ever wonder how a restaurant adds a new dish without rebuilding its kitchen?
Each person has one job. The chef cooks, the waiter serves, the cashier takes payment. If the cashier also cooks, one bad day breaks everything.
New dish? Add a recipe card. Nobody rewrites the kitchen rules. A design round gives you about an hour to build something small, like a parking lot, using this same habit.

show.title: The habit
items: Add a card, do not rewrite rules
Swap a chef, nothing else changes
Small system, built in an hour

check.q: In the restaurant analogy, what does adding a new dish by adding a recipe card represent?
opts: Rewriting the whole system
Extending behaviour by adding a new piece without editing old ones
Hiring more cashiers
Removing the waiter
check.why: Adding a card leaves existing rules untouched, which mirrors extending software by adding a class instead of changing working code.

work: Pick one class you own and list every job it does; circle any that could be separate.
Next time you add a feature, try adding a new class or function before editing an existing branch.

p04.title: Building a parking lot in sixty minutes

beats.say: You have sixty minutes to build a parking lot. Where do you start?
Spend the first five minutes asking questions. Which operations: park, leave, pay? How many spots? What might change, like pricing?
Then split into classes. The lot finds spots. A ticket records entry time. A pricing strategy computes the fee. One class, one job.
Hourly rate, flat rate, weekend rate each become a small class with the same method. The lot calls that method and never checks which kind it is. Finish with a demo and one change request.

check.q: Why does the lot call one fee method on any pricing class instead of checking its type?
opts: It runs faster
New pricing types can be added without editing the lot
Types cannot be checked in Python
It saves memory
check.why: Because every pricing class offers the same method, the lot stays unchanged when you add a new one.

work: Practise a parking lot or rate limiter with a timer: five minutes of questions, then code.
Write down the one thing most likely to change in your design and hide it behind a small interface.

p04.title: Why working code still fails

beats.say: Why do interviewers fail candidates whose code works?
Because of the if elif chain. Every new pricing type means editing the working function, and each edit can break old cases. Open for extension, closed for modification means adding a class instead.

show.title: The smell
show.text:
if kind == 'hourly': ...
elif kind == 'flat': ...
elif kind == 'weekend': ...

beats.say: Another trap: the lot builds its own price calculator inside. Then you cannot test it with a fake. Pass in anything that matches a Protocol, which is just a list of methods it must have. That is dependency inversion.
Also ask about two cars arriving at once. Without a lock, both can grab the last spot. And do not invent ten patterns for a two-class problem.

show.title: More gotchas
items: Race: two cars, one last spot
Use a lock around spot assignment

check.q: What is the main testing benefit of passing a pricing object into the lot instead of creating it inside?
opts: Fewer lines of code
You can inject a fake with a known fee
Pricing runs in parallel
It removes the need for classes
check.why: Injected dependencies can be replaced by fakes, so you test the lot alone with predictable fees.

work: Review your last design for hidden constructors inside classes and move them to arguments.
Ask in every round what happens if two requests arrive at the same instant.

p04.title: When clean design is too much

beats.say: When is clean object design the wrong answer?

A Strategy class for every rule costs files, names and indirection. If there are two rules and they rarely change, a plain function is cheaper and easier to read. Add the pattern when the third variant appears.
Observer sounds nice for notifications, but it hides who reacts and in what order. If a subscriber fails, does the sender fail too? Decide, and say so.
Also state the limit. An in-memory design lives in one process. At many servers, you need a shared store and locks, so say what you would change. Show judgment, not pattern count.

show.title: Say the limits
items: Many servers need a shared store

check.q: When is a plain function a better choice than a Strategy class hierarchy?
opts: When there are many variants that change often
When there are very few stable rules
When you need testing
When using Protocols
check.why: With few, stable rules the extra classes add indirection without benefit; introduce the pattern once variants grow.

work: For each pattern in your design, write one sentence on the change it protects against.
End every design answer by naming what breaks at ten servers and what you would swap in.

p04.title: Parts, not family trees

beats.say: Why do engineers say build with parts, not family trees?
Think of a family tree. A child inherits from a parent, who inherited from a grandparent. Change something at the top, and every descendant feels it.

show.title: A change at the *top* ripples down

beats.say: Now think of LEGO. A car has wheels, an engine and a body. Each piece snaps in. Swap the wheels and nothing else changes.

chip.text: Swap one part, the rest stays

beats.say: Code works the same way. Composition means an object has parts. Inheritance means an object is a kind of another thing. Parts are easier to swap, so they break less.

show.title: Two ways to relate things
items: Parts swap easily and break less

check.q: A Pipeline is built from a source, steps and a sink passed in. Which idea is this?
opts: Inheritance, because Pipeline is a kind of source
Composition, because Pipeline has parts
Neither, it is just a function
check.why: The Pipeline holds other objects as parts it has, which is composition. It is not a kind of source.

work: Look at one class in your codebase and say aloud whether it is a kind of something or has something.
Find a base class with many subclasses and list what would break if you changed the base.

p04.title: How a Pipeline is composed

beats.say: How does one small class run any pipeline you can imagine?
Pipeline holds three things: a source, a list of steps, and a sink. It does no reading or writing itself. It only coordinates.
Run loops over rows. Say the source gives one thousand rows and you have three steps. Each row passes through all three steps, then the sink writes it. That is three thousand step calls.
Want to read from an API instead of a CSV? Pass a different source. The Pipeline code does not change a single line, because it only calls read.

show.title: Swap the source
show.text:
Pipeline(CsvSource(path), steps, sink)
Pipeline(ApiSource(url), steps, sink)
show.note: Pipeline code is unchanged

check.q: You switch from a CSV source to an API source. What changes in Pipeline.run?
opts: Nothing, it only calls read
You add a branch for the API
You make ApiSource inherit from CsvSource
check.why: Pipeline depends only on the read method, so any object offering it can be plugged in without touching run.

work: Rewrite one script that mixes reading, cleaning and writing so each part is a separate object or function.
Write a Pipeline test that passes a list of three dicts as the source.

p04.title: Duck typing, Protocols and gotchas

beats.say: What happens if you pass a source with no read method?

show.sub: Python will not warn you early

beats.say: Python does duck typing. It never checks the class, only whether the method exists. So the failure is an AttributeError, and it fires when run reaches that call, maybe after half your data moved.
A Protocol writes the expected method down, such as read returning rows. Your type checker catches the mistake before you run. But at runtime Python still does not enforce it, so tests matter.

show.title: Protocol
show.note: Checked by the type checker, not at runtime

beats.say: Also watch shared state. If a step keeps a counter inside itself, two pipelines using that step will mix their numbers. And a source that returns a generator can be read only once.

show.title: Gotchas
items: Protocol checks happen in the type checker only
Steps holding state get shared by reuse
Generators are consumed after one read

check.q: You add a Protocol called Source and run with an object lacking read. When does it fail?
opts: At class definition, Python enforces Protocols
In the type checker if you run one, otherwise at runtime when read is called
Never, Python skips missing methods
check.why: Protocols are for static checkers. Python itself only fails with AttributeError when the missing method is actually called.

work: Run a type checker such as mypy in CI so Protocol mistakes fail before deploy.
Make steps stateless, or build a fresh one per pipeline.
Have sources return a fresh iterator on each read call.

p04.title: When to compose, when to inherit

beats.say: When is inheritance still the right answer?
Use it for one shallow level: an abstract base that holds shared logic, like retries, with subclasses filling in one method. Python then refuses to build a subclass that forgets it.

chip.text: Shared logic, one method to fill

beats.say: Choose composition when behaviours vary independently, like source, rules and sink. Three sources times four sinks is twelve subclasses, but only seven parts when composed.
The cost is wiring and indirection. Someone must assemble the parts, and a stack trace crosses many small objects. For a one-off script, a plain function beats both.

show.title: Costs of composition
items: Tiny scripts do not need either

beats.say: The reward is testing. You pass in a fake source with ten rows and need no real system.

check.q: You have 3 sources and 4 sinks that vary independently. What is the best design?
opts: 12 subclasses, one per pair
One base class with flags for every case
Compose a pipeline from 3 source and 4 sink parts
check.why: Composition needs only 7 parts that combine freely, while subclassing multiplies into 12 and grows with each addition.

work: Limit inheritance in your code to one level from an abstract base.
Inject sources and sinks into jobs so tests can pass in fakes.
Before adding a class, ask if a plain function would do.

p05.title: Busy line or wrong number

beats.say: You call a friend and the line is busy. Should you try again? Now imagine you dialed a number that does not exist. Should you try again?
A busy line fixes itself. Wait a bit, and it is free. That is a transient error, one that goes away on its own. Network blips and rate limits are like this. So you retry.

A number that does not exist will never connect. Redialing a hundred times just wastes your afternoon. A missing field or a bad file is the same. Do not retry. Raise the error right away so someone fixes it.
Between tries, wait a little longer each time, so you never hammer a struggling line.

show.title: Wait longer each time
items: Give up after a few tries

check.q: Which failure is worth retrying?
opts: A missing column in a file
A short network blip
A typo in a dictionary key
check.why: A network blip passes by itself, so waiting and retrying works. The other two are bugs or bad data and fail the same way every time.

work: List the errors your jobs hit last month and mark each as transient or a bug.
Check that your code raises bad data errors immediately instead of looping.

p05.title: Backoff and jitter in numbers

beats.say: A thousand clients all fail at once. If every one retries after exactly two seconds, what happens?

The server gets another thousand requests in the same instant, and falls over again. That is a retry storm. The fix is exponential backoff. Wait one second, then two, then four, then eight. Each wait doubles, giving the server room to recover.

Backoff alone still lines clients up. So add jitter, a random extra wait. Client one waits two point three seconds, client two waits one point seven. Now the thousand retries spread across a window instead of landing together.
Cap the attempts, say five, then raise the last error. Retry only transient types like connection and timeout errors.

show.title: The shape of it

check.q: Why add jitter on top of exponential backoff?
opts: So the waits are longer
So clients do not all retry at the same moment
So errors are logged
check.why: Without randomness, clients that failed together still retry together on every round. Jitter spreads them out.

work: Add random jitter to every retry loop you own.
Cap attempts and total wait time so retries always end.

p05.title: Retry traps interviewers probe

beats.say: Your retry loop catches every exception. What could go wrong?

A KeyError is a bug. Retrying it five times just delays the crash by thirty seconds and hides the cause. So catch only a named tuple, like connection error and timeout error. Anything else propagates at once.

Second trap: the operation itself. If a payment call timed out, it may have succeeded. Retrying could charge twice. Retried work must be idempotent, meaning running it twice has the same effect as once.
Third, off by one errors. After the last failed attempt, do not sleep. Just raise the original error. And to test it, inject sleep, so tests record the waits instead of actually waiting.

show.title: Edge cases
items: No sleep after the final attempt
Pass sleep in; tests use a list append

check.q: A payment call times out. What must be true before you retry it?
opts: The call is idempotent or carries a unique key
The wait is exactly one second
You catch every exception
check.why: A timeout does not tell you the work failed. Without idempotency, a retry may repeat a side effect like a charge.

work: Search your code for bare except blocks around retries and replace them with named exceptions.
Add idempotency keys to retried writes and payments.
Write a test that passes a fake sleep and asserts the exact delays.

p05.title: When retries make outages worse

beats.say: Three services call each other, and each retries three times. How many requests hit the database?
Up to twenty seven, from one user click. Retries multiply across layers, and they hit a database that is already struggling. Retry at one layer only, usually the layer closest to the failing call.

Add guardrails. A retry budget caps retries at, say, ten percent of traffic. A circuit breaker stops calling a dependency that is clearly down. And a total deadline stops retries outliving the user's patience.

show.title: Guardrails
items: Retry budget: about 10 percent of traffic

beats.say: For long outages, in process retries are the wrong tool. Put the job on a queue with a dead letter queue, so failed work waits and can be replayed hours later.

check.q: A dependency is down for two hours. What is the best design?
opts: Retry in each service up to ten times
Queue the work with a dead letter queue and replay later
Remove the timeout
check.why: In-process retries cannot outlast a long outage and add load. A queue holds the work durably, and a dead letter queue lets you replay it once the dependency recovers.

work: Map which layers in your call chain retry and pick one owner.
Add a circuit breaker and a total deadline to your busiest outbound call.
Route permanently failing jobs to a dead letter queue with an alert.

p05.title: The kitchen that hides its mistakes

beats.say: What if your program hit a problem, and quietly carried on as if nothing happened?
Picture a kitchen sorting order tickets. One ticket has no price. A good cook sets it aside, writes it on a list, and keeps cooking. That is catching one specific problem you know how to handle.
A bad cook throws a blanket over the whole kitchen. Burnt toast, a fire, a missing chef: all ignored. Dinner goes out wrong and nobody knows. That is catching every error.
So in code, name the exact problem you expect and handle only that. Let anything surprising stop the job with a loud message. A loud failure is cheaper than quiet wrong data.

show.title: The habit
items: Let surprises stop the job loudly

check.q: A cook finds one ticket with no price. Which response matches good error handling?
opts: Throw away every ticket and start again
Set that ticket aside, note it on a list, keep cooking
Ignore it and hope nobody notices
check.why: Handle the specific, expected problem visibly and carry on. Hiding it or overreacting both cause worse outcomes.

work: Find one place in your code that catches every error and list what it could hide.
Write down the exact problems you expect in your data, such as missing fields or bad numbers.

p05.title: How Python picks an except clause

beats.say: Ten thousand rows, and one has the amount abc. What does Python do when int fails to read it?

show.title: One risky line

beats.say: Python raises a ValueError. That stops the line and Python scans the except clauses from top to bottom, picking the first one whose type matches.

A missing amount key raises KeyError instead, so it lands in a different branch: log a warning, set amount to None. For bad text, raise your own BadRow, chained from the original error, so the traceback keeps the real cause.
The else block runs only when nothing failed. The finally block always runs, for cleanup. Keep the try around that one line, so you always know what failed.

check.q: A row has no amount key at all. Which clause runs in the example?
opts: except ValueError
except KeyError
else
check.why: A missing dictionary key raises KeyError. Python matches by exception type, not by what you meant.

work: Shrink any try block that wraps more than the one line that can fail.
Use raise ... from e whenever you wrap an error in your own type.

p05.title: Bare except and other traps

beats.say: Why does a job with a bare except refuse to stop when you press Control C?

show.sub: a bare except is the cause

beats.say: Because Control C raises KeyboardInterrupt, which sits beside Exception, not under it. A bare except catches it. Even except Exception swallows a NameError from a typo, so a bug becomes a skipped row and quietly wrong data.
Make BadRow a subclass of ValueError. Old callers catching ValueError still work, new callers can catch BadRow alone. Order your clauses specific first, because the first match wins.
If you skip a row, count it and log it, or send it to a dead-letter store. Otherwise a five percent loss looks exactly like a healthy run.

show.title: Never swallow silently
items: Log the row id and reason
Or send it to a dead-letter store

check.q: Why is except Exception around a whole job still dangerous?
opts: It catches Control C
It also swallows bugs like NameError, turning them into silent wrong data
It makes the job slower
check.why: Exception does not include KeyboardInterrupt, but it does include programming bugs, which then hide as skipped rows.

work: Search your repo for bare except and except Exception and review each one.
Add a skipped-row counter and log it at the end of every job.

p05.title: Fail fast or skip: the architect call

beats.say: A million rows arrive, two thousand are bad. Do you fail the whole job, or skip them?

It depends on what wrong data costs. For payments, fail fast. For clickstream, quarantine bad rows in a dead-letter store, but set a threshold, say one percent. Above that, abort, because something upstream broke.

chip.text: Cost of wrong sets the policy

beats.say: Catch only at boundaries, where you can decide to retry, skip or abort. Retry transient errors like timeouts, never bad data, since retrying a bad row never fixes it.

show.title: Where to catch
items: Only at boundaries that can decide

beats.say: Raising an exception per bad row is slow at millions of rows. For bulk loads, validate with a schema or a set-based check first, and route failures in one pass.

check.q: A nightly job quarantines bad rows. Suddenly 40 percent are bad. What should it do?
opts: Keep quarantining and finish
Abort and alert, since a threshold breach signals an upstream break
Retry each bad row three times
check.why: A sudden jump means a systemic cause, not stray bad rows. Retrying bad data never fixes it, and finishing hides the break.

work: Set a bad-row percentage threshold per pipeline, based on what wrong data costs.
Alert on dead-letter volume, not just job failure.
Move bulk validation into a schema check instead of per-row try blocks.

p05.title: Logging is a ship's logbook

beats.say: Why does a ship's captain keep a logbook instead of just shouting updates across the deck?
A shout has no time, no urgency, and no name attached. A logbook entry says when it happened, how serious it was, and who wrote it.

Python's print is the shout. It just dumps text on screen. Logging is the logbook. Every message automatically carries a timestamp, a severity level, and the name of the part of the program that wrote it.

Severity works like a dial. Debug is fine detail for investigating. Info is normal milestones. Warning is something odd. Error is a failure. The person running the program turns the dial up or down, and nobody edits the code.

show.title: The severity dial
items: Operators turn the dial, no code change

check.q: What does a log message give you that print does not?
opts: Faster output
A timestamp, a severity level and the source
Automatic encryption
check.why: Logging attaches time, level and source to every message, and lets operators control detail without editing code.

work: Find one print call in your pipeline code and replace it with a log call.
Decide which of your messages are milestones and which are only detail.

p05.title: How a log line gets made

beats.say: How do you turn one line of code into a log line with a time, level and source?
At the top of each module, get a logger named after the module. Then configure once, at startup: set the level to info, and a format with time, level, name and message.
Now call info with loaded 50000 rows into orders. It prints with a timestamp, the word INFO, and the module name. A debug call is silently dropped, because debug sits below info.
Pass values as arguments, not inside an f string. Logging only builds the text if the message passes the level check, so a million skipped debug calls cost almost nothing.

show.title: Lazy formatting
items: Pass the format and the values separately
Text is built only if the level passes
A million skipped debug calls stay cheap
An f string always builds the text first

check.q: Why pass values as arguments instead of using an f string in a log call?
opts: The text is built only if the message passes the level check
It makes the log line colored
It stops the traceback being printed
check.why: Arguments are formatted lazily, so skipped messages cost almost nothing.

work: Configure logging once in your entry point, with time, level and name in the format.
Create a logger per module using the module name.

p05.title: Logging traps that bite in production

beats.say: You caught an error, logged it with error, and the traceback vanished. Why?
Error records only your message. Inside an except block, call log dot exception instead. It logs at error level and attaches the full traceback, the chain of calls that led to the failure.
Second gotcha: basic config does nothing if the root logger already has handlers, so a library that configures first silently wins. Configure once, in the entry point, never inside library modules.

show.title: Config gotcha
items: Basic config is skipped if handlers already exist
A library that configures first silently wins
Configure only in the entry point
Library modules just get a logger

beats.say: Third: secrets and personal data. A logged password or email lives in log storage for months and is copied to many systems. Log ids, never the values. And in production, log JSON fields like run id, table, and rows so you can search and count them.

check.q: You catch an exception in a pipeline step and want the full traceback in the logs. What do you call inside the except block?
opts: log.info with the error text
log.exception
print the error
check.why: log.exception logs at error level and attaches the traceback automatically.

work: Search your code for except blocks that log only a message and switch them to log.exception.
Check that no log call includes tokens, passwords or personal data.

p05.title: Logs have a bill and a limit

beats.say: Is logging every row a good idea at ten million rows an hour?
No. Log volume is a bill. Log stores charge per gigabyte ingested, and slow synchronous handlers can stall your pipeline. Log milestones and counts per batch, not per row. Sample the rest.

chip.text: Log per batch, sample the rest

beats.say: Logs are not metrics. If you want an alert when rows loaded drops, emit a metric, a number that is cheap to store and fast to query. Use logs to explain why, metrics to tell you that.

chip.text: Alert on metrics, diagnose with logs

beats.say: Standardize across teams: one JSON schema, a run id on every line, and a correlation id passed between services. Then one search follows a failure across the whole pipeline, and your on-call tooling gets clean evidence to diagnose from.

show.title: Standardize
items: One JSON schema for every team
A run id on every line
A correlation id passed between services
One search follows a failure end to end

check.q: You need an alert when rows loaded per hour drops sharply. What is the best fit?
opts: Log each row and count lines by hand
Emit a metric and alert on it, keeping logs for the cause
Raise the log level to debug
check.why: Metrics are cheap and fast to query for alerting. Logs then explain why it happened.

work: Estimate your monthly log volume in gigabytes and what it costs.
Define a shared JSON log schema with run id and correlation id.
Move count-based alerts from log searches to metrics.

p05.title: A robot inspector for your code

beats.say: How do you know your code still works after you change it? You could check by hand every time. Or you could hire a tiny robot inspector.

Think of a bakery. Before any tray goes out, a worker checks one thing: is this cookie sweet, round, and cooked? A test is that check, written as code. pytest is the worker who walks the whole kitchen and runs every check.

chip.text: A test is a check written as code

beats.say: You only need two habits. Name your files starting with test underscore, and name your checks the same way. Then write assert, which just means, I claim this is true. If the claim is false, pytest shouts and tells you which one.

show.title: Two habits
items: Name files and checks starting with test_
Write assert: I claim this is true
False claim means pytest shouts and names it

check.q: What does the word assert mean in a pytest test?
opts: Run this file twice
Claim that something is true, and fail loudly if it is not
Skip this check for now
check.why: An assert states a claim. If the claim is false, pytest reports the failure and shows which check broke.

work: Pick one small function you rely on and write one test for it in a file starting with test_.
Run pytest after your next change instead of checking by hand.

p05.title: How pytest finds and runs tests

beats.say: How does pytest know what to run, and how do you test three bad inputs without writing three tests?

pytest walks your folders and picks up files named test underscore star dot py. Inside, it runs every function starting with test. Plain assert is enough. If parse amount of rupee twelve fifty returns twelve point five, it passes. Otherwise you see both values side by side.

Parametrize runs one test over many inputs. Give it three bad strings and you get three separate results, each named. A fixture builds shared data, like a list of two sample rows, and pytest hands it to any test that asks by name.

chip.text: Fixture is passed in by name

check.q: You want to check that three different bad strings all raise BadAmount. What is the cleanest way?
opts: Write one test with a loop that stops at the first failure
Use parametrize so each input is its own named test result
Copy the test three times
check.why: Parametrize gives one test body and a separate pass or fail for each input, so you see exactly which input broke.

work: Replace any copy-pasted tests that differ only by input with one parametrized test.
Move repeated sample data into a fixture.

p05.title: What your passing tests still miss

beats.say: Your tests all pass, yet production breaks. What did they miss?

Usually the edges. Empty input, None, duplicates, boundary values, and the failure path. Test that a bad row lands in the dead letter list, not just that good rows load. Use pytest raises to prove the right error is thrown, not just any error.

show.title: Test the edges
items: Failure path: bad row goes to dead letter

beats.say: Keep tests isolated. tmp_path gives each test its own temporary folder, so files never leak between tests. monkeypatch swaps an environment variable or function, then restores it afterward. Without that, one test's change can break another, and failures depend on run order.
Also compare floats with pytest approx, because point one plus point two is not exactly point three.

check.q: A test passes alone but fails when the whole suite runs. What is the most likely cause?
opts: pytest is too slow
Shared state, such as a changed environment variable or file, leaking between tests
The assert keyword is broken
check.why: Tests that share state depend on run order. tmp_path and monkeypatch give each test its own clean, restored setup.

work: Use tmp_path for any test that writes files, and monkeypatch for environment variables.
Add a test for empty input and one for the failure path to each pipeline function.

p05.title: Choosing how much to test, and where

beats.say: Why do pipelines with a thousand passing tests still ship bad data?

show.text: Code tests are not data tests

beats.say: Because code tests check logic, not the data. Build three layers. Many unit tests of pure functions, running in milliseconds. A few integration tests against a real local database or DuckDB. Then data quality checks on real tables, which catch what no fixture imagined.

The trade-off is speed against realism. Mocks are fast but can lie about how the database behaves. So mock only at the edges you don't own, like a paid API, and use real DuckDB for your SQL. Keep the pure logic separate from input and output, so most of it needs no setup at all.

chip.text: Mock only what you don't own

check.q: Your pipeline's SQL transforms are heavily mocked and all tests pass, but a join duplicates rows in production. What is the best fix?
opts: Add more mocks of the database
Run the SQL in an integration test against real DuckDB and add a data quality check for duplicate keys
Delete the unit tests
check.why: Mocks cannot show how real SQL behaves. A real local engine tests the join, and a data quality check catches duplicates on actual tables.

work: Separate pure transformation functions from code that reads or writes, so they can be unit tested without setup.
Add one DuckDB integration test per critical SQL transform.
Add a duplicate-key and null check on your most important output table.

p05.title: Why it worked on my laptop

beats.say: Why does a program work on your laptop, then break on the server?
Think of a kitchen. Each project gets its own kitchen, with its own pots and ingredients. That is a virtual environment. It stops one project's tools from messing with another's.
The recipe card lists exact brands and amounts. That is pinning. Next month, a new brand cannot spoil dinner.
And the safe combination is never written on the recipe. It sits in a drawer, outside the card. That is config from the environment.

check.q: In the kitchen analogy, what does pinning dependencies protect you from?
opts: A new release of a library changing behaviour unexpectedly
Someone reading your password
Your laptop running out of disk space
check.why: Pinning fixes exact versions, like an exact brand on the recipe, so a new release cannot silently change a working job.

work: Check that every project you run has its own virtual environment, not the system Python.
Find one password or URL written inside code and note where it should live instead.

p05.title: Layout, venv, lock and config step by step

beats.say: How do you make a Python job run the same way on every machine?
First, create a virtual environment: python three, dash m, venv, dot venv. It is a private folder holding its own packages, so installs never touch the system Python.

show.title: Isolate
show.note: Packages now install into .venv only

beats.say: Second, lay out the project. A source folder holds the package, a tests folder holds the tests, and pyproject dot toml lists name, version and dependencies. Third, pin versions in a lock file, so version two point one stays two point one, even after two point two ships.
Fourth, read settings from the environment. Code asks for WAREHOUSE URL at startup. Dev, test and prod each set a different value, and the code never changes.

check.q: Why does the job read WAREHOUSE_URL from the environment?
opts: It makes Python run faster
The same code can run in dev, test and prod with different values
It removes the need for a virtual environment
check.why: Config outside the code lets one unchanged build target different systems just by setting different values.

work: Create a pyproject.toml and a lock file for one job and rebuild its environment from scratch.
Replace one hard-coded connection string with an environment variable and add it to .env.example.

p05.title: Import side effects, silent defaults, leaked secrets

beats.say: What happens when you import a file that loads data on the first line?

It runs. Importing executes the whole file. So a test that imports your module could hit the real warehouse. Wrap the entry point in if name equals main, so it runs only when executed directly, not when imported.

Environment lookups have a trap too. Square bracket access fails loudly with a KeyError if the variable is missing. A get with a default silently carries on, and might point a job at the wrong database. For required settings, fail fast at startup.
And secrets: committing a dot env file puts the password in history forever. Deleting it later does not help. Commit dot env dot example with placeholders, and rotate any leaked key.

show.title: Secrets in *Git*
items: Leaked once means rotate the key

check.q: A required variable is missing in production. Which approach is safest?
opts: os.environ.get with a default pointing at dev
os.environ with square brackets, so the job fails at startup
Catch the error and carry on with an empty string
check.why: Failing fast with a KeyError stops the job before it does any damage, whereas a silent default can write to the wrong place.

work: Add a main guard to every module that currently does work on import.
Run a secrets scanner over your repository history and rotate anything it finds.

p05.title: Where config lives and how far layout scales

beats.say: Is an environment variable always the right home for config?

For a handful of settings, yes. It is simple and works everywhere, containers included. But environment variables are plain text, visible to anyone who can inspect the process, and they get dumped into crash logs.

show.title: Env vars: *good* and *risky*
items: Plain text, visible to process inspectors

beats.say: At scale, use a secrets manager. Jobs fetch short-lived credentials at runtime, access is audited, and rotation needs no redeploy. Cost is one more dependency, and a failure mode if it is down.

Same for layout. One package per job is simple. With fifty jobs, share a library, but version it, or one change breaks everyone. Pin each job, and rebuild the lock on a schedule so you still get security fixes.

show.title: Layout at *fifty jobs*
items: Each job pins its own lock file
Scheduled lock rebuilds for security fixes

check.q: When is a secrets manager worth its extra dependency over plain environment variables?
opts: Never, environment variables are always better
When you need auditing, rotation without redeploys, and many jobs sharing credentials
Only when the project has fewer than three settings
check.why: Auditing, short-lived credentials and easy rotation matter as jobs and people multiply; for a few settings the extra moving part is not worth it.

work: List which of your secrets could be rotated today without a redeploy.
Decide a schedule for rebuilding lock files so pinned jobs still receive security patches.

p05.title: The library book promise

beats.say: Ever left a tap running or a fridge door open? Code does that too, and it costs real money.

A with block is like borrowing a library book with a promise attached. You take the book, you read, and the librarian makes sure it goes back on the shelf, even if you spill coffee on it or run out in a panic.

In code, the book is a file, a lock, or a database connection. If you forget to close them, they stay stuck open, and other work waits in line. The with block does the closing for you, every single time.

show.title: Things that must be given back

check.q: What is the main promise of a with block?
opts: Your code runs faster
Cleanup runs even if the body fails
Errors are never raised
check.why: With guarantees the teardown step, such as closing a file or releasing a lock, whether the body succeeds or fails. It does not speed things up or hide errors.

work: Find places in your code that open files or connections without a with block.
Replace manual close calls with with statements.

p05.title: What with really calls

beats.say: What actually happens when Python meets the word with?

First it calls a method named enter. That does the setup, like opening a file or starting a transaction. Then your indented code runs. When it ends, Python calls exit, and exit gets three things: the error type, the error, and the traceback. On a clean finish, all three are None.

chip.text: Clean exit: all three are None

beats.say: Here is a transaction. Enter sends BEGIN. Exit sends COMMIT if the error type is None, and ROLLBACK otherwise. So a hundred row load either lands whole or not at all.
For short cases, use the contextmanager decorator. Code before yield is setup. Code after is teardown. Wrap yield in try finally so teardown runs on errors too.

show.title: Generator version

check.q: In a class based context manager, what does exit receive when the body finishes without error?
opts: Three None values
A True flag
The return value of the body
check.why: Exit gets exc_type, exc and tb. On a clean exit all three are None, which is how a transaction knows to commit.

work: Write a small Transaction class and watch exit receive None versus an error.
Turn a repeated setup and teardown pair into a contextmanager function.

p05.title: Swallowed errors and missing finally

beats.say: What happens to your error if exit returns True?

It vanishes. Returning True tells Python the exception is handled, so the program carries on as if nothing broke. Return False, or nothing, and the error continues upward. A transaction class should almost always return False, otherwise a failed load looks like a success.

With the contextmanager decorator, there is a trap. An error is thrown into the generator at the yield line. Without try and finally, the teardown after yield never runs, and a lock stays held forever.

show.title: Generator trap
items: Errors are thrown in at yield

beats.say: Also, if exit itself raises, the new error takes over, and the original is only attached as context. Keep teardown simple.

show.sub: A failing exit hides the real cause

check.q: A contextmanager function has cleanup after yield but no try and finally. The body raises. What happens to the cleanup?
opts: It still runs
It is skipped
It runs twice
check.why: The exception is raised at the yield line, so code after it is skipped unless it sits in a finally block.

work: Audit your exit methods for return True and justify each one.
Check every contextmanager function wraps yield in try and finally.

p05.title: When with is the wrong tool

beats.say: When is a with block the wrong tool?

It only guards one scope. If a resource must outlive the function, like a connection pool shared by a service, or a stream handed to a caller, a with block closes it too early. Give the pool an owner, and close it at shutdown.
Also, a rollback cannot undo side effects outside the database. An email sent or a file uploaded inside the transaction stays. Keep those after commit, or make them idempotent.
For many resources, use ExitStack to enter a dynamic number of them and unwind in reverse. For async code, use async with. Prefer with over try finally, because reviewers see the cleanup in one line.

check.q: A transaction block uploads a file to cloud storage, then the database commit fails and rolls back. What is true?
opts: The upload is undone automatically
The upload stays, so do it after commit or make it idempotent
The upload never ran
check.why: Rollback only covers the database. External side effects remain, so order them after commit or design them to be safely repeated.

work: List side effects inside your transaction blocks and move them after commit.
Use ExitStack where the number of files or connections varies.
Give long lived pools a clear owner and a shutdown hook.

p06.title: Many kitchens, not one cook

beats.say: Imagine one chef chopping a thousand onions. Hiring a second chef in the same tiny kitchen doesn't help, if they must share one knife. So what does?
Give each chef their own kitchen, their own knife, their own board. Now four chefs chop four piles at once. In Python, each kitchen is a process, and it can use its own processor core.

chip.text: All cores work at the same time

beats.say: But there is a price. Opening a kitchen takes time, and passing ingredients between kitchens means packing them in boxes and copying them. So send a short order, like a pile number, and get back a small note, like the onion count.

chip.text: Copying big boxes erases the gain

check.q: In the kitchen picture, what is the best thing to hand each separate kitchen?
opts: The whole warehouse of onions
A short note saying which pile to chop
A copy of every other kitchen's results
check.why: Passing data between processes means copying it, so small inputs and small results keep the copying cost low and the parallel gain intact.

work: Think of one slow job at work that is pure calculation and could be split into independent piles.
Write down what each worker would receive and return, and check both are small.

p06.title: Eight cores, eight locks

beats.say: You have eight cores and eight hundred files, each taking two seconds of pure CPU. Why do threads take about twenty-six minutes, while processes take about three?
Each process has its own interpreter and its own GIL, the lock that lets only one thread run Python code at a time. Eight processes means eight locks, so eight cores work at once.
ProcessPoolExecutor starts one worker per core by default. Pool dot map sends each file path to a worker, which parses it and returns counts. Then you merge the counts.
Arguments and results are pickled, meaning turned into bytes and copied across. So pass paths, and return summaries.

show.title: Keep the traffic small
items: Pickled means turned into bytes and copied
Send a path, not the file contents

check.q: Why can eight processes beat eight threads on pure Python number crunching?
opts: Processes have faster memory
Each process has its own GIL, so all cores run Python at once
Threads cannot use more than one file
check.why: Threads in one process share a single GIL, so only one runs Python code at a time. Separate processes each have their own interpreter and GIL.

work: Benchmark your CPU-heavy loop with one worker, then with a process pool, and compare real timings.
Change the worker function to take a file path and return a small summary.

p06.title: Why your pool hangs on a Mac

beats.say: Your pool code works on Linux, then hangs or crashes on a Mac. Why?

show.text: Works on Linux. Breaks on macOS.

beats.say: On macOS and Windows, workers start by spawn. A fresh interpreter imports your script from the top. Without the main guard, each worker would try to start more workers, and everything blows up. So wrap the launch in if name equals main.

show.title: The main guard
show.note: Spawned workers re-import this file

beats.say: Functions must be top level, because pickle sends them by name. A lambda or nested function fails to pickle, and you get an error.
And watch size. Sending a two gigabyte DataFrame to each of eight workers copies sixteen gigabytes, and erases the gain. Startup also costs around a tenth of a second per worker, so tiny tasks lose.

check.q: Your pool task takes five milliseconds and you submit a million of them one by one. What is the likely result?
opts: Near-perfect speedup on all cores
Slower than a plain loop, because pickling and messaging dominate
It fails because of the GIL
check.why: Each task pays for pickling and inter-process messaging. When the work per task is tiny, that overhead exceeds the work. Batch tasks into larger chunks.

work: Add the main guard to every script that creates a process pool, and test it on macOS or Windows.
Give each task enough work, such as a whole file or a range of rows, to outweigh the copy cost.

p06.title: When a process pool is not the answer

beats.say: When should you not reach for a process pool?
It stops at one machine. Eight cores gives at best eight times faster, and memory is multiplied by the worker count. Past that, you need a cluster.

The shape you wrote, split, process, merge small results, is MapReduce. Spark executors work the same way: each task handles one partition and returns a partial result. So the design scales out when data outgrows one box.

But first, measure. If time goes to waiting on networks, use threads or asyncio. If NumPy or the database does the work in native code, you may need no processes. Choose processes for proven Python CPU work with small inputs and outputs.

show.title: Choose by bottleneck
items: Waiting on network: threads or asyncio
Native vectorised code: often no pool needed
Python CPU work, small data: processes
Beyond one machine: Spark or similar

check.q: A job is slow because it waits on thousands of API calls. What should you choose?
opts: A process pool with one worker per core
Threads or asyncio, since the wait is not CPU
Pickle the responses to speed things up
check.why: Waiting on I/O releases the GIL and uses no CPU, so threads or asyncio overlap the waits cheaply. Processes add copying and memory cost for no benefit.

work: Profile a slow job and label it CPU-bound, I/O-bound or native-code-bound before picking a tool.
Note the point where one machine's cores or memory run out, and what you would move to next.

p06.title: The buzzer and the kitchen

beats.say: Ever ordered at a food court and been handed a buzzer?
The buzzer is a promise of food later. Meanwhile you are free to do other things. In Python, that promise is called a future.
The kitchen has a fixed number of cooks. That is the pool. Extra orders wait in line, so the kitchen is never swamped.
When a buzzer goes off, you collect that meal. If the cook burned it, you only find out at pickup. And you can swap cooks sharing one kitchen for separate kitchens, without changing how you order.

show.title: Same way to order
items: Buzzer goes off: collect the meal
Burned meal: you learn at pickup

check.q: In the food court analogy, what does a future correspond to?
opts: The cook
The buzzer, a promise of a result later
The kitchen
The queue of waiting customers
check.why: A future is a placeholder you hold while the work happens elsewhere. It later holds a result or an error, just like a buzzer leads to your meal.

work: Spot one place in your code where you wait for slow calls one after another.
Say out loud what the future, the pool and the result are in that code.

p06.title: Submit, futures and as_completed

beats.say: You have one hundred URLs to fetch. How do you finish in seconds, not minutes?
Each fetch waits about half a second on the network. One after another, that is fifty seconds. A pool of eight threads overlaps the waiting, so it takes about six seconds.
Calling submit returns a future at once. It is a placeholder that later holds a result or an error. Calling result on it waits if needed, and re-raises any worker exception.
Map gives results in input order. As completed gives them the moment each finishes, so one slow URL never blocks the rest.

show.title: Pick your order
items: map: input order, first error on reach
submit plus as_completed: first done, first handled
Per-item try and except only with submit

check.q: You want to log each failed URL and keep going while others finish. What fits best?
opts: pool.map and one try around the loop
submit with as_completed and try around each result call
A single thread in a for loop
ProcessPoolExecutor with map
check.why: With submit and as_completed you handle each future when it finishes, and a try around result lets one failure be logged without stopping the others.

work: Time a sequential fetch loop, then the same with eight workers, and compare.
Replace a map call that hides failures with submit and as_completed plus per-item logging.

p06.title: Silent errors and hung pools

beats.say: Your worker threw an error, so why did your program stay silent?
With submit, the exception is stored inside the future. It only surfaces when you call result. If you never call it, the failure vanishes. Always wrap result in a try block.

Map is different. It raises the first error when you reach that item in order, and the remaining results are lost to your loop. Also, leaving the with block waits for every pending job, so a hung task hangs your program. Set timeouts.

show.title: Map and the with block
items: map raises at the failing item, in order
Later results are lost to your loop
Leaving with waits for all pending jobs
A hung task hangs the program: set timeouts

beats.say: Threads cannot stop a running job. Cancel only works on jobs still waiting in the queue. And processes need arguments and results that can be pickled, meaning turned into bytes, which costs time.

show.title: Limits
items: Cancel works only on queued jobs
Process pools need picklable inputs and outputs

check.q: You submit 50 jobs and never call result on the futures. One job raises an error. What happens?
opts: The program crashes immediately
The error is stored in the future and goes unnoticed
The pool retries the job automatically
All other jobs are cancelled
check.why: The exception lives inside the future until result or exception is called. Ignoring the futures means silent failure.

work: Audit every submit call and confirm each future has result called inside a try block.
Add a timeout to result calls and to any network call inside workers.

p06.title: When a pool is the wrong tool

beats.say: Is a thread pool the right tool for ten thousand calls?
Probably not. Each thread costs memory, so pools stay in the tens. For thousands of network calls, asyncio handles them on one thread with far less overhead.
For CPU work, swap in a process pool. But pickling and startup cost mean tiny tasks get slower. Batch work into chunks, and size workers to your core count.

show.title: CPU-bound work
items: Pickling and startup hurt tiny tasks

beats.say: Also respect the other side. Eight workers hitting one API can trigger rate limits, so pool size is a throttle. For retries, queues, and scheduling across machines, choose a task queue or Spark instead. One pool is for one machine.

check.q: You must make 20,000 small HTTP calls and later scale across several machines with retries. What is the best choice?
opts: ThreadPoolExecutor with 2,000 workers
ProcessPoolExecutor with map
asyncio for the calls, and a task queue or distributed framework to spread them
A single sequential loop
check.why: Asyncio handles huge counts of waiting I/O cheaply, and an executor cannot span machines or provide retries, so a queue or distributed framework fits the scale-out need.

work: Write down the rate limit of each API you call and set pool size below it.
Benchmark a process pool with chunked batches against per-item tasks before adopting it.

p06.title: Waiting versus working, in a kitchen

beats.say: Why can't ten extra cooks make water boil faster?

Because boiling is waiting. While the pot heats, one smart cook chops onions. That is concurrency: juggling jobs while one of them waits. Programs wait too, on web calls, database answers and file downloads.
Chopping is different. The cook is busy every second, so juggling does not help. You need more hands working at the same instant. That is parallelism. In a computer, those hands are processor cores.
So before picking a tool, ask one question. Is my program mostly waiting, or mostly working? Waiting calls for juggling. Working calls for more cores.

check.q: A program spends most of its time waiting for web replies. What helps most?
opts: Doing other work while waiting
Buying a CPU with more cores
Rewriting the loop to be shorter
check.why: The processor is idle during waiting, so overlapping the waits gains the most. More cores would sit idle too.

work: For a slow job at work, say out loud whether it is waiting or computing before touching code.
List three jobs in your pipelines that mostly wait on APIs, databases or storage.

p06.title: Concurrency or parallelism: the numbers

beats.say: A crawler makes one hundred API calls, each taking two hundred milliseconds. How long does it take?

One after another, twenty seconds. But the program only computes for about one millisecond per call. The rest is waiting on the network. With twenty calls in flight at once, using threads or asyncio, the same job finishes in about one second.

Now flip it. Eight files, each needing ten seconds of pure parsing. The core is never idle, so interleaving gains nothing. Eight processes on eight cores finish in about ten seconds instead of eighty.
Best of all, use an engine that is already parallel, like DuckDB, Polars or Spark. Then you write no concurrency code at all.

show.title: Prefer a parallel engine
items: DuckDB and Polars use all local cores
No threads or locks in your code
