check.q: Eight files each need ten seconds of pure CPU parsing, and you have eight cores. Which approach gets close to ten seconds in total?
opts: Asyncio with eight tasks
Eight processes
One thread per file in plain Python
check.why: Pure computing keeps a core busy, so overlapping does not help. Separate processes use separate cores at the same instant.

work: Time one slow step with a stopwatch, then compare time spent waiting against time spent computing.
Before writing a worker pool, check whether DuckDB or Polars can do the transformation directly.

p06.title: Where threads, processes and asyncio bite

beats.say: Why can ten Python threads run a pure loop no faster than one?

The global interpreter lock lets only one thread run Python code at a time. Threads still help with waiting, because a thread releases the lock while it waits on the network. For computing, it just adds switching overhead. Use processes, each with its own lock.

Processes have costs too. Data sent between them is copied, so shipping big objects can cost more than the work saved. Asyncio has its own trap: one blocking call, like a slow library read, freezes every other task, because they share one thread.

show.title: Hidden costs
items: Processes: data is copied between them
Processes: extra memory and startup time
Asyncio: one blocking call freezes all tasks

beats.say: And more concurrency is not always better. Fire a thousand requests at once and the server answers with rate limit errors. Cap the number in flight, and retry with backoff.

check.q: An asyncio crawler stalls completely whenever one task parses a large file with a normal blocking function. Why?
opts: Asyncio tasks each use their own process
The blocking call holds the single thread running every task
The network connections were closed
check.why: Asyncio runs all tasks on one thread, so a call that never yields stops the event loop until it finishes.

work: Add a semaphore or pool size limit to any crawler that has no cap on requests in flight.
Search async code for blocking calls and move heavy ones to a process pool.

p06.title: When not to write concurrency code

beats.say: When is writing concurrency code the wrong answer?

Often. First measure. Profile where the time goes. If a query spends ninety percent of its time in one slow database scan, threads change nothing; an index or a better plan does. Concurrency adds bugs, hard debugging and memory cost.

For heavy transformation, prefer a parallel engine. DuckDB or Polars use every core on one machine. Spark spreads work across machines when data outgrows one box. Each worker you add also costs money, so scale only past the measured limit.

show.title: Scale in order
items: Cluster: Spark, when data outgrows a box

beats.say: Keep concurrency for waiting work: crawlers, fan out API calls, object store reads. Use asyncio for thousands of connections, threads for a few dozen with simple blocking libraries. Bound both by the other system's limits.

show.title: Where concurrency fits
items: Waiting work: crawlers, API fan out, storage reads
Threads: a few dozen, blocking libraries
Always cap by the other side's limits

check.q: A nightly job joins and aggregates 40 GB of Parquet on one large machine and is slow. What is the best first move?
opts: Wrap the Python loop in a thread pool
Measure, then use a parallel engine such as DuckDB or Polars
Move straight to a Spark cluster
check.why: The work is computing, so threads will not help. A parallel engine uses all cores with no concurrency code, and a cluster is justified only after measuring a real limit.

work: Make profiling output a required step before approving any concurrency pull request.
Write down the limits of your busiest upstream API so every crawler uses a matching cap.

p06.title: One waiter, twenty tables

beats.say: How can one waiter serve twenty tables at the same time?
He takes an order, hands it to the kitchen, and does not stand there waiting. He walks to the next table. When the kitchen rings the bell, he comes back and delivers the food.
That waiter is asyncio. The tables are tasks. The bell is the moment a slow answer arrives. One person, many jobs, because most of the time is spent waiting.

show.title: The mapping
items: Waiting, not working, is the big cost

beats.say: But if the waiter stops to cook a dish himself, every table sits hungry. Slow work that blocks is the danger.

show.sub: The waiter cannot cook and serve

check.q: In the waiter analogy, why can one waiter serve many tables?
opts: He works much faster than normal
He moves on while the kitchen is slow
He has many helpers
He cooks every meal himself
check.why: Most of the time is spent waiting on the kitchen. Using that wait to serve other tables is what asyncio does.

work: List the slow waiting steps in one of your jobs, such as API calls or database reads.
Ask whether each waiting step could run while others wait.

p06.title: Ten thousand calls in four minutes

beats.say: Ten thousand API calls, each taking half a second. How long if you make them one by one?

show.sub: 10,000 calls x 0.5 s, one at a time

beats.say: About eighty three minutes. With asyncio, a coroutine runs until it reaches await on something slow, like a network call. Then it hands control back to the event loop, which starts another task.
A semaphore caps how many are in flight, say twenty. With twenty at a time, ten thousand calls at half a second each take about four minutes.
Gather collects the results in input order. All of it runs on one thread, switching only at await.

show.title: Pattern
show.text:
sem = asyncio.Semaphore(20)
async with sem:
    await fetch(client, i)
await asyncio.gather(*tasks)

check.q: With a semaphore of 20 and 0.5 second calls, roughly how long do 10,000 calls take?
opts: About 4 minutes
About 83 minutes
About 0.5 seconds
About 20 seconds
check.why: 10,000 divided by 20 is 500 rounds of 0.5 seconds, about 250 seconds.

work: Time a sequential batch of calls, then the same batch with a semaphore.
Pick a limit from the API's documented rate limit, not a guess.

p06.title: The one line that freezes everything

beats.say: Why can one line of code freeze two hundred running tasks?

show.text: One blocking call = all tasks stop

beats.say: Because asyncio switches tasks only at await. Call time dot sleep or requests dot get, and the thread is stuck. The event loop cannot run anything else until it returns.
Fix it by using async libraries like httpx, asyncpg, or aiobotocore. For blocking code you cannot replace, use asyncio dot to thread, which runs it on a worker thread.
Also, gather without a semaphore launches all ten thousand at once, and you hit rate limits or run out of sockets. And heavy CPU work blocks the loop too, since it never awaits.

show.title: Other traps
items: No semaphore: rate limits, socket exhaustion
gather returns results in input order

check.q: A coroutine calls requests.get inside an async function. What happens?
opts: Only that task waits
Other tasks run faster
Every task on the loop stalls until it returns
Python raises an error
check.why: requests.get never awaits, so the single thread never returns to the event loop.

work: Search your async code for requests, time.sleep and sync database drivers.
Wrap unavoidable blocking calls in asyncio.to_thread.
Always bound concurrency with a semaphore.

p06.title: When asyncio is the wrong tool

beats.say: When is asyncio the wrong choice?
It shines for many waiting calls: thousands of requests, small memory, no thread per call. Match the semaphore to the downstream rate limit, such as an agent running five hundred LLM test cases.
It does nothing for CPU heavy work. Use processes there. If your libraries are only blocking, threads are simpler than rewriting everything.
The cost is async spreading through the codebase, harder debugging, and one blocking call hurting everyone. Measure first: if the job is not wait-bound, asyncio buys nothing.

show.title: Costs
items: One blocking call hurts all tasks

check.q: A job is slow because it parses large files with heavy computation. What fits best?
opts: asyncio with a big semaphore
Processes across CPU cores
More coroutines with gather
asyncio.sleep between files
check.why: CPU-bound work needs real parallelism. asyncio only overlaps waiting on one thread.

work: Profile first to see whether time goes to waiting or computing.
Set concurrency from the downstream rate limit and measure the result.
Use threads when only sync libraries exist and scale is modest.

p06.title: The kitchen with too many orders

beats.say: What happens when a thousand customers shout orders at one tiny kitchen at the same time?

The kitchen collapses. Orders pile up, cooks panic, and everyone waits longer. A computer service does the same when too many requests arrive at once. It starts refusing them, with an error called four twenty nine, which means too many requests.

Two simple rules fix it. First, a limit on how many orders the cooks handle at once, say three. That is a semaphore, a counter of free seats. Second, a ticket machine that hands out one ticket per second. No ticket, you wait.
And if the kitchen is slow, the waiter stops taking new orders instead of stacking paper slips on the counter. That is backpressure.

check.q: In the kitchen story, what does backpressure mean?
opts: Cooks work faster when orders pile up
The waiter stops taking new orders while the kitchen is busy
Customers get refunds
The kitchen hires more cooks
check.why: Backpressure makes the faster upstream side slow down to match the slower downstream side, instead of letting work pile up.

work: List the outside services your code calls and write down each one's documented rate limit.
Find one place where your code fires requests as fast as it can, and note what would happen at ten times the load.

p06.title: Token bucket and semaphore

beats.say: How can a limiter allow a burst of three calls, yet still average only one call per second?

show.text: Burst of 3, average of 1 per second

beats.say: It uses a token bucket. The bucket holds at most capacity tokens, here three. Tokens drip in at rate one per second. Every call spends one token.

At time zero the bucket is full, so three calls go straight through. Now it is empty. At half a second, only half a token has refilled, so the next call must wait. At one second there is one whole token, and the call goes.
A semaphore is different. It does not count time, only calls in flight. Limit ten, and the eleventh call waits until one finishes. Use both: rate for the speed, semaphore for the pile.

show.title: Two different caps
items: Token bucket caps calls per second

check.q: A bucket has capacity 3 and rate 1 per second. It is empty now. When can the next call go?
opts: Right away
After about 1 second
After 3 seconds
Never
check.why: One token refills each second, and each call spends one, so the next call waits roughly a second.

work: Pick one API client and add a token bucket sized to its published limit.
Add a semaphore to cap in-flight calls so slow responses cannot stack up.

p06.title: Why pipelines run out of memory

beats.say: Why does a pipeline run fine for an hour, then die with an out of memory error?

show.text: Fine for an hour, then out of memory
show.sub: A silent gap between two stages

beats.say: Because the reader is faster than the writer. If the queue between them has no size limit, the gap fills memory. Say the reader makes ten thousand rows a second and the writer takes six thousand. Four thousand extra rows pile up every second.
The fix is a bounded queue, with max size one thousand. When it is full, the reader's put call blocks, so the reader simply sleeps. Slowness travels upstream by itself.

Gotchas. A token bucket without a lock lets two threads spend the same token. Retrying after a four twenty nine with no pause makes things worse, so honour the Retry After header and add random jitter. And a huge bound is no bound at all.

check.q: A reader outpaces a writer through an unbounded queue. What most likely happens?
opts: The writer speeds up
Memory grows until the process crashes
The queue drops the oldest rows safely
Nothing, queues are free
check.why: Without a bound, the surplus accumulates in memory. A bounded queue blocks the reader instead.

work: Replace any unbounded queue in your pipelines with one that has a maxsize.
Make your retry code read Retry After and add jitter.

p06.title: Limiting across many machines

beats.say: Your rate limiter works on one machine. What breaks when you run it on fifty?

show.sub: What is the real limit now?

beats.say: Each machine has its own bucket, so the real limit is fifty times higher. You can split the quota, a fixed share per machine. That is simple, but wastes capacity when load is uneven. Or keep shared counters in Redis. That is accurate, but adds a network hop to every call and a new point of failure.
Decide what happens if Redis is down. Fail open and risk overload, or fail closed and block everyone.
Where possible, prefer pull. A Kafka consumer asks for data when ready, so it needs no limiter at all. Save limiters for the edge, where you cannot control callers.

check.q: You run 50 workers, each with its own bucket at 10 calls per second, against an API limited to 100 per second. What happens?
opts: You stay under the limit
You can send up to 500 per second and get throttled
Each bucket shares tokens automatically
The API raises its limit
check.why: Local buckets are not coordinated, so the total is 50 times 10. Split the quota or share state.

work: Write down the global limit of each dependency and divide it by your worker count.
Decide whether each limiter should fail open or closed, and record why.
Prefer pull-based designs like Kafka consumers where you control both sides.

p06.title: Time it before you fix it

beats.say: Your nightly job takes an hour. Which part is slow? Most people guess, and most people guess wrong.

Picture a restaurant with slow dinners. You blame the chef and hire a second one. Then you time every step with a stopwatch. The chef takes ten minutes. Walking to a faraway storeroom for each ingredient takes forty.
A second chef would have changed nothing. Measuring means timing each step first, so you fix the part that actually hurts.
Then fix in order of biggest win. First a smarter method, like moving the storeroom closer. Then do less work. Adding more cooks comes last.

check.q: Dinners are slow. What should you do first?
opts: Hire more cooks
Time each step to find the slowest one
Buy a bigger stove
check.why: Timing shows where the time really goes. Extra cooks do nothing if the delay is the storeroom walk.

work: Before changing a slow job, write down how long each stage takes.
Ask teammates what they think is slow, then check it with a timer.

p06.title: Profile with cProfile and timeit

beats.say: How do you find the slow line in a Python job without guessing?

Run the job under cProfile, sorted by cumulative time. It lists each function and the total seconds spent inside it, including everything it calls. Read the top twenty lines. Usually one or two functions own most of the time.

To compare two ways of writing one line, use timeit. It repeats the line thousands of times and reports a steady average, so one noisy run cannot fool you. For example, turning a list of a hundred thousand numbers into a set.
The loop is simple. Profile, change one thing, then measure again. If the number did not drop, your guess was wrong.

check.q: Which tool tells you which functions in a whole job use the most time?
opts: timeit
cProfile
head
check.why: cProfile reports time per function across the run. timeit only benchmarks one small snippet.

work: Profile your slowest pipeline step this week and note the top three functions.
Change one thing at a time and record the before and after time.

p06.title: Fix in order: biggest wins first

beats.say: Why does changing the algorithm beat any amount of tuning?
Say you join ten thousand orders to ten thousand customers with a nested loop. Each order scans every customer. That is one hundred million comparisons.
Instead, build a dictionary of customers by id once. Now each order is one lookup. About twenty thousand steps in total. Thousands of times less work, with no new hardware.
Spark makes the same choice. A nested loop join is the slow scan. A hash or broadcast join is the dictionary. After that come doing less work, vectorised engines, and only last, concurrency.

check.q: A nested loop join over 10,000 by 10,000 rows is slow. Best first fix?
opts: Add more threads
Build a dictionary keyed on the join column
Buy a faster disk
check.why: It cuts about 100 million comparisons to about 20,000 lookups. Threads only split the same huge amount of work.

work: Look for loops inside loops in your code and replace lookups with dicts or sets.
Check Spark plans for nested loop joins and aim for hash or broadcast joins.

p06.title: Why a profile can mislead you

beats.say: Your profile says one function is slow. Why might it still mislead you?
Cumulative time counts everything a function calls, so the top entry is often just the caller. Total time, called tottime, shows time spent in the function itself. Read both columns.

show.title: Two columns
items: Top cumtime is often just main

beats.say: Profiling adds overhead, and tiny test data hides the real hotspot. A join that looks fine on a thousand rows can collapse on a hundred million. Profile with realistic volume.

Micro-benchmarks lie too. Warm caches and tiny inputs flatter code. And a pandas apply with a Python function is still a Python loop, row by row, so it will not speed up like a native column operation.

check.q: Which column shows time spent only in a function's own body?
opts: cumtime
tottime
ncalls
check.why: tottime excludes callees. cumtime includes them, so it flatters callers like main.

work: Profile with production-sized data, not a ten-row sample.
Read tottime and cumtime together before deciding what to fix.

p06.title: When to stop, and what to choose

beats.say: When a job is slow, should you reach for Spark?
Usually not. Spark adds a cluster, network shuffles, and a lot to operate. A vectorised engine like DuckDB or Polars on one big machine often handles hundreds of gigabytes, faster and cheaper.

Concurrency is the last lever because it adds bugs: races, retries, harder debugging. Threads or asyncio help only when you wait on I/O. Processes help only when you are CPU bound. The profile tells you which.

show.title: Match tool to bottleneck
items: Waiting on I/O: threads or asyncio
Too big for one machine: Spark

beats.say: Also ask if it is worth it. A five minute nightly job nobody waits on may not deserve a week of engineering. Set a target, measure against it, and stop when you reach it.

show.sub: Engineer time costs more than compute

check.q: A job is CPU bound on 200 GB of columnar data. What is the sensible first step after fixing the algorithm?
opts: Rewrite with asyncio
Try a vectorised engine like DuckDB on one large machine
Move straight to a Spark cluster
check.why: asyncio helps I/O waits, not CPU work. A vectorised engine is cheaper and simpler than a cluster at this size.

work: Write a target runtime before optimising, and stop once you hit it.
Before proposing Spark, test the job in DuckDB or Polars on one large machine.

p06.title: One chopping board: the GIL

beats.say: Why would hiring more cooks sometimes not speed up dinner at all?
Picture a kitchen with only one chopping board. Python has a similar rule called the Global Interpreter Lock, or GIL. Only one thread, a worker inside your program, can run Python code at any moment.
If the job is chopping, extra cooks just queue for the board. But if a cook is waiting for the oven, they step away and hand the board over. Waiting for a website or database works the same way.
So threads help when your program mostly waits, and don't help when it mostly computes.

check.q: A Python script spends most of its time crunching numbers in pure Python. What do extra threads do?
opts: Make it much faster
Give little or no speedup
Make it use less memory
check.why: Only one thread runs Python code at a time because of the GIL, so pure CPU work gains nothing from threads.

work: Before adding threads, ask whether the job mostly waits or mostly computes.
Explain the GIL to a teammate using the one-chopping-board picture.

p06.title: Why threads speed up I/O

beats.say: You run a hundred web requests, one after another, at half a second each. Why can fifty seconds shrink to a few?
A thread that waits on the network releases the GIL. Another thread then runs and sends its own request. With sixteen workers in a thread pool, sixteen requests wait at the same time.

In code, you make a thread pool executor with sixteen workers, and call map with your fetch function over the urls. Results come back in input order. A hundred half-second calls finish in about three to four seconds.

show.title: Thread pool
show.text:
with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=16) as pool:
    pages = list(pool.map(fetch, urls))

beats.say: Pure Python math is different. Two threads crunching numbers take as long as one, or longer, because they swap the lock back and forth.

check.q: Why do 16 threads fetch URLs faster than a loop?
opts: Each thread runs Python on its own core
Waiting threads release the GIL so others can send requests
The GIL is turned off for network code
check.why: While a thread waits on the network it releases the GIL, so many requests wait in parallel even though only one runs Python at a time.

work: Time a loop of 50 HTTP calls against a thread pool of 16 and compare.
Use pool.map when you need results in input order.

p06.title: Races, locks and the GIL's limits

beats.say: If only one thread runs at a time, how can two threads still corrupt a counter?
The GIL can switch threads between bytecode steps. Adding one to a counter is read, add, write. Two threads can both read forty-two, both write forty-three, and one update is lost.
Fix it two ways. Best: give each thread its own data, return a result, and let the main thread merge. Or guard the shared dict with a threading lock, so only one thread touches it at a time.

show.title: Two fixes
items: Each thread returns its own result; main thread merges
Or wrap shared state in a threading Lock

beats.say: Also know this. NumPy, hashing and compression release the GIL, so threads can use many cores there. And Python 3.13 added an optional free-threaded build with no GIL, but it is opt-in, and libraries are still catching up.

show.title: Good to know
items: C extensions can release the GIL
Standard build still has the GIL

check.q: Which design best avoids lost updates across threads?
opts: Rely on the GIL to protect shared dicts
Each thread returns its own result and the main thread merges
Add more threads so updates average out
check.why: The GIL can switch threads mid-update. No shared mutable state means no race; otherwise protect it with a Lock.

work: Review thread code for shared counters or dicts and replace them with returned results.
Where sharing is needed, wrap updates in a threading Lock.

p06.title: Threads, processes or asyncio?

beats.say: Your pipeline is slow. Do you add threads, processes, or something else?

Measure first. If the time is spent waiting on I/O, threads are cheap and share memory, so sixteen to a few dozen workers is a fine start. Beyond that, the remote service's rate limits become the real limit.

If it is pure-Python CPU work, threads give nothing. Use separate processes, which each have their own GIL, but pay for startup and for copying data between them. Or move the hot loop into NumPy or a compiled library.
For thousands of connections, asyncio uses less memory than threads. And don't bet on free-threaded Python yet. The standard build still has the GIL.

check.q: A job is CPU-heavy pure Python and runs on 8 cores. What is the best first choice?
opts: A pool of 64 threads
Multiple processes
A single thread with a Lock
check.why: Each process has its own GIL, so work runs on multiple cores. Threads would still share one GIL.

work: Profile a slow job to see whether it waits or computes before choosing a model.
Check API rate limits before raising thread counts.
Test your key libraries against the free-threaded build before relying on it.

r01.title: From best cook to menu designer

beats.say: Why do some excellent engineers stop getting promoted? Because the job changes, not just the skill.

show.sub: Senior to staff is a change of role

beats.say: Think of a restaurant. A senior engineer is the best cook. Give them an order, and the dish comes out perfect.
A staff engineer is closer to the person who designs the menu. They notice customers keep complaining about slow dinners, and decide that is the problem worth fixing.
They also write the recipe book, so every kitchen makes the sauce the same way. And they guide other cooks without being their boss.

check.q: In the restaurant picture, what best describes the staff engineer?
opts: The fastest cook on the line
Someone who decides which problem to fix and writes the recipe others follow
The manager who assigns every order
A cook who works only on their own dish
check.why: Staff work is about finding the right problem and shaping how many teams work, not just cooking faster.

work: Write down one problem you noticed that nobody asked you to solve.
Ask a senior colleague how they chose what to work on last quarter.

r01.title: Project, domain, strategy: how scope grows

beats.say: Five teams report active users, and you get five different numbers. Who fixes that?
A senior engineer fixes their own pipeline. A staff engineer notices the pattern and defines the real problem: no single definition exists.

show.title: Fix a *pipeline* or fix the domain

beats.say: Then they write a design document, because documents decide what gets built. Other senior engineers read it and execute, with no formal authority needed, because the argument is sound.
The time horizon stretches too. Seniors plan a quarter, about three months. Staff write strategy for two or three years, and lead migrations that long.

check.q: Five teams compute active users five different ways. What is the staff-level move?
opts: Fix your own team's number and move on
Define one shared metric in a design doc and get teams to adopt it
Ask a manager to order everyone to match
Build a sixth dashboard
check.why: Staff work defines the cross-team problem and uses a document to give others one definition to build on.

work: Pick one metric at work with competing definitions and list who computes each.
Draft a one page problem statement before proposing any solution.

r01.title: Fixing a class of failures, and the traps

beats.say: You fixed the same outage three times. Why is that a warning sign at staff level?

show.sub: Fixing incidents is the senior habit

beats.say: Because staff owns the whole class of failure. After the second one, you ask what makes it impossible: a schema check, a quota, a runbook turned into automation. Then you attach a reliability or cost number to it.

Watch for common traps. Becoming the hero who does everything, so you are the bottleneck. Writing a document nobody reviewed, so nobody follows it. Or drifting so far from code that your designs stop being realistic.

show.title: Staff traps
items: Hero mode: you become the bottleneck
Unreviewed doc: no buy-in, no adoption
No coding: designs lose touch with reality

check.q: The same pipeline fails for the same reason a second time. What should a staff engineer do?
opts: Fix it faster and write a better apology
Add a guardrail that makes that class of failure impossible and track a target
Wait for a third time to be sure
Assign it to the newest engineer
check.why: Staff ownership means removing the class of incident, with a measurable reliability or cost target, not just repairing instances.

work: Review last quarter's incidents and group them by root cause class.
Share your next design doc with reviewers before you build, not after.

r01.title: Choosing what is worth your years

beats.say: In the hiring manager round they ask: how do you choose what to work on? What is a strong answer?

Rank problems by impact on money, risk, or speed, against the effort. A migration that saves two million dollars a year but needs eighteen months of five engineers may lose to a small fix this quarter.
Say no to your own pet projects too. A new standard nobody asked for costs adoption effort. Prefer the boring option when the pain is small.

show.title: When not to lead a big change

beats.say: Prepare three stories: scope across teams, influence without authority, and a decision with a cost you could measure.

check.q: A migration saves two million dollars a year but takes five engineers eighteen months, while a small fix removes most of the pain in a quarter. What is the best reasoning?
opts: Always pick the larger saving
Compare impact against effort and risk, and often take the small fix first
Avoid anything that costs engineers
Let the loudest team decide
check.why: Architects weigh impact against effort, risk and adoption cost. A cheap fix can beat a bigger but slower prize.

work: Write a ranked list of your candidate projects with impact, effort and risk.
Prepare three stories with numbers: scope, influence, and cost.

r01.title: Three documents that settle decisions

beats.say: Why do the best engineers write so much? Because a decision nobody wrote down gets argued again, and again, and again.
Think of a family road trip. A design doc is the route plan you show everyone before leaving. It says why you are going, the roads you rejected, and what you do if the car breaks down.
An architecture decision record is a sticky note on the fridge. One page. We took the coast road because of the ferry. Two years later, nobody has to guess why.

show.title: Decision record
items: The good and the bad it brings

beats.say: A technical strategy is the whole year's travel plan. It names a few big destinations and the trips you are skipping. A plan that skips nothing is only a wish list.

check.q: What is the main job of an architecture decision record?
opts: Explain why a choice was made, long after the people have moved on
List every task for the next sprint
Replace the design doc for large projects
check.why: It is a one-page memory of context, decision and consequences, so nobody has to guess why the system looks the way it does.

work: Find one decision in your team nobody can explain and write a one-page record for it.
Next time you plan a project, write down what you are deliberately not doing.

r01.title: Anatomy of a design doc people approve

beats.say: What goes into a design doc that people actually approve?

Open with the problem, using numbers. For example, the nightly load takes six hours and misses the nine a.m. dashboard deadline twice a week. Then goals, and non-goals: what you are deliberately not doing.

show.title: Start here
items: Context: why now, who is hurt, with numbers
Non-goals: what we will not do

beats.say: Next comes the proposal, with a diagram, data model and interfaces. Then at least two alternatives, each with a reason why not. Without alternatives, reviewers assume you never looked.
Finish with risks, rollout with rollback, cost including the cost of doing nothing, and open questions. Lead with the conclusion on page one, so a busy reader can answer yes or no.

show.title: Close with
items: Risks and how you would know

check.q: Why must a design doc include at least two alternatives with reasons for rejecting them?
opts: To make the document longer
To show the proposal was chosen, not just the first idea
Because the template requires exactly three options
check.why: Alternatives prove you explored the space. Reviewers then trust the proposal and can challenge specific trade-offs.

work: Rewrite your last proposal's first paragraph so it states the conclusion and one number.
Add a cost-of-doing-nothing line to your next design doc.

r01.title: Why good designs still get rejected

beats.say: Why do design docs fail even when the design is good?

First failure: fake alternatives. If the other options are strawmen, a sceptic spots it and distrusts everything else. Second: a vague problem. Pipelines are slow cannot be checked. Six hours, twice late a week, can.

show.title: Doc failures
items: Sections reviewers cannot answer yes or no

beats.say: Decision records rot when nobody writes the bad consequences. Record both sides. Example: Iceberg over Delta for multi-engine reads; consequence, we run our own compaction. Never edit old records. Mark them superseded and add a new one.
Last, show the doc first to your most sceptical reviewer, privately. Their objections cost ten minutes now, instead of a week in the open review.

check.q: An old ADR is now wrong because the team changed direction. What should you do?
opts: Edit it to match the new decision
Delete it to avoid confusion
Mark it superseded and write a new ADR linking to it
check.why: The history of why you chose then, and why you changed, is the value of the record. Rewriting it destroys that.

work: Add a consequences section listing at least one bad outcome to every ADR you write.
Send your next draft privately to the harshest reviewer before the group review.

r01.title: When to write, when not to, and what to cut

beats.say: When should you not write a full design doc?
Skip it for work that is cheap to reverse, like a two day change behind a flag. A short ADR is enough. Heavy documents for small choices slow the team and teach people to ignore them.
Write the full doc when a change is costly to undo, like a new lake format or a migration touching forty pipelines. Its cost section covers build, run, and the cost of doing nothing.

A strategy covers one to three years: where we are, with data, the few big bets, what we stop doing, and how we measure progress. If nothing is stopped, you have not chosen. Pick the biggest cost, and say no to the rest.

check.q: Which sign most clearly shows a technical strategy is weak?
opts: It is only three pages long
It lists priorities but stops nothing
It includes metrics for progress
check.why: Strategy is choice. If no work is dropped or declined, it is a wish list that spreads the team thin.

work: Create a simple rule for your team: reversible changes get an ADR, costly ones get a full doc.
Review your current roadmap and name two things you would explicitly stop.

r01.title: Leading without being the boss

beats.say: How do you change what ten teams do when none of them report to you?
Think of a town with a dangerous crossroads. You are not the mayor. Shouting gets nowhere. But if you count the accidents and put the numbers on a big board, people start to see the problem.
Next, ask the shopkeepers who will object what worries them, and fix the plan. Then paint a safe crosswalk, so walking the right way is the easiest way. Nobody needs persuading to use it.

show.title: Win people, then make it easy
items: Fold their worries into the plan
Paint the crosswalk: the easy path

beats.say: Finally, let a neighbour cut the ribbon and take the credit. Influence means people want to follow, not that they must.

check.q: In the crossroads story, what is the best first move for someone with no authority?
opts: Demand the mayor build a roundabout
Count the accidents and show everyone
Paint your own crosswalk quietly
Wait until people complain
check.why: Making the problem visible with data turns a personal opinion into a shared fact, which is the base for any influence without authority.

work: Pick one pain you keep complaining about and find a number that measures it.
List who would object to your idea and ask each one what worries them.
Name one person who can present your next idea instead of you.

r01.title: The influence playbook, step by step

beats.say: Why does nobody fix a pipeline problem that fails forty runs every week?

Because nobody sees it. Build a dashboard first. Show failed runs, the engineer hours lost, and the cost. Or list the five different revenue definitions finance is using. Data turns an opinion into a fact.
Then write a short design doc. Send it early to the three people most likely to say no. Their objections go into the doc, so they become co-authors, not blockers.
Last, make the right thing easy. A template or library that sets up a pipeline in ten minutes beats a month of meetings. Adoption stops depending on persuasion.

show.title: Make the right thing the *easy* thing

check.q: Why send a design doc early to the people most likely to object?
opts: It lets you claim they were consulted
It shortens the review meeting
Their objections improve the design and they become supporters
It avoids needing any data
check.why: Early feedback is cheap to absorb. Objectors who shaped the doc have ownership in it, so they are less likely to block it later.

work: Build one chart of failed runs or cost before you pitch your next change.
Share your next draft with your toughest critic before the review.
Turn a repeated manual setup into a template others can copy.

r01.title: Why good advice sometimes changes nothing

beats.say: Why do some architects give great advice and still change nothing?
A common failure is presenting a finished design on review day. People feel ambushed and say no. Share drafts early, when changing your mind is still cheap.

Mentoring needs structure. Hold regular one to ones. Hand over a stretch piece with a safety net, like you reviewing the design before build. Review designs, not only code, because design mistakes cost far more to fix.

show.title: Mentor deliberately
items: Stretch work with a safety net

beats.say: When you lose an argument, disagree and commit honestly. State your data, accept the decision, support it fully, and write down what evidence would reopen it. Quiet sabotage destroys trust.

check.q: You lost a design argument. What does honest disagree and commit look like?
opts: Comply but let the project slip to prove your point
Keep arguing in every meeting
Support it fully and record what evidence would reopen the decision
Escalate to a manager after the decision
check.why: Committing means real support. Recording the reopen trigger keeps the decision evidence-based without turning disagreement into sabotage.

work: Share your next design as a rough draft a week before any review.
Give a junior a stretch task and agree when you will check in.
Write a reopen condition in the decision log next time you lose a debate.

r01.title: When influence is the wrong tool

beats.say: When is persuasion the wrong tool, and a rule the right one?

show.sub: Choose on the cost of being wrong

beats.say: Paved paths cost real engineering time, maybe two people for a quarter. Build one only when many teams repeat the same work. For one team, a conversation is cheaper.

Influence does not scale through you. If every design needs your review, you become the bottleneck. Train senior engineers to run reviews, give them the presentation, and sponsor them for visible work.
For risks like security or data privacy, choose a firm policy over persuasion. Mandates are fast but breed resentment. Paved paths are slower but stick. Pick by how costly a wrong choice is.

show.title: Mandate or paved path
items: High-risk areas like privacy: firm policy

check.q: When is a firm mandate better than a paved path?
opts: When a wrong choice is costly, such as a privacy or security risk
When only one team has the problem
When you want the team to feel ownership
When you have no time to write a doc
check.why: Mandates are fast and certain, which matters when a mistake is costly. For ordinary choices, paved paths build lasting adoption with less resentment.

work: Count how many teams repeat the same work before proposing a paved path.
List the reviews that only you do and hand one to a senior engineer.
Decide which two risks in your platform deserve a firm policy.

r01.title: The story bank, like a toolbox

beats.say: Why do strong engineers freeze when asked about a time they failed? Because they never practised telling it out loud.

show.text: Why freeze on a question you already lived?

beats.say: Think of a story bank as a toolbox. You do not invent a tool when the job starts. You reach in and pick one. About twelve stories cover almost every question, because questions keep repeating the same themes: conflict, failure, influence, cost.
Each story follows STAR. Situation: what was going on. Task: what was your job. Action: what you did. Result: what changed. Tell it like the plot of a short film, not a diary.
Keep it under three minutes, say I for your part, and finish with a number. People remember numbers.

show.text: Under 3 minutes. Say I. End with a number.

check.q: Why prepare about twelve stories instead of one answer per possible question?
opts: Questions are unlimited, so more is always better
Questions repeat a few themes, so a small bank can be reused
Interviewers ask for exactly twelve stories
Stories should be memorised word for word
check.why: Behavioural questions cluster around a handful of themes such as conflict, failure and influence, so one well-built story can be adapted to several prompts.

work: List ten projects from your career and note which theme each fits
Write one sentence each for situation, task, action and result of your best story
Tell one story aloud to a friend and time it

r01.title: Building stories that fit three minutes

beats.say: How do you squeeze a whole career into twelve stories of under three minutes each?

Start with themes. Influence without authority, big delivery, failure, conflict, ambiguity, raising the bar, cost, mentoring, customer focus, and prioritisation. One story can cover two themes, so twelve stories are enough to cover ten.
Then budget the time. About thirty seconds for situation and task, ninety seconds for action, and forty seconds for result and lesson. Action gets the most time because that is what is scored.
The result needs a number: hours saved, cost cut, incidents down, people affected. Then prepare a follow-up two levels deeper, because interviewers dig two or three times.

check.q: In a three-minute story, which part should get the most time?
opts: Situation, to set the scene fully
Action, what you personally did
Result, repeated for emphasis
Task, to define the goal
check.why: Interviewers score your own decisions and actions, so about ninety seconds should go to what you did and why.

work: Map each of your stories to one or two themes and find the gaps
Add a concrete number to the result of every story
Write two deeper follow-up questions for each story and answer them

r01.title: Why a good story still gets marked down

beats.say: You told a great story and still got marked down. What went wrong?
The most common cause is we. If you say we built it, the interviewer cannot tell what you did, so they have nothing to score. Say I for your part, and name the team honestly for the rest.
Second, failure stories that are secret boasts. A real failure names your mistake, what it cost, and what you changed afterwards. Third, no number and no lesson means no proof.

show.title: Traps
items: Failure that is really a boast

beats.say: Expect the dig. Why that choice? What would you do differently? A thin story falls apart at level three. Amazon scores Leadership Principles in every round, so map each story to a principle.

check.q: Which failure story is strongest?
opts: A deadline slipped because another team was late
You worked a weekend and saved the launch
You made a wrong design call, it cost two days of outages, and you added a review step
You say the failure was being too much of a perfectionist
check.why: A strong failure names your own mistake, its real cost with a number, and a lasting change you made.

work: Rewrite each story replacing we with I where it was your work
Check every failure story for owned mistake, cost and change
Tag each story with the Amazon principles it could prove

r01.title: What staff-level stories must prove

beats.say: At staff level, what is the interviewer really measuring in a story?
Scope and judgment, not effort. They want proof you changed what a team or organisation did, weighed trade-offs, and said no to something important. A heroic weekend fix signals senior, not staff.

Your analyst background is leverage. Defining a metric people trust, or translating between engineers and stakeholders, is what cross-functional means. It appears in sixty-three percent of staff postings.

show.sub: of staff postings ask for cross-functional work

beats.say: There is a trade-off. A polished script sounds fake, a loose story rambles. Memorise the outline and the number, not the sentences. If AI tools are allowed in coding rounds, narrate your approach and verify the output aloud.

show.title: Practice rules
items: Narrate your approach with AI tools

check.q: Why is a story about a heroic weekend fix weak for a staff interview?
opts: It shows too much technical depth
It shows effort but not scope, trade-offs or organisational change
Weekend work is always penalised
It has no situation
check.why: Staff roles are judged on influence and judgment across teams. Individual heroics show execution, not that you changed how others work.

work: Pick your three stories with the widest scope and rehearse those first
Turn one analyst story into a metric-trust or translation story with a number
Practise a coding task with an AI assistant while explaining and checking its output aloud

r01.title: A promise, not a hope

beats.say: Is the revenue table reliable? If your answer is usually, that is a hope, not a promise.
Think of a train timetable. The measurement is how late the train arrives. The promise is nine out of ten trains within five minutes. Everyone can check it.

Data works the same way. Measure how late the table lands. Promise it lands by six in the morning on ninety nine days out of a hundred. The few late days are your allowance for trouble. Spend that allowance, and fixing things comes before new features.

check.q: What turns 'the table is usually fine' into a real reliability promise?
opts: Asking the team to try harder
A measured number with a target, such as on time 99 days in 100
Adding more dashboards
Running the pipeline twice
check.why: A promise needs something measured and a target everyone can check. Effort and extra runs do not give you either.

work: Pick your three most important tables and write down when each should land.
Ask the owner of each how often it landed on time last quarter.

r01.title: Cost is a bill you can read

beats.say: Your cloud bill doubled. Is that bad news or good news?
Picture an electricity bill for a whole apartment block. One total tells you nothing. You need to know which flat uses the most, and the biggest few usually cause most of the bill.

chip.text: Few spenders, most of the bill

beats.say: Then you can switch off lights nobody uses, and run the washing machine less often. And you report cost per person, not just the total. If the block gained twice the residents, a doubled bill is fine. Data teams call this unit cost.

show.title: Read the bill well
items: Report cost per person, not the total
Doubled bill with doubled residents is fine

check.q: Why report cost per person (unit cost) instead of only the total bill?
opts: It makes the bill smaller
It separates growth in use from waste
It removes the need for tags
It is required by the cloud provider
check.why: A bigger total can come from more use. A unit cost shows whether each unit of work got cheaper or dearer.

work: Find out who owns the three largest items on your cloud bill.
Pick one unit, such as cost per terabyte processed, and write it down monthly.

r01.title: SLI, SLO and the error budget

beats.say: How many late days a year is ninety nine percent allowed to have?
Start with the SLI, the thing you measure. For the daily revenue table, it is minutes from midnight until the table lands.
The SLO is the target: ninety nine percent of days by six in the morning India time. That leaves an error budget of about three days a year.
Burn through it, say four late days by September, and the team stops shipping features until reliability work is done. The number ends the argument.

check.q: The team has used its whole error budget by September. What follows?
opts: Lower the SLO quietly
Reliability work comes before new features
Ignore it until next year
Add a new SLI
check.why: The point of an error budget is that spending it all pauses feature work in favour of reliability.

work: Write an SLI, SLO and budget for one critical table in a single line each.
Track late days against the budget on a team dashboard.

r01.title: Finding and cutting the spend

beats.say: A team's warehouse bill hits forty thousand dollars. Where do you even start?
First, attribute. Tag every job and read the query logs, so each dollar belongs to a team, a table or a job. Then rank them. The top ten spenders are usually most of the bill.

Then pull four levers. Scan less, with partitions and only the columns you need. Compute cheaper, with spot nodes for batch jobs. Store less, with lifecycle rules that delete old files. Run less often: does that dashboard really need hourly refresh?

show.title: Four levers
items: Compute cheaper: spot nodes for batch
Run less often: question the freshness

beats.say: Moving one dashboard from hourly to daily cuts its runs from twenty four to one a day.

check.q: Which lever cuts cost by questioning the business need rather than the technology?
opts: Spot nodes
Partitioning
Running less often, such as hourly to daily
Compaction
check.why: Reducing refresh frequency removes work entirely. The other options make the same work cheaper.

work: Pull last month's query logs and list the ten most expensive queries or jobs.
Ask each dashboard owner whether hourly freshness is really needed.

r01.title: Disaster recovery: RPO, RTO and the catch

beats.say: Your main region goes dark. Can you restore the pipelines, and how much data is gone?
Two numbers answer that. RPO is how much data you can lose, say fifteen minutes of events. RTO is how long until it works again, say four hours.
Copying files to a second region is the easy part. The catalog and orchestration state must be recoverable too. Without the table metadata and the job history, copied files are just a pile of bytes.
Most pipelines can be rebuilt by replaying raw data. Anything with no replayable source cannot, so protect it first. And rehearse the failover, because an untested plan is only a guess.

show.title: Recovery checklist
items: Rehearse the failover on a schedule

check.q: You replicate object storage to a second region. What is still missing for a real recovery?
opts: Nothing, the files are the data
Recoverable catalog and orchestration state, plus a rehearsal
A faster network
More dashboards
check.why: Without table metadata and job state, you cannot tell what the files mean or what to run. An untested failover may also fail.

work: Run a failover drill for one pipeline and record the real recovery time.
List every pipeline with no replayable source and decide how to protect it.

r01.title: Cost traps that fool you

beats.say: Your costs rose twenty percent. Did the team get worse, or did the business grow?
Raw totals cannot tell you. Unit costs can: cost per terabyte processed, per dashboard, per trained model. If data grew thirty percent and cost rose twenty, efficiency actually improved.

Watch the traps. Untagged jobs land in a mystery bucket nobody owns. Spot nodes can be reclaimed in the middle of a job, so batch work must be safe to retry. And partitioning too finely creates thousands of tiny files, which makes queries slower and costlier.

check.q: Data volume grew 30% and total cost rose 20%. What is the fair conclusion?
opts: Efficiency got worse
Unit cost fell, so efficiency improved
Nothing can be concluded
Cost must be cut by 20%
check.why: Cost grew more slowly than the work done, so cost per unit fell.

work: Find the untagged share of your bill and assign owners.
Check that every spot-run batch job is safe to retry.

r01.title: How much reliability to buy

beats.say: Should every dataset get five nines and a second region?

No. Each extra nine costs far more than the last, in standby capacity, duplicate storage and engineer time. Tier your datasets instead. A finance close table gets a tight target and a rehearsed failover. An internal experiment table gets a loose one.
Pick the recovery style by RPO and RTO. If four hours is fine, rebuild from replicated raw data in the second region. Only pay for a hot standby when minutes matter.
Let the business sign the targets. They are choosing how much risk to buy.

check.q: A table's RTO is four hours and raw data is replicated. What is the usual best-value recovery design?
opts: Hot standby in two regions
Rebuild in the second region from replicated raw data
No recovery plan
Manual copy by email
check.why: Rebuilding meets a four hour target at far lower standing cost. Hot standby is for minute-level needs.

work: Tier your datasets into three levels and attach an SLO to each tier.
Get the business owner of each Tier 1 table to sign its RPO and RTO.

r01.title: Governing cost across many teams

beats.say: How do you cut cost across twenty teams without becoming the person who says no?
Make cost visible, not policed. Give each team a dashboard of its spend and unit cost, and let owners decide. Central mandates are slow; informed owners fix the waste themselves.
Spend your own time on the top ten spenders. Chasing the long tail of small jobs costs more engineer time than it saves.

Know when not to optimise. Saving two hundred dollars a month is a bad trade if it takes an engineer two weeks. Also count the hidden costs: cross region transfer, and the risk of cheaper but flakier nodes.

show.title: When not to optimise
items: Saving is smaller than the engineer time
Cheaper nodes that fail more often

check.q: Which approach scales best for cost control across many teams?
opts: A central team approves every query
Per-team visibility of spend and unit cost, with focus on the top spenders
Cut every budget by 10%
Ban spot nodes
check.why: Visibility lets owners act themselves, and focusing on the top spenders gives the largest savings for the effort.

work: Publish a per-team cost and unit cost view and review the top ten monthly.
Set a minimum saving, for example per engineer-week, before starting an optimisation.

r01.title: The kitchen that never closes

beats.say: How do you move a restaurant kitchen without ever closing during dinner?
You don't. You build the new kitchen next door and keep cooking in the old one. For a while, both kitchens cook every order.
Each night, you taste the dishes side by side. If they match for two weeks straight, you send real orders to the new kitchen, one table at a time.
The old kitchen stays ready as a fallback, so a bad night means flipping back. Only when nobody orders from it do you lock the door. In data, this is called the strangler fig pattern.

chip.text: Delete the old only when nobody uses it

check.q: In the kitchen story, why keep the old kitchen running after the new one opens?
opts: So you can switch back quickly if the new one has problems
Because the new kitchen cannot cook without it
To double the number of dishes served
Because closing it is against the rules
check.why: The old kitchen is the fallback. Keeping it alive makes each move small and reversible, so a bad night costs little.

work: Name one system you would migrate and write down what would be its fallback.
Ask your team who still uses the old system today, and how you know.

r01.title: Six steps of a safe migration

beats.say: You have four hundred Hive tables to move to Iceberg. Where do you even start?

show.sub: Hive tables to move to Iceberg

beats.say: Start with an inventory. List every table, job and consumer, using query logs to see who really reads what. Rank them by risk and dependency, so small leaf tables go first and the scary ones go last.
Next, build beside. New pipelines write new tables while the old ones keep running. Every day, reconcile: compare row counts, sums, and key-level diffs between old and new.

Cut over only when the gate passes, for example numbers match within tolerance for fourteen days in a row. Move one consumer group at a time, with a tested switch back. Finally, find remaining readers, announce dates, and delete.

check.q: Which is the best cutover criterion for a migrated table?
opts: The new pipeline has been running for a month
Numbers match within tolerance for 14 consecutive days
The engineer who built it feels confident
The old system is getting expensive
check.why: A measurable, repeatable reconciliation result is something others, even a Finance director, can verify and sign. Time or confidence alone proves nothing.

work: Pull query logs and rank your tables by how many consumers read them.
Write the cutover rule in your design doc as a number and a duration, not a feeling.

r01.title: When matching counts still lie

beats.say: Your row counts match, so is the migration safe? Not yet.

Counts can match while content differs. A bad join might drop one row and duplicate another. Rounding can drift a sum. So also compare sums, and run key-level diffs that list keys missing on either side or with different values.

Then explain every difference. Some are bugs in the new system. Often they are bugs in the old one, which the business has trusted for years. Some are intended, like a new rule rejecting unknown cities. Write each down, with an owner, or the gate means nothing.
Rollback fails if untested. Keep the old pipeline running for a fixed window, and make sure a switch back works per table, without losing writes made on the new side.

chip.text: Untested rollback is not a rollback

check.q: Reconciliation shows a small set of keys whose values differ between old and new. What should you do first?
opts: Ignore it, since the row counts match
Overwrite the new table with the old values
Find out whether each difference is a new bug, an old bug, or intended, and record it
Extend the double run by a year
check.why: Differences are often old bugs or deliberate changes. Classifying and documenting each one keeps the cutover gate honest and gives owners something to approve.

work: Add a key-level diff to your reconciliation job, not only counts and sums.
Keep a log of every explained difference with a category and an owner.
Rehearse a rollback on one table before you need it.

r01.title: The cost of doing it safely

beats.say: When is the right migration plan no migration at all?

show.sub: the cheapest table is the one you delete

beats.say: The double run is the big cost. Both systems bill you for months, plus engineers' time on reconciliation. Put that number in the design doc up front, or finance will find it for you, angrily.

A big bang cutover is shorter, but one surprise hits everyone at once and rollback is hard. Strangler fig costs more and takes longer, yet each step is small and reversible. Choose big bang only for small, low-risk, well-understood systems.

Run it on a calendar: announce, migrate, freeze, delete, with a named owner for each consumer group. Use the inventory to retire tables nobody reads rather than migrating them. Sign-off criteria like fourteen matching days let a Finance director say yes.

check.q: A small, low-risk internal table has one known reader and no downstream dependents. Which approach is most defensible?
opts: A months-long dual run with daily reconciliation
A direct cutover, since the blast radius is tiny
Never migrate it and keep it forever
Wait until all other tables are done
check.why: The strangler fig buys safety at the cost of a long double run. When the blast radius is tiny and the system is well understood, a direct cutover is cheaper and still safe.

work: Add a double-run cost line, with months and dollars, to your next migration design doc.
Use query logs to propose tables to retire instead of migrate.
Assign a named owner to every consumer group on the migration calendar.

s00.title: The platform you will build

beats.say: Over this program you build one data platform for Meridian, a ride-hailing and food delivery company. Every module adds one layer while the rest keeps running.

show.sub: built a layer at a time

beats.say: Rider and driver apps send events to Kafka. Orders change in Postgres, and Debezium captures each change. Spark processes both, in batch and in streams, into Iceberg tables on object storage.
dbt turns those tables into clean models that Trino, Snowflake and Databricks serve to dashboards. Airflow schedules every step, and an on-call agent reads failures and reports them.

show.note: Airflow schedules it; an agent watches it

check.q: Which tool captures every change in the Postgres orders table?
opts: Airflow
Debezium
dbt
check.why: Debezium reads the database log and turns each insert, update and delete into an event.

work: Draw your current platform in the same left-to-right way: sources, transport, processing, storage, serving
Mark which box has no owner or no monitoring

s00.sec: From a platform to a data foundation
s00.title: From a platform to a foundation

beats.say: A platform that one engineer runs is not yet a foundation a company can build on. Other teams need to use it without asking you every time.

show.sub: other teams use it without you

beats.say: Three things make the difference. Golden paths: a template that creates a new pipeline in minutes. Governance: every dataset has an owner, a class like personal or public, and a rule for who may read it and how long it is kept.
And the platform run as a product: onboarding, docs, published service levels, and showing each team what it costs. Modules O1 to O5 teach this.

check.q: What is a golden path?
opts: A ready-made template that sets up a new pipeline the approved way
The fastest network route
A dashboard for executives
check.why: It makes the right way the easy way: tests, logging and CI come with the template.

work: List what a new team must ask you before building a pipeline today: each item is a golden path to build
Give every important table a named owner

s01.title: Why build a bad pipeline first

beats.say: Why would anyone build a deliberately bad pipeline first?

Picture plumbing a new house. You could buy beautiful taps first. But you only find leaks when water runs through every pipe and joint. So a plumber first connects one plain pipe from the street to the sink, and turns the water on.

A walking skeleton is that plain pipe for data. Trip events go in one end, get counted, and land in a table you can ask questions of. Every piece is the simplest thing that works. Meridian, a ride company, wants completed trips per city, per hour, by Friday.
The leaks are rarely inside one tool. They hide at the joints, where one tool hands data to the next. A thin pipeline running end to end shows you those joints early.

show.title: Where problems live
items: Thin and end to end shows them early

check.q: Why build every stage as the simplest thing that works before improving any of them?
opts: Simple tools are always cheaper
It exposes problems at the joints between tools early
It removes the need for testing later
check.why: Problems mostly appear where tools hand data to each other. A thin end to end version shows those early, before you polish any one part.

work: Before polishing any one component, get a dummy record flowing from source to final query.
List each hand-off in your current pipeline and ask what could break at each.

s01.title: The skeleton pipeline, step by step

beats.say: What is the smallest pipeline that can answer: how many trips completed, per city, per hour?

show.text: Completed trips per city, per hour

beats.say: First, a script makes fake trip events, around one hundred a second, and writes them to a Kafka topic called trip events. Kafka is a log. It keeps events in order, so other tools can read them whenever they are ready.

Every hour, Airflow, a scheduler, starts a Spark job. Spark reads that hour, keeps only completed trips, groups by city, and writes Parquet files to object storage. Parquet stores data by column, so queries read only what they need.

Then plain SQL counts completed trips per city. Airflow also checks the row count. One hour is about three hundred sixty thousand events, so zero rows means something broke, and the run should fail loudly.

check.q: What is the job of the row count check in the Airflow DAG?
opts: It speeds up the Spark job
It makes a silent empty result fail loudly
It deletes duplicate events from Kafka
check.why: A job can succeed technically yet write nothing. A row count check turns that silent failure into a visible one.

work: Add a minimum row count assertion to the end of one scheduled job.
Draw your own pipeline as boxes and label what format sits between each pair.

s01.title: Where the skeleton breaks

beats.say: Your hourly job died halfway and Airflow retried it. Did Meridian just count trips twice?

show.sub: the joints are where it breaks

beats.say: Possibly. If the retry appends new files beside the half-written ones, those trips are counted twice. The fix is idempotency. Rerunning the same hour overwrites that hour's partition, so the answer is the same however many times it runs.

Next, small files. A job that writes every few minutes leaves thousands of tiny Parquet files. Each one costs a metadata lookup, so queries slow down. Compact them into files of a few hundred megabytes.
Last, late data. A trip completed at 10:59 may arrive at 11:05. An hourly job that cut off at 11:00 misses it. Decide whether you group by event time or arrival time, and how long you wait.

show.title: Late data decisions
items: Event time: when the trip happened
Arrival time: when we saw it
Wait window before closing the hour

check.q: An hourly Spark job fails halfway and is retried. What makes the retry safe?
opts: Appending output files on every run
Overwriting that hour's partition so reruns give the same result
Running the job twice and averaging the counts
check.why: Idempotent writes mean a rerun replaces the same output, so retries cannot create duplicates.

work: Check whether your retried jobs overwrite a partition or append, and fix any that append.
Measure file count and average file size on your largest table.
Write down your lateness rule: event time or arrival time, and the wait window.

s01.title: Is the skeleton the right design?

beats.say: Meridian only needs hourly counts. So why run Kafka, Spark and Airflow at all?

show.text: Do you need all of this?

beats.say: Honestly, at one hundred events a second, one Postgres table and a cron job would answer this. Kafka and a Spark cluster cost money around the clock, and someone must be on call for them.
The skeleton is not the final design. It is a test rig. You swap one part at a time, such as batch for streaming, and rerun the same end to end check to see what that one swap changed.

show.title: Swap one part at a time

beats.say: Keep Kafka when several teams need replay or the rate hits tens of thousands a second. Otherwise, choose the boring option, and say why in the interview.

show.title: Choose by need
items: Replay or many consumers: keep Kafka
Tens of thousands of events a second: keep Kafka
Otherwise: the boring option, and justify it

check.q: What is the best use of the walking skeleton once it works?
opts: Ship it unchanged as the final design
Use it as a test rig and swap one component at a time
Rebuild everything at once for production
check.why: Changing one part at a time against the same end to end check shows exactly what each choice costs or gains.

work: For your current stack, write the simplest alternative and the volume at which it would stop working.
Keep one end to end test that you rerun after every component change.

s01.title: The conveyor belt of the terminal

beats.say: How can one line of typing sort a forty gigabyte log on a laptop with only sixteen gigabytes of memory?
Think of a factory conveyor belt. Items pass one at a time. Each worker does one small job, then hands the item along. Nobody ever holds the whole pile.

show.title: A *belt* moves one item at a time

beats.say: The terminal pipe works the same way. One tool reads a line. The next counts it. The next sorts the counts. The file flows through like items on a belt, so memory stays small.
And Git is your saved history, like versions of a document, so you can try changes safely.

check.q: Why can a pipe handle a file bigger than memory?
opts: It compresses the file first
It processes the file a line at a time and passes results along
It copies the file to the cloud
check.why: Each tool reads a small piece, does its job and hands it on, so the whole file is never held in memory.

work: Run head dash n 3 on a data file before loading it anywhere.
Try a two-step pipe on a small file to feel the streaming idea.

s01.title: Counting values with a pipe

beats.say: You have a three million row trips file. How do you find the most common value in column three without opening it?
Cut pulls out column three, one line at a time. Sort groups equal values side by side. Uniq dash c collapses each group into a count.
Then sort dash r n orders the counts from biggest to smallest, and head keeps the top ten. Only ten lines reach your screen.

show.title: Value counts
show.text: cut -d, -f3 trips.csv | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head

beats.say: Before that, use head dash n three with jq to peek at records, and wc dash l to count rows. Peek first, so you never load a huge file blindly.

check.q: In the value count pipe, what does the first sort do?
opts: Puts the biggest counts first
Places equal values next to each other so uniq can count them
Removes duplicate rows
check.why: Uniq only merges neighbouring identical lines, so sort must bring equal values together first.

work: Run a value count on a low-cardinality column of a real file.
Use du dash sh with sort dash h to find what is eating disk.

s01.title: Git commands for the right situation

beats.say: You pushed a bad commit to main. Do you rewrite history, or add to it?
On shared branches, add to it. Git revert creates a new commit that undoes the old one. Everyone's copies still match, so nothing breaks for teammates.
Rewriting is for local work only. Git reset soft head tilde one removes your last local commit but keeps the changes staged. Do it before you push, never after.

Start each change on its own branch with git switch dash c. Park half-done work with git stash. When something broke and you don't know when, git bisect binary searches history. A thousand commits needs about ten checks.

check.q: A bad commit is already pushed to shared main. What is the safest fix?
opts: git reset --soft HEAD~1 and force push
git revert with the commit id
Delete the repository and re-clone
check.why: Revert adds a new commit that undoes the change, so teammates' history is never rewritten.

work: Practice revert, stash and bisect on a throwaway repository.
Name branches by change, such as feature slash ingest.

s01.title: Why a tidy one-liner can lie

beats.say: Why can your tidy one-liner give a wrong answer on a perfectly healthy CSV?
Cut splits on every comma. If a quoted field contains a comma, like Smith, John, the columns shift and your counts are quietly wrong. Use a real CSV tool for those files.
Also, wc dash l counts newlines, not records. A record spanning lines, or a missing final newline, changes the number. And grep dash c counts matching lines, not distinct events.

Streaming has limits too. Sort must see everything before it outputs, so it spills temporary files to disk. Fill that disk and the job fails. Uniq only merges neighbours, so skipping sort gives wrong counts.

check.q: Why might a pipe over a 40 GB file still fail even though it streams?
opts: Pipes cannot read large files
Sort must see all data and can fill the temporary disk
Head loads the whole file
check.why: Sort cannot output until it has read everything, so it spills to temp files; a full disk stops the job.

work: Check free space in the temp directory before sorting very large files.
Use a CSV-aware tool when fields may contain quoted commas.

s01.title: When to leave the shell behind

beats.say: When does a shell one-liner stop being the right tool?

When you need repeatable, tested, scheduled logic. A one-liner has no schema, no retries and no review trail. Once a check matters to the business, move it into a pipeline job, or a SQL query in an engine like DuckDB or Spark.

Remote storage adds cost. Listing an S3 prefix recursively makes paged list calls, slow and billed across millions of objects. Pulling data down just to count it adds transfer charges. Prefer inventory reports, or query the data where it lives.

show.title: Cost on object storage
items: Recursive ls is many list calls
Use S3 inventory or query in place

beats.say: For history, rebase keeps main linear but rewrites commits, so use it only on your own branch. Choose merge when others share the branch.

check.q: Which is the best way to count objects in a huge S3 prefix regularly?
opts: Recursive ls from a laptop each time
Download everything and run wc
Use an inventory report or query the data in place
check.why: Inventory or in-place queries avoid millions of list calls and transfer costs, and they can be scheduled.

work: Promote any shell check that people rely on into a tested, scheduled job.
Set a team rule: rebase only unpushed personal branches.

s01.title: A library and a coat check

beats.say: What if your files were stored like books in a library, with one librarian who knows where every page is?
That librarian is the NameNode in HDFS. A big file is cut into chunks, and each chunk is copied onto three different shelves. If one shelf collapses, the librarian notices and makes a new copy.

Object storage, like S3, is different. It is one giant coat check. You hand over a bag, get a tag, and later show the tag to get the bag back. There are no folders, only long tag names with slashes in them.

check.q: In the coat check picture of object storage, what is a folder?
opts: A real shelf holding many bags
Just part of a long tag name
A second librarian
A copy of the bag
check.why: Object storage is a flat map from key to object. Slashes in a key are only characters, so a folder is only a naming habit.

work: Explain HDFS and S3 to a colleague using the library and coat check pictures.
Look at one S3 path in your project and point out which parts are really just the key.

s01.title: How HDFS keeps a file alive

beats.say: How does a one gigabyte file survive a machine dying?

show.sub: one machine dies. Is it gone?

beats.say: HDFS cuts it into eight blocks of 128 megabytes. Each block is copied to three different machines, so the cluster holds twenty four block copies.

show.title: Block copies for a 1 GB file

beats.say: The NameNode keeps the map of which DataNode holds which block, in memory. To read, you ask the NameNode for locations, then pull bytes straight from the DataNodes.

chip.text: Metadata and data take separate paths

beats.say: DataNodes send a heartbeat every three seconds. If one goes silent, the NameNode orders new copies of its blocks, so every block is back to three copies.

check.q: A client wants to read a file in HDFS. Where do the file bytes come from?
opts: Through the NameNode
Directly from DataNodes after asking the NameNode for locations
From the standby NameNode
From a temporary directory
check.why: The NameNode only answers where blocks are. Keeping bytes off it stops it becoming a bottleneck.

work: Work out how many blocks and copies a 10 GB file creates on your cluster.
Check the replication factor and block size configured for your main data directory.

s01.title: Flat keys and the slow rename

beats.say: Why can renaming a folder take a blink on one system and an hour on another?
Object storage is a flat map from a key to an object. A key like raw, trip events, date, part one dot parquet is one long string. The slashes are just characters.
So renaming a folder means copying every object to a new key, then deleting the old one. Ten thousand files means twenty thousand calls, and the whole thing is not atomic.
In HDFS the same rename is one metadata change inside the NameNode. It is instant, and it happens all or nothing.

check.q: Why is renaming a prefix on S3 slow?
opts: The NameNode is overloaded
Each object must be copied and the old one deleted
S3 locks the whole bucket
Rename compresses the data
check.why: There are no real directories. A rename is a copy and a delete per object, so cost grows with file count.

work: Find any job in your pipelines that renames output directories on S3.
Count how many objects sit under one output prefix to estimate the cost of a rename.

s01.title: A million tiny files

beats.say: Why can a million tiny files hurt a cluster that stores petabytes?

show.sub: the disks are empty, yet the cluster is sick

beats.say: Every file and every block is an object in NameNode memory, roughly 150 bytes each. Ten million small files means about twenty million objects, around three gigabytes of heap, before any real data moves.
The disks sit nearly empty, but the NameNode runs out of memory. Each small file also becomes its own task, so jobs spend more time starting than working.

chip.text: Memory, not disk, is the limit

beats.say: The fix is compaction: merge small files into files of hundreds of megabytes. And remember the NameNode is the one part you cannot lose, so run a standby.

show.title: Defences
items: Aim for hundreds of MB per file

check.q: What is the main resource that millions of small files exhaust in HDFS?
opts: Disk space on DataNodes
NameNode memory
Network bandwidth between racks
Replication factor
check.why: Each file and block is a NameNode memory object, so file count matters more than total bytes.

work: Report file count and average file size for your busiest directories.
Schedule a compaction job for any directory with files under 64 MB.

s01.title: Half a result on object storage

beats.say: A job finished, yet a reader saw only half of its output. How?

show.sub: a reader saw some files, not all

beats.say: Old Hadoop jobs wrote to a temporary directory, then renamed it into place. On HDFS that is one atomic step, so output appears all at once.
On S3 that rename is a copy and delete per object. A reader listing the folder midway sees some files new and some missing. A crash leaves a half result behind.
Table formats like Iceberg and Delta commit by swapping one small metadata pointer. Readers see the old version or the new one, never a mix.

show.title: Pointer swap commit
items: Readers see old or new, never both

check.q: Why do Iceberg and Delta avoid the half result problem?
opts: They rename faster
They commit by atomically swapping a small metadata pointer
They replicate files three times
They lock the bucket
check.why: Data files are invisible until the pointer changes, so a single small atomic update publishes everything.

work: Check whether any job publishes by renaming a prefix on S3, and flag it as a risk.
Read how your table format commits, and write down what a reader sees mid-write.

s01.title: Choosing HDFS or object storage

beats.say: When would you still pick HDFS over S3 for a new design?
