show.sub: default to one, justify the other

beats.say: Default to object storage. Compute and storage scale separately, so you can switch compute off at night and pay only for bytes. HDFS bills for the whole cluster, and three copies mean one terabyte of data uses three terabytes of disk.

show.title: Disk needed for 1 TB of data

beats.say: HDFS still wins on premises, where you already own the machines, or when you need data next to compute and cheap, fast renames and appends.
Object storage also charges per request, so millions of tiny files become a slow bill. Use large Parquet files plus a table format.

check.q: Which reason best justifies choosing object storage for a new analytics platform?
opts: Atomic directory renames
Compute and storage scale and are paid for independently
No need to think about file sizes
Data always sits next to the compute
check.why: Separating compute from storage lets you scale or switch off compute while paying only for stored bytes. Renames are weaker, and file size still matters.

work: Estimate the monthly cost of your cluster against bytes stored plus requests on S3.
Write a one page note listing where your platform depends on atomic rename, and what replaces it.

s01.title: The receipt roll that never tears

beats.say: What if a messaging system never threw a message away after you read it?

show.sub: Kafka does not delete on read

beats.say: Picture a shop's receipt roll. Every sale is printed at the bottom, one after another, and nothing is ripped off. That is Kafka: a log, which just means a list you only ever add to.
Each receipt has a number, called its offset. Each reader keeps a bookmark at the last number they read. Accounting reads at its own pace. Marketing reads the same roll too.
If a report turns out wrong, move the bookmark back and read again. The roll is still there. That is replay, and it is why data engineers love it.

show.title: Why it matters
items: Many readers, each with a bookmark

check.q: In the receipt roll analogy, what does moving a bookmark back let you do?
opts: Delete old receipts
Read the same messages again
Make the roll shorter
check.why: Reading does not remove messages, so resetting your position replays them. That is Kafka's replay.

work: Explain Kafka to a colleague using the receipt roll in one minute.
List two teams in your company who could read the same stream independently.

s01.title: Topics, partitions and keys

beats.say: Meridian produces millions of trip events. How does Kafka keep one trip's events in order?

The stream is a topic, called trip events. A topic is split into partitions. Each partition is an ordered log on a broker, which is a Kafka server. Every message gets an offset, its position: zero, one, two.

The producer picks the partition. With a key, it hashes the key, meaning it turns it into a number. Then it divides by the partition count and keeps the remainder. Same trip id, same number, same partition.
So requested, accepted, started and completed for trip forty-two all land in one partition, in order. Order holds inside a partition, and nowhere else.

check.q: Why do all events for one trip_id arrive in order?
opts: Kafka sorts every topic globally
The key hashes to the same partition, and a partition is ordered
Consumers sort by timestamp
check.why: Same key gives the same partition, and Kafka guarantees order only inside a partition.

work: Check which key your busiest topic uses and what ordering it protects.
Write down the partition count of each topic you own.

s01.title: Consumer groups and replay

beats.say: A topic has six partitions and you start ten consumers. How many actually work?
A consumer group shares the partitions among its members. Each partition goes to exactly one consumer in the group. So six partitions keep six consumers busy, and the other four sit idle.
The group records progress by committing offsets, which means saving the note: I have read up to here. If a consumer crashes, another one picks up from the last commit.
Reading does not delete. Messages stay for the retention period, say seven days. Fix a Spark bug, reset the offsets, and read the same data again.

show.title: Replay
items: Messages kept for retention, say 7 days
Fix the bug in the Spark job
Reset offsets, reprocess the same data

check.q: A topic has 4 partitions and a group has 6 consumers. What happens?
opts: All 6 share the work equally
4 work and 2 are idle
Kafka adds 2 partitions automatically
check.why: Each partition is read by one consumer in the group, so parallelism is capped at the partition count.

work: Compare consumer count to partition count for each of your groups.
Find out your topics' retention and whether it covers your longest outage.

s01.title: Changing partitions and committing safely

beats.say: You double a topic from six to twelve partitions. Why might trip events now arrive out of order?

The key maps to a partition using the partition count. Change the count and the same trip id can hash somewhere new. New events go to a different partition than old ones, and two consumers may handle them at once.
Keyed randomly, it is worse. A consumer can see completed before started, because order only exists inside one partition.

show.title: Random keys
items: Events for one trip spread across partitions

beats.say: Another gotcha: commit offsets before you finish processing, and a crash loses messages. Commit after, and a crash means duplicates, so make your writes safe to repeat.

show.title: Commit timing
items: Commit before work: crash loses data
Commit after work: crash repeats data
Make writes idempotent, safe to repeat

check.q: Why is adding partitions to a keyed topic risky?
opts: Old messages are deleted
The key may map to a different partition, breaking per-key order
Consumers stop committing offsets
check.why: The partition is derived from the key and the partition count, so a new count moves keys.

work: Pick a partition count with headroom up front so you never have to change it.
Make your sink writes idempotent, then test by replaying one hour.

s01.title: When Kafka is the wrong tool

beats.say: Kafka is great, so why not use it for everything?
Partition count is your parallelism ceiling and hard to change safely. Size it with headroom, but not into the hundreds per topic, because each partition costs broker memory and slows recovery.
A hot key is another limit. If one big customer is the key, one partition gets most of the traffic, and one consumer becomes the bottleneck no matter how many you add.
Retention costs disk. A hundred megabytes a second for seven days is about sixty terabytes, before replication.
For a nightly batch from one database, files or a table are simpler. Choose Kafka when many readers need ordered, replayable events.

show.title: Choose Kafka when
items: Otherwise files or tables are simpler

check.q: Which workload is the weakest fit for Kafka?
opts: Many teams reading the same ordered trip events
One nightly export from a single database to a warehouse
Replaying a day of events after a bug fix
check.why: A single nightly batch has no need for multiple readers, ordering or replay, so files or a table are simpler and cheaper.

work: Estimate retention disk as rate times seconds times replication for your busiest topic.
Check partition traffic for skew from hot keys.

s01.title: Spark as a restaurant kitchen

beats.say: You tell Spark to filter a billion rows, and nothing happens. Is it broken?

show.sub: A filter on a billion rows, and silence

beats.say: No. Picture a restaurant kitchen. The driver is the head chef. She reads your order and writes the plan. The executors are the cooks. Each cook works on one tray of ingredients at a time. That tray is called a partition.

chip.text: A partition is one tray of data

beats.say: Saying filter or join is just writing on the order pad. Nothing is cooked yet. These notes are called transformations. Saying count, show, or write is like shouting serve it. That is an action, and now the cooks start.

Why wait? Because the chef sees the whole order first. She will not peel carrots nobody ordered, and she trims ingredients early. Spark skips unused columns and filters early too, so less work gets done.

show.title: Why laziness helps
items: The chef sees the whole order first
Filter early, so less work is done

check.q: You write a filter and a join on a big table, but never call count, show or write. What does Spark do?
opts: Runs both immediately and stores the result
Nothing yet, it only records the plan
Runs the filter but waits on the join
check.why: Filter and join are transformations, which are lazy. Work starts only when an action such as count, show or write is called.

work: Explain to a teammate the difference between a transformation and an action using the kitchen picture.
Next time a Spark cell returns instantly, check whether it contained any action at all.

s01.title: Tracing the hourly job end to end

beats.say: When your job reads a Kafka topic and writes Parquet, what actually runs, and when?

Your code builds a plan: read, parse the JSON, filter to the time window, add date and hour columns. All transformations, so nothing has run. The write at the end is the action. Only then does the driver optimise the plan and cut it into tasks.

Say the topic has twelve partitions. Spark reads each one as a separate data partition, so twelve tasks. With four cores across the executors, four tasks run at once, so three waves. Each task parses its slice and writes Parquet files into the date and hour folders.
Because the whole plan is visible, the optimiser drops columns nobody uses, and the time filter runs right after parsing, so rows outside the window never reach the write.

show.title: What the optimiser does
items: Runs the time filter right after parsing
Rows outside the window never reach the write

check.q: A topic has 12 partitions and the cluster has 4 cores in total. Roughly how does the read stage run?
opts: 12 tasks in one wave
12 tasks in about 3 waves of 4
4 tasks in 12 waves
check.why: One task per input partition gives 12 tasks. Four cores run four at a time, so about three waves.

work: Open the Spark UI for a job and match each stage's task count to its input partitions.
Compare task count with total cores to see how many waves your job needs.

s01.title: Silent wrong answers in the skeleton

beats.say: Your count says one million rows, and your write saves a different number. How?

show.text: Count is not what you wrote

beats.say: Every action re-runs the plan from the source. Count reads Kafka. Write reads it again. With ending offsets set to latest, new events may have arrived between the two runs. Fix it by pinning explicit end offsets, or cache the result.

Bad data is quieter. If a JSON line is malformed, from json returns null, not an error. A timestamp that fails to parse also becomes null, and the time filter then drops that row. No exception, no warning, just missing events.
Two more traps. Collect pulls every row into the driver's memory, so a big table crashes it. And partitioning by date and hour with many tasks writes many tiny files, which slows every later read.

show.title: Two more traps
items: Collect on a big table crashes the driver
Many tasks times many folders means tiny files
Tiny files slow every later read

check.q: A malformed JSON line reaches from json in your job. What most likely happens?
opts: The job fails with a parse exception
The row becomes null fields and may be silently dropped by a later filter
Spark retries the line until it parses
check.why: In default mode from json returns null instead of failing, and a null timestamp then fails the time filter, so the row disappears without any error.

work: Count rows that parse to null and compare to total rows before writing; alert if the gap is nonzero.
Pin explicit start and end offsets for each batch run.
Check output folders for file counts and sizes after each run.

s01.title: Is Spark the right tool here?

beats.say: Is Spark the right tool for an hourly job that reads a few gigabytes?

show.sub: An hourly job, a few gigabytes

beats.say: Maybe not. Spark pays a fixed cost: starting a cluster, scheduling, shuffling over the network. For a few gigabytes, one machine running DuckDB or plain SQL can finish sooner and cost far less. Spark wins when data outgrows one machine, or work needs many cores.

show.title: Rough time for a small job

beats.say: If you keep Spark, fix the reading. Scanning from earliest each hour grows cost forever. Record the end offsets of each run, and start the next run there. Or use streaming with an available-now trigger, which keeps offsets in a checkpoint and stops when caught up.

chip.text: Cost tracks new data, not history

beats.say: If you need seconds of latency, hourly batch is the wrong shape; consider a continuous stream engine like Flink. Choose by data size, latency needed, and who runs the cluster.

show.title: Choose by three questions
items: Who runs and pays for the cluster?

check.q: Your hourly job rereads the whole topic from earliest and runtime grows each week. What is the best fix?
opts: Add more executors
Track end offsets per run, or use a checkpointed available-now stream
Switch the output format to CSV
check.why: Rereading history makes cost grow with all data ever written. Resuming from saved offsets makes cost follow only new data.

work: Estimate your hourly data volume and test whether a single machine tool finishes it faster.
Store end offsets alongside each output batch so reruns are repeatable.
Write down the latency target before choosing between batch and streaming.

s01.title: Airflow as a kitchen manager

beats.say: How does a kitchen get the soup ready before the lunch rush, every single day, without anyone shouting orders?

show.text: Soup ready by noon. Every day.

beats.say: A recipe card lists the steps and their order. Chop, then boil, then serve. Airflow calls that card a DAG: a set of tasks, the order between them, and a schedule.
A manager watches the clock and says what should start now. That is the scheduler. Someone then assigns each job to a cook or a station. That is the executor.
And a logbook records every step. When the soup is late, you can see exactly which step failed.

chip.text: Late soup? Find the failed step

check.q: In the kitchen analogy, what does the scheduler do?
opts: Cooks the food
Decides which jobs should start now
Stores the leftover ingredients
check.why: The scheduler is the manager watching the clock and deciding what should run. Workers, chosen by the executor, do the actual work.

work: Draw one of your nightly jobs as boxes and arrows, showing which step must finish before the next.
Write down who or what decides when each job starts today, and where its history is recorded.

s01.title: Why a run starts after its interval

beats.say: The nine to ten o'clock run starts just after ten, not at nine. Why would a scheduler wait?
Because each run covers a data interval. The hourly run for nine to ten can only begin once that hour is over, so all of its data exists.

chip.text: Hour is complete, data is complete

beats.say: The scheduler checks each DAG, finds tasks whose upstream tasks succeeded, and queues them. The executor picks where they run: a local process, Celery workers, or one Kubernetes pod per task.
Every attempt is recorded as queued, running, success or failed, so you can see exactly what happened and when.

check.q: Why does the 09:00 to 10:00 hourly run start just after 10:00?
opts: The scheduler is always an hour slow
The run needs the whole interval to be complete first
Executors only start work on the hour
check.why: A run covers a finished data interval. Waiting until 10:00 passes means all the data for that hour exists.

work: For each DAG, write down its data interval and when its run really starts.
Check which executor your team runs and why it was chosen.

s01.title: Tasks, operators and XCom in code

beats.say: How do two tasks hand work to each other without sharing a disk?

show.text: Task A finishes. Task B needs its result.

beats.say: In the example, ingest runs the Spark job for one hour and returns a row count. Check receives that number and fails the run if it is zero.
That number travels through XCom, Airflow's small message store. A row count or a file path fits. A million rows does not, because XCom lives in the metadata database.
Big data stays in storage. Tasks pass only a pointer to it. Retries are set to two, with two minutes between attempts, so a network blip heals itself without paging anyone.

show.title: Habits
items: Pass a path or a count

check.q: What should you pass between tasks using XCom?
opts: A file path or a row count
The full table of results
A copy of the Spark cluster logs
check.why: XCom is stored in the metadata database, so it suits small values like a path or count. Large data belongs in storage.

work: Find any task that returns a large object and change it to write to storage and return the path.
Set sensible retries and a retry delay in default args.

s01.title: The now() trap

beats.say: A task failed at ten past ten, retried at quarter to eleven, and wrote different data. Why?

show.text: Same task. Same run. Different data.

beats.say: The task asked the clock. Calling now gives a different answer on every attempt, so the retry processed a different hour.
The fix is to use the interval Airflow passes in: data interval start and data interval end. Same run, same hour, on every attempt. That makes a retry safe to repeat.
The same rule powers catch up and backfill. A backfill reruns chosen dates on purpose. With now, last Tuesday's backfill would quietly process today.

check.q: A backfill of last Tuesday processed today's data. What is the most likely cause?
opts: The executor was too small
The task read the current time instead of its data interval
XCom was too large
check.why: Tasks that call now ignore which interval the run is for. Using the interval boundaries makes reruns and backfills reproducible.

work: Search your DAG code for now, today and utcnow, and replace them with interval values.
Make writes overwrite the hour's partition so a retry cannot duplicate rows.

s01.title: Catchup surprises

beats.say: You deploy a new hourly DAG with a start date one year ago. Why does the cluster suddenly melt?
Catchup is true. The scheduler creates a run for every missed hour since the start date. That is about eight thousand seven hundred sixty runs, all wanting workers at once.
That is why the example sets catchup false. Only new intervals run. Choose true only when history should be built, and cap how many runs go at once.

show.title: Safer defaults
items: Use true only to build history

beats.say: Remember too that a retry reruns the same task. Writes must be safe to repeat: overwrite that hour's partition, do not append.

check.q: What does catchup true do for a DAG whose start date is far in the past?
opts: Skips all old intervals
Creates a run for every missed interval
Runs only the latest interval twice
check.why: Catchup makes the scheduler create a run for each missed interval since the start date, which can be thousands.

work: Review every DAG for catchup and set false unless history is wanted.
Set a limit on concurrent active runs before any large backfill.

s01.title: When Airflow is the wrong tool

beats.say: When is Airflow the wrong tool? Knowing that separates a good architect from a fan.

Pick the executor by isolation and cost. Local runs on one machine, fine for a laptop. Celery keeps a pool of workers always on, so tasks start fast, but you pay for idle time. Kubernetes gives each task its own pod and dependencies, but adds seconds of startup.

Airflow is not a streaming engine. It starts batch runs per interval, so second-level latency belongs to Kafka and Flink. It is also not a data processor. Spark does the heavy lifting. Airflow triggers, waits and records.
At thousands of tasks an hour, the metadata database and scheduler become the bottleneck. Keep tasks coarse.

show.title: Scale limits
items: Metadata database load grows with task count
Scheduler loop slows with many DAGs

check.q: Which workload is the weakest fit for Airflow?
opts: A nightly warehouse load
Second-by-second event processing
An hourly Spark job with a row count check
check.why: Airflow orchestrates batch runs per interval. Second-level streaming latency belongs to engines like Kafka and Flink.

work: Write a one-page note on why your team picked its executor and what the idle or startup cost is.
Move any heavy data processing out of Airflow tasks into Spark or the warehouse.
Track task counts per hour and metadata database load as an early warning.

s01.title: The detective and the runner

beats.say: Can an AI actually do things, or does it only talk?

show.sub: How an AI gets things done

beats.say: Picture a brilliant detective locked in a room. She cannot leave. She writes notes: bring me the case file. You are the runner. You fetch it and slide it under the door.
She reads it and asks for another. That back and forth is the agent loop. The model only asks. Your code does every action.
She stops when she can answer, or when you call time. Without a limit, she could send you out forever, and you pay for every trip.

check.q: In an agent loop, who actually runs the tool?
opts: The model, inside the AI service
Your own code, after the model asks
The user, by hand every time
check.why: The model only replies with a request naming a tool and arguments. Your code runs it and sends back the result.

work: Explain the loop to a teammate using the detective and runner picture.
List which actions in your pipelines you would let a model request, and which stay human only.

s01.title: Five steps of the agent loop

beats.say: What really happens when an AI model uses a tool? Five steps, in a loop.

You send the conversation plus a list of tools. Each tool has a name, a description, and a schema that describes its inputs. The model replies with text, or a request to call one tool with chosen arguments.
Your code runs that function, adds the result to the conversation, and calls the model again. Each turn, the model sees everything so far.
For a failed Airflow task, that is often three turns. List the failed logs. Read the last eighty lines of one. Then answer. The loop ends when the reply is not a tool request, or after six turns.

check.q: When does the loop stop normally?
opts: When the tool returns any result
When the reply is not a tool request
After exactly one model call
check.why: A reply that is plain text instead of a tool request means the model has its answer. Your max turns limit is the backstop.

work: Trace one real agent run and count turns and tool calls.
Write each tool description so a stranger could tell when to use it.

s01.title: Never trust the path

beats.say: Who chooses the file path your code reads? The model does. So what if it asks for a password file?

Treat anything the model supplies as untrusted input, like a web form. The code first resolves the path to its real absolute form, then checks the log folder is a parent. Resolving first matters, because dot dot segments would slip past a simple text check.
A blocked path raises an error. That error is not a crash. It goes back to the model as a tool result marked as an error, with the message. The model reads it and tries a valid path instead.

check.q: A tool raises an error because the model chose a bad path. What should the loop do?
opts: Crash the whole job
Return the message as an error tool result
Silently skip and answer anyway
check.why: Sending the error back lets the model see what went wrong and choose another path, while the failure stays contained.

work: Audit every tool argument and decide what could be abused if the model were tricked.
Add a test that feeds a path with dot dot segments and confirm it is rejected.

s01.title: Limits and honest answers

beats.say: What happens if the model never decides it is finished?

It keeps calling tools. Every turn resends the whole conversation, so each call costs more than the last. A limit of six turns caps the spend. When it is hit, return a clear stopped message, never a guess.
Second trap: models want to please. If the prompt demands a cause and the logs show none, the model invents a believable one. So the prompt says: if the logs do not show the cause, say so.

show.title: Allow "I don't know"
items: Prompt gives explicit permission to say unknown

beats.say: Asking for the exact log line helps too. A claim you can check against evidence is hard to fake.

check.q: Why tell the model it may say the logs do not show the cause?
opts: It saves tokens on every call
A model forced to give a cause may invent one
It lets the model skip calling tools
check.why: Without permission to be uncertain, the model fills the gap with a plausible but unsupported cause.

work: Set a max turns value on every agent loop and log when it is reached.
Require evidence, such as a quoted line, in answers and spot check a few.

s01.title: Agent or plain pipeline?

beats.say: Do you need an agent, or just one model call?

If the steps never change, find the failed log, read it, summarise, write plain code and call the model once. It is cheaper, faster and easier to test. Use a loop only when the next step depends on what the last one found.
A loop costs more. Each turn takes seconds and resends a growing history, so three turns cost well over one call. Keep tool output small, like eighty lines, not whole files.
Read-only tools limit damage to a wrong answer. A tool that changes things needs a human approval step in front of it, plus a budget and an audit log. Add capabilities one at a time.

show.title: Grow power slowly
items: Read-only: worst case is a wrong answer
Budget and audit log on every run

check.q: When is a full agent loop the better choice over a fixed pipeline?
opts: When every run follows the same steps
When the next step depends on what was found
When you want the lowest possible cost
check.why: Loops earn their extra cost and risk only when the path varies with the findings. Fixed paths are cheaper as plain code.

work: Review each LLM workflow you own and mark whether the steps are really fixed.
Define approval, budget and audit rules before adding any tool that changes state.

s01.title: The elevator button and the tip jar

beats.say: Why does pressing an elevator button five times still bring just one elevator?
Because the button only says, I want to be here. Pressing again changes nothing. That property has a name: idempotent. Doing it twice leaves the same result as doing it once.
Now picture a tip jar. Every coin you drop makes the total bigger. If a data job works like a tip jar and gets run twice, every row is counted twice.

And data jobs do get run twice. They retry after failures, people rerun them after fixing bugs, and teams refill a whole month of history. So build jobs like the elevator button: same request, same result.

show.title: Why jobs run again
items: Manual rerun after a bug fix

check.q: Which job is idempotent?
opts: Adds 100 rows to a table each time it runs
Replaces the 09:00 data with the same 100 rows each time
Sends a counter that goes up by one per run
check.why: Replacing the same data leaves the same result after one run or ten. Adding or counting up changes the result on every run.

work: List which of your jobs get retried or rerun, and note how each one writes.
Ask of every job: if this ran twice, would the numbers change?

s01.title: Three ways a rerun stays safe

beats.say: You rerun the nine o'clock hour, and suddenly every trip event appears twice. Why?
The naive write uses append mode. Append just adds new files. Say the hour holds one million rows. Run it twice and the partition holds two million.
Fix one: overwrite the partition you own. The nine o'clock run replaces the nine o'clock folder, and nothing else. Set partition overwrite mode to dynamic first.
Fix two: merge on a key. Match rows on event id. Update the ones that exist, insert the ones that do not. Rerun it ten times and you still get one million rows.

check.q: The 09:00 job runs three times with the same input. Which write gives one million rows each time?
opts: Append mode
Overwrite of the 09:00 partition
Appending, then counting rows later
check.why: Overwriting the partition replaces its content, so the count stays at one million. Append adds a copy on each run.

work: Find one job that uses append and decide whether overwrite or merge fits it.
Rerun a single hour twice in a test and compare row counts.

s01.title: Where idempotent writes bite back

beats.say: One config line decides whether a rerun fixes one hour or wipes the whole table. Which one?

By default, overwrite is static. Writing the nine o'clock hour deletes every partition in the table first, then writes just that one. A month of history, gone. Setting partition overwrite mode to dynamic replaces only the partitions present in the new data.

The second trap is de-duplicating on read. Keeping one row per event id downstream makes the numbers look right, but the lake still holds duplicates, storage grows, and every reader must remember the rule. It is a second line of defence, not a fix.

show.title: Dedupe on read hides it
items: Every reader must remember the rule

beats.say: Third, merge needs a table format, because plain Parquet files cannot update a row in place.

check.q: You overwrite hour 09 with the default static mode on a table partitioned by date and hour. What happens?
opts: Only hour 09 is replaced
Every partition in the table is deleted, then hour 09 is written
The write fails because the partition exists
check.why: Static overwrite clears the whole table before writing. Dynamic mode limits the replacement to the partitions in the new data.

work: Check that dynamic partition overwrite is set in every job that uses overwrite.
Test an overwrite on a copy of the table before trusting it in production.

s01.title: Choosing how to make reruns safe

beats.say: An interviewer asks how you make a pipeline safe to rerun. What is the two-part answer?

First, bind every run to a fixed interval. The run for nine o'clock always processes nine o'clock, from the scheduled time, never from the clock on the wall. Second, every write replaces or merges, never blindly appends.

Choose by shape. Event data that lands by time suits partition overwrite: it is cheap, with no key lookups. Merge fits when late or corrected rows touch old partitions, but it rewrites files and costs more at scale.
Keep de-duplication downstream as a safety net, and alert on duplicate counts. If you cannot name a key, do not pick merge; overwrite a coarser partition instead.

show.title: Guardrails
items: Dedupe downstream as a safety net
No stable key? Overwrite a coarser partition

check.q: Late corrections arrive for rows in partitions from last week. Which write fits best?
opts: Append the corrections
Merge on a key
Overwrite the whole table daily
check.why: Merge updates the exact rows that changed, even in old partitions. Append creates duplicates, and a full overwrite is costly and risky.

work: For each pipeline, write down its run interval and its write strategy in one line.
Add a duplicate-count check on the event key and alert when it is above zero.

s01.title: Airflow is the head chef

beats.say: How does a company make sure fifty data jobs run in the right order, every night, without someone watching?
Think of a restaurant kitchen. The head chef does not cook. She calls out orders: start the sauce, then plate the fish, and if the oven breaks, tell someone. Airflow is that head chef for data jobs.
The cooks are the real engines, like Spark or the warehouse. Airflow only says what runs, when, and in what order. It retries a failed step, sends an alert, and keeps a record of every run.

show.title: What the chef does
items: Keeps a record of every run

beats.say: Compare that with cron, a plain alarm clock. It rings at a time, but it knows nothing about order, failures or history.

check.q: In the kitchen picture, what is Airflow's job?
opts: Doing the heavy cooking itself
Deciding what runs, when, and checking the result
Only ringing at a fixed time
check.why: Airflow orchestrates: the engines such as Spark or the warehouse do the work, while Airflow handles order, retries, alerts and history.

work: List your nightly jobs and write down which depend on which.
Find one job still run by cron and note what happens when it fails.

s01.title: Intervals, start times and backfills

beats.say: An hourly job covers nine to ten o'clock. When does it actually start?

Just after ten. A run covers a data interval, and it fires once that interval is finished, because the data is only complete then. Its logical date is the interval start, nine o'clock. Old code treated that date as now, a classic bug.

show.title: A run fires at the *end* of its interval

beats.say: Now backfill last week. Airflow creates one run per hour, a hundred and sixty eight in all, each with its own interval, and feeds them through the concurrency limits.
This is safe only if each run reads and overwrites just its own hour. That is idempotency: rerun it and nothing doubles.

check.q: An hourly DAG's 09:00 to 10:00 run starts when?
opts: At 09:00, when the hour begins
Just after 10:00, when the interval is complete
Whenever the scheduler is free, regardless of time
check.why: A run covers a data interval and fires at its end, once the data is complete. The logical date is the interval start.

work: Search your DAGs for execution date used as the current time and replace it with the data interval.
Make every load overwrite its own partition, then test by rerunning one day twice.

s01.title: Why heavy DAG files hurt everyone

beats.say: Why can one badly written DAG file slow down every pipeline in Airflow?
Because the DAG processor re-reads every DAG file about every thirty seconds, looking for changes. Any code at the top of the file runs on every read.
Say the top calls an API or queries a database. That call now happens thousands of times a day, and a slow one delays how fast the scheduler sees all DAGs, or hits the parse timeout.

show.title: A slow call *delays the scheduler's view*

beats.say: The fix: keep the top level to definitions only, and do real work inside tasks. Then watch the DAG processing duration metric.

show.title: The fix
items: API calls and queries go inside tasks

check.q: Where should a database query for a DAG's config run?
opts: At module level in the DAG file
Inside a task
In an import at the top of the file
check.why: Module-level code runs on every parse, about every 30 seconds, for every file. Work inside a task runs only when the task runs.

work: Grep your DAG folder for requests, database connects and big imports at module level.
Add an alert on DAG processing duration.

s01.title: Sensors that hog workers

beats.say: A sensor waits six hours for a file. What does that cost?
In poke mode it holds a worker slot the whole time, doing nothing. Twenty waiting sensors can starve the real tasks. Reschedule mode frees the slot between checks.

A deferrable operator goes further. It hands the wait to the triggerer, a separate process that runs thousands of waits as lightweight async coroutines. A worker is picked up again only when the event arrives.
In Airflow three, assets remove many sensors altogether. A DAG simply runs when an upstream task updates the asset.

check.q: Why is a deferrable operator better than a poke-mode sensor for a long wait?
opts: It checks the file more often
It frees the worker slot and waits in the triggerer
It skips the file check entirely
check.why: The triggerer runs thousands of waits cheaply as async coroutines, and a worker is used only after the event arrives.

work: Count sensors in poke mode and move long waits to deferrable operators.
Where upstream is another DAG, try asset-based scheduling instead of a sensor.

s01.title: Celery or Kubernetes executor

beats.say: Celery or Kubernetes: how do you pick an Airflow executor, the part that actually runs tasks?
Celery keeps warm worker processes pulling tasks from a queue. Tasks start fast, which suits many short jobs. But all tasks share the workers' image and resources, and you size the pool yourself.

chip.text: Fast start, you size the pool

beats.say: Kubernetes starts one pod per task. You get isolation, a custom image and resources for each task, and scaling to zero. The price is pod start time, seconds or more, on every task.
Many platforms run both: light, fast tasks on Celery, heavy or unusual ones in pods.

show.title: Hybrid setup
items: Heavy or odd tasks in pods

check.q: Which workload fits Celery best?
opts: A few tasks needing custom images and scale to zero
Thousands of short tasks that share one environment
A GPU job needing its own container
check.why: Celery's warm workers start tasks fast, ideal for many short, similar tasks. Heavy or special tasks fit pods better.

work: Measure your task duration and pod start time before choosing an executor.
Move one heavy or oddly-dependent task into its own pod and compare.

s01.title: When to say no to Airflow

beats.say: When should an architect say no to Airflow?

Streaming or sub-minute work: use Kafka with Flink or Spark streaming. Moving the data inside tasks: let Spark, the warehouse or a copy tool do it, and keep tasks thin. A lone dbt project: the warehouse or dbt Cloud can schedule it.
Airflow is the control plane of batch, not the data plane. It tells engines what to run and checks the result. Its cost is the always-on scheduler, database and workers.
Move off when work turns event-driven, when Dagster or warehouse pipelines cover everything you schedule, or when a managed service is cheaper.

show.title: Time to move off
items: Dagster or warehouse pipelines cover it all

check.q: A team runs one dbt project and nothing else. What is the best call?
opts: Deploy a full Airflow cluster for it
Let the warehouse or dbt Cloud schedule it
Replace dbt with Spark tasks
check.why: A single dbt project does not need cross-system orchestration, so a built-in scheduler avoids running an always-on Airflow.

work: Audit your DAGs for tasks that move data themselves and push that work to Spark or the warehouse.
Estimate the monthly cost of your scheduler, database and workers against a managed option.

s01.title: What Airflow 3 changes

beats.say: What changed in Airflow three that an upgrade plan must cover?

show.sub: what must your upgrade plan cover?

beats.say: Tasks no longer talk to the metadata database directly. They go through the Task SDK and an API server, which is safer and lets tasks run in other environments and languages.
DAGs are versioned, so a run keeps the code it started with, and the UI shows which version ran. Datasets became assets with event-driven scheduling.
SubDAGs and execution date are gone, so budget a code pass before upgrading.

check.q: What does DAG versioning in Airflow 3 give you?
opts: Faster parsing of all files
A run keeps the code version it started with
Automatic removal of old DAGs
check.why: Each run stays tied to the DAG code it started with, and the UI shows which version ran, which helps debugging.

work: Scan your code for SubDAGs and execution date before planning an upgrade.
Check whether any task connects straight to the metadata database.

s02.title: Fast means reading less

beats.say: How do you find one recipe in a library of a million books without reading them all?
You don't. You skip. First you walk to the right shelf, ignoring every other aisle. Then you glance at book spines, and pass over any that can't match.
Inside a book, you flip past chapters whose titles don't fit. And in a table, you read only the one column that answers you.

show.title: Keep skipping
items: Skip chapters that do not fit
Read only the column you need

beats.say: A database works the same way. Fast never means reading quicker. It means reading less. Each skip saves bytes, and bytes are the real cost.

check.q: What is the main way a query engine becomes faster on huge data?
opts: Reading the same bytes with a quicker reader
Skipping bytes it does not need to read
Copying all data into memory first
check.why: Time is spent reading and moving bytes, so the biggest win is to avoid reading bytes that cannot affect the answer.

work: Pick one slow query and write down how many bytes it scans.
Ask which shelf, spine, chapter and column it really needed.

s02.title: Four levels of skipping

beats.say: Finance wants eighteen months of trips queried in under ten seconds. How do you scan three terabytes that fast?
You don't scan it. Level one: partitions. Data is foldered by date, so a one week question opens seven folders out of about five hundred and fifty.

Level two: files. Each file has minimum and maximum statistics, so files that cannot match are skipped. Level three: row groups. Each chunk of rows also stores a minimum and maximum, and the engine skips chunks outside your filter.
Level four: columns. Parquet stores columns separately, so a query naming two of forty columns reads about five percent. Stack the four skips and three terabytes becomes a few gigabytes.

check.q: A query uses 2 of 40 columns in a columnar file. Roughly how much column data is read?
opts: All of it
About half
About 5 percent
check.why: Columnar formats store each column separately, so only the named columns are read: 2 of 40 is 5 percent.

work: Name which of the four levels each of your big tables supports.
Run an explain on a date-filtered query and check bytes scanned.

s02.title: Why pruning silently fails

beats.say: Why does a filter on a date sometimes still read every file?

Minimum and maximum only help if values are clustered. If every file holds trips from every day, each range covers everything, and nothing is skipped. Sorting or clustering on the filter column fixes that.
Wrapping the column in a function, like casting a timestamp to a string, can stop the engine comparing it with the statistics, so pruning silently fails. Filter on the raw column.

show.title: Keep the column bare
show.text:
bad:  where cast(pickup_ts as string) = '2025-03-01'
good: where pickup_ts >= '2025-03-01' and pickup_ts < '2025-03-02'

beats.say: Over-partitioning hurts too. Partitioning by user creates millions of folders and tiny files, and listing them costs more than the data you skipped. A table format keeps file statistics in one manifest, so there is no listing.

show.title: Gotchas
items: Too many partitions means tiny files

check.q: Every file contains rows from every day, and you filter on one day. What happens?
opts: Min/max skips most files
Almost no files are skipped
The engine errors out
check.why: Each file's range spans all days, so no file can be excluded. Clustering by date makes ranges narrow.

work: Check whether your filter columns are sorted or clustered within files.
Search queries for functions wrapped around partition or filter columns.
Count files per partition and compact tiny ones.

s02.title: Choosing a layout

beats.say: If skipping bytes is everything, why not partition and sort on every column?

Because every layout favors one question. Partition by date and date queries fly, but a query by driver still touches every folder. Pick the column most queries filter on, with a few hundred to thousands of values.

Use partitions for coarse cuts, and sorting or clustering inside files for the rest. A table format adds file statistics, so you skip files without listing folders. The price is compaction jobs that rewrite small files.
Don't bother under a few gigabytes; just scan. For single-row lookups, use a key-value store. And on pay-per-byte engines, fewer bytes read is a smaller bill.

check.q: Most queries filter by date, some by driver. Which layout is best?
opts: Partition by driver
Partition by date, cluster by driver inside files
Partition by date and driver together
check.why: Date has few values, so it suits partitions. Driver has many values, so clustering avoids millions of tiny partitions while still narrowing ranges.

work: Review the top ten queries and pick the layout key from their filters.
Schedule compaction and track average file size.
Skip tuning for tables under a few gigabytes.

s02.title: Drawers and pigeonholes

beats.say: How do you find one day's receipts in a warehouse holding ten years of paper? You certainly don't open every box.
Partitioning means labeling one drawer for each day. Ask for October eleventh, and you open one drawer and ignore the rest. Skipping drawers is called pruning, and it saves the most work.
But don't label a drawer per customer. Five million customers means five million nearly empty drawers, and walking between them takes forever.
For customers, use sorting pigeonholes instead. Give every name a number from one to sixteen, and always drop it in the same hole. Now one customer's mail lives in one place.

check.q: Which column is the better choice for labeling drawers, meaning partitioning?
opts: Customer id, with millions of values
Date, with a few hundred values
A random number for each row
check.why: Drawers only help when there are few of them and you ask for them by label. Date fits. Customer id would create millions of nearly empty drawers.

work: List the columns your biggest tables are filtered on most often.
Count how many distinct values each of those columns has.
Name one column that would make far too many drawers.

s02.title: How pruning and buckets work

beats.say: A query asks for one day of trips. How does the engine avoid reading a whole year of data?

The table is split into directories, one per date value, like dt equals 2026-10-11. The query filter matches one directory name, so the engine lists only that folder. Three hundred sixty-five days becomes one. That is partition pruning.
Bucketing handles columns with millions of values. The engine hashes rider id, then takes the remainder after dividing by sixteen. That remainder picks one of sixteen files in each partition.
If two tables use the same bucket count on the join key, bucket five meets bucket five directly. No shuffle, which means no sending data across the network.

check.q: Two tables are both bucketed on rider id with 16 buckets. What does the engine gain on a join by rider id?
opts: It can join matching buckets directly without a shuffle
It can skip all partitions
It no longer needs to read any files
check.why: Matching rows are guaranteed to sit in the same bucket number in both tables, so each pair joins locally. Files still get read, and partition pruning is a separate feature.

work: Check whether your daily big join could use matching bucketed tables.
Open a query plan and find the shuffle step on the join.
Confirm which tables are partitioned by date today.

s02.title: Where partitioning bites back

beats.say: Why can a partitioned table end up slower than an unpartitioned one?

Because each partition should hold at least hundreds of megabytes. Partition by rider id and you get five million directories of tiny files. Listing them and opening each file costs more than reading the data.
Pruning also only works if the query filters on the partition column. Filter on a different column and the engine reads every directory.

Bucketing has its own trap. The bucket count is fixed at write time. Join a sixteen bucket table to a thirty-two bucket one, and the engine may shuffle after all. Both tables must be bucketed the same way.

check.q: A table is partitioned by date, but most queries filter only on city. What happens?
opts: Pruning works because date is a partition column
The engine reads every date directory
The engine builds buckets automatically
check.why: Pruning needs a filter on the partition column. Without a date filter, every directory is read.

work: Check the average file size in each partition and flag any under 100 megabytes.
Compare how many buckets each joined table uses.
Review whether query filters match the partition column.

s02.title: Choosing partitions or buckets

beats.say: Partition by date and bucket by rider. Is that always the right call?
Rule of thumb: partition by what you filter on with low cardinality. Bucket by what you join on with high cardinality.
Partitioning is cheap and gives the biggest saving, so start there. But every extra partition column multiplies directories. Date plus city plus device can explode into millions.

Bucketing costs more. Writers must hash and sort, the count is baked in, and growth means rewriting. Use it for a join repeated daily on the same key, or for rider lookups. For a one-off join, a shuffle is cheaper than the commitment.

show.title: Bucket only when it pays
items: Changing the count means a rewrite

check.q: A team joins two huge tables on rider id once a quarter. What is the sensible choice?
opts: Bucket both tables on rider id with 16 buckets
Partition both tables by rider id
Accept the shuffle for that rare job
check.why: Bucketing adds write cost and a fixed layout. For a rare join, one shuffle costs less than that commitment, and partitioning by rider id would create millions of tiny files.

work: Review the table layouts and mark each as filter-driven or join-driven.
Bucket only the joins that run daily on the same key.
Set a minimum partition size target and alert when files fall below it.

s02.title: The catalog and the boxes

beats.say: Imagine a warehouse with a million boxes and no labels. How do you find last Tuesday's invoices?
You keep a catalog book at the front desk. For each shelf it says what the boxes hold, what the columns mean, and where to walk. That book is the metastore. The boxes are just files.
Shelves are grouped by date, so a question about Tuesday walks to one shelf only. Nobody checks a box when it is put away. The catalog's description is applied only when you open it.

chip.text: Checked on opening, not on storing

beats.say: Throw away the catalog entry and the boxes stay, if the shelf is external. If the warehouse owns the boxes, they are shredded too. So for shared data, keep it external.

show.title: Who owns the boxes?
items: External: drop removes only the catalog entry
Managed: drop shreds the files too

check.q: You drop an external table. What happens to its files?
opts: They are deleted
They stay; only the catalog entry goes
They are moved to a trash folder
check.why: An external table only has a metastore entry that Hive owns. The files belong to you, so dropping removes just the catalog record.

work: List which of your lake tables are managed and which are external.
Make shared lake tables external before anyone runs a drop.
Write down who owns each table's storage folder.

s02.title: How a Hive query finds its files

beats.say: When you run a query on a Hive table, where does the engine learn which files to read?
It asks the metastore, a small database. For a sales table it returns the schema, the location, and the partition list, like date equals 2026-11-01.
Now filter on one date. The engine prunes the other 364 partitions and lists only that directory, maybe 200 files. Without the filter it reads all 365 days. Pruning is the whole speed trick.
Then it opens the files and applies the schema while reading. That is schema-on-read. A bad row is not rejected on write. It shows up as a null or an error at query time.

check.q: Why does filtering on the partition column make a query faster?
opts: The engine prunes partitions and lists only matching directories
The metastore caches the results
The files are compressed more
check.why: Partition values live in the directory path, so the engine can skip whole folders without opening them.

work: Check that your biggest queries filter on the partition column.
Look at an explain plan and count the partitions scanned.
Add a check at write time, since nothing validates files for you.

s02.title: Half-written partitions and slow planning

beats.say: A job writes 200 files, fails after 120. What does a reader see?

Half a partition. Hive has no atomic commit across files, so readers see the 120 files as if they were complete. Totals are silently wrong. The usual fix is writing to a temporary directory and swapping it in, but that swap is still not atomic on object storage.

Planning has a cost too. The engine lists every partition directory, and on object storage each list call is a slow network request. With 100,000 partitions, planning can take minutes before any data is read.
Last gotcha: drift. Files copied in outside Hive are invisible until you run M S C K repair table, which registers the new partitions.

check.q: A copy tool drops a new date folder straight into storage. Queries do not see it. Why?
opts: Schema-on-read rejects the files
The metastore does not list that partition yet
The engine caches old file sizes
check.why: The partition list lives in the metastore. Folders added outside Hive stay invisible until registered, for example with MSCK REPAIR TABLE.

work: Register new partitions as the last step of every ingest job.
Write to a temporary location and publish only after success.
Track partition counts per table and alert when they climb.

s02.title: Drop, update and repartition traps

beats.say: Someone runs drop table on a table. Did you just lose a year of data?

It depends on the type. For a managed table, Hive owns the files, so drop deletes them. For an external table, only the metastore entry goes, and the files stay. That is why lake data should almost always be external.
Two more limits. Updating one row means rewriting its whole partition, maybe gigabytes, because files are never edited in place.

show.title: No row-level changes
items: Fix one row, rewrite the partition

beats.say: And the partition scheme is frozen. Moving from daily to hourly means rewriting the whole table, since the directory layout is the partitioning.

check.q: You must correct one wrong row in a 5 GB Hive partition. What is required?
opts: Edit the row in place
Rewrite the partition's files
Update the metastore entry only
check.why: Hive tables are plain immutable files with no row-level changes, so the fix means rewriting the partition.

work: Audit tables for managed type and convert to external.
Keep partitions sized so a rewrite is affordable.
Choose partition granularity carefully before data lands.

s02.title: When to leave Hive tables behind

beats.say: Your team wants a new lake table. Do you reach for Hive tables?
Rarely, for new builds. The Hive layout is cheap and every engine reads it, so it is fine for append-only, rarely changing data, like raw landing zones and logs.

But it breaks where you need updates, deletes, concurrent writers or reliable reads during writes. Table formats like Iceberg and Delta keep a transaction log of files, which gives atomic commits, and avoid directory listing.
Even then, the metastore often stays as the catalog, so engines can find tables. Choose by write pattern, not habit, and plan migration before partitions pass tens of thousands.

show.title: Decision rule
items: Migrate before partitions hit tens of thousands

check.q: Which workload most clearly justifies moving off plain Hive tables?
opts: Append-only clickstream logs
Frequent row updates with concurrent writers
A table queried by one engine
check.why: Updates and concurrent writers need atomic commits and row-level changes, which table formats provide and Hive layout lacks.

work: Classify tables by write pattern: append-only or mutable.
Pilot Iceberg or Delta on your most update-heavy table.
Set a partition count threshold that triggers migration review.

s02.title: Rows or columns: the phone book

beats.say: Imagine a phone book with ten million people. You only want the list of everyone's city. How much of the book must you read?
A row format is the normal phone book. Each person's name, city and fare sit together on one line. Great when you want one whole person. But for just the city, you must flip through every page.

A column format is a book regrouped. One section holds only cities, another only fares. Want cities? Open one section and ignore the rest. That is why analytics, which touches a few columns, loves it.
The catch: rebuilding one whole person means visiting every section. So columns suit reading, rows suit writing records one by one.

show.title: The trade
items: Columns: fast to read a few fields across many records
Rows: fast to write or fetch one whole record

check.q: A query totals one column across millions of records. Which layout reads the least data?
opts: Row format
Column format
They read the same amount
check.why: A column format keeps all values of one column together, so the reader opens just that section and skips the rest.

work: List the five most common queries on your biggest table and count how many columns each touches.
Check whether your analytics tables are stored in a row format such as CSV or JSON.

s02.title: Inside a Parquet file

beats.say: A query needs 5 columns out of 80. How does a Parquet file let you read only those, and skip most of the rows too?

A file is split into row groups, about 128 megabytes each. Inside each group, every column is stored as its own chunk. At the end sits a footer with the schema and, for every chunk, its minimum, maximum and null count.

The reader opens the footer first. It learns where each chunk starts, so it fetches just the five columns it needs. That is column pruning. Reading five of eighty means roughly a sixteenth of the bytes.
Now filter fare greater than 5000. If a row group's maximum fare is 900, nothing inside can match, so the reader skips it entirely. That is predicate pushdown.

check.q: What lets a reader skip a row group without reading its data?
opts: The min and max statistics in the footer
A sorted file name
The dictionary of each page
check.why: The footer records min, max and null count per column chunk, so if the filter value falls outside that range the group cannot contain a match.

work: Open a Parquet footer with a tool such as parquet-tools and read the row group statistics.
Compare bytes scanned for a query selecting five columns versus select star.

s02.title: Why columns compress so well

beats.say: A city column holds ten million values but only ten different cities. How small can that get?
Because similar values sit together, Parquet builds a dictionary. Each city name becomes a small number, zero to nine. Instead of repeating a long string, the file stores a tiny integer.
Next comes run-length encoding. If the same city repeats a million times in a row, the file stores the pair: city three, one million times. Just two numbers.
But runs only form if equal values are neighbours. So sort by city before writing. Sorting also tightens each group's minimum and maximum, which makes pushdown skip far more. Sort once, win twice.

show.title: Sort before you write
items: Equal values sit together, so runs get long
Tight min and max per group, so more skipping

check.q: Why does sorting by a column before writing Parquet help?
opts: It makes the footer smaller
It groups equal values for run-length encoding and tightens min and max statistics
It turns the file into a row format
check.why: Sorted data forms long runs that compress well and gives each row group a narrow value range, so pushdown can skip more groups.

work: Pick the column most often used in filters and sort the table by it on write.
Compare file size and scan time before and after sorting one table.

s02.title: When Parquet pruning fails

beats.say: Your Parquet table has min and max statistics, yet the query still reads every row group. Why?

show.sub: why does the query read everything?

beats.say: Statistics only help when values are clustered. If fares are random, every group spans from 1 to 9000, so no group can be ruled out. Unsorted data quietly turns pushdown into a full scan.

show.title: Random data: every group looks alike

beats.say: The opposite trap is tiny files. A streaming job writing a file every minute makes thousands of small files. Each one needs its own footer read and a storage request, and row groups far under 128 megabytes waste the layout. Compact them regularly.

Also remember: a column where almost every value is different, like event id, gets no useful dictionary, so it compresses poorly. And a footer lives at the end, so a writer must finish the file before anyone can read it.

show.title: Two more gotchas
items: Nearly unique columns, like event id, compress poorly
The footer is written last, so unfinished files are unreadable

check.q: A table's queries filter on fare but still scan every row group. What is the most likely cause?
opts: Fares are scattered randomly, so each group's min and max cover the whole range
Parquet does not support filters
The footer is missing the schema
check.why: Min and max only rule out a group when its range excludes the filter value. Random data makes every range wide, so nothing is skipped.

work: Check the average file size in your largest table and schedule compaction if it is far below 128 MB.
Cluster or sort data by the main filter column when you write it.

s02.title: Why Avro for messages

beats.say: Why would you pick a row format for Kafka messages when columns compress so well?
Messages arrive one at a time. A columnar file needs a batch to build column chunks and a footer, so writing one record at a time is slow. Avro just appends each record whole, which is fast.

Avro also carries its schema with the data. The writer's schema says how the bytes were written; the reader's schema says what the consumer wants. Clear rules resolve the two, so adding a field with a default won't break old readers.

chip.text: New field with default is safe

beats.say: The cost: to total one column, Avro must read every whole record. So land data as Avro, then convert to Parquet for analytics.

check.q: Which change is safe under Avro schema resolution?
opts: Adding a new field with a default value
Renaming a field with no alias
Changing a string field to a map
check.why: A new field with a default lets readers fill in the value for older data, so compatibility holds. Renames without aliases and type changes break resolution.

work: Check which compatibility mode your schema registry enforces for your key topics.
Add a job that converts landed Avro into Parquet for analysts.

s02.title: Choosing a file format

beats.say: Parquet, ORC or Avro? The answer has two halves.

For analytics tables in a lake, choose columnar, and default to Parquet. It is supported by nearly every engine, handles nested types, and avoids lock-in. Choose ORC only if your estate is centred on Hive, where its built-in indexes pay off.

show.title: Analytics: columnar
items: Default to Parquet: pruning, pushdown, support everywhere

beats.say: For records moving between systems one at a time, choose Avro, for fast writes and enforced schema compatibility. JSON and CSV are fine for exchange with outside parties, but never for large analytics: they are text, have no pruning, and compress badly.

show.title: Movement: row
items: Avro for Kafka and landing zones
JSON and CSV only for outside exchange

beats.say: So the architecture is usually both: Avro at the edges where data arrives, Parquet in the lake where it is queried. Don't use columnar for tiny, record-by-record lookups, and budget for compaction jobs.

check.q: You are designing an estate with Kafka ingestion and a lake queried by analysts. What do you choose?
opts: Parquet everywhere, including Kafka messages
Avro for messages and landing, Parquet for lake tables
CSV for both, for simplicity
check.why: Avro suits fast single-record writes with strict schema rules, while Parquet suits analytic reads through pruning, pushdown and compression.

work: Write a one-page format decision note stating where each of Avro and Parquet is used and why.
Estimate compaction cost for your streaming tables before choosing write frequency.

s02.title: Why tiny files are slow

beats.say: Why would ten thousand tiny files take hundreds of times longer to read than one big file holding the same data?

show.sub: same data, hundreds of times slower

beats.say: Picture moving house. One big box takes one trip. Ten thousand envelopes mean ten thousand trips, and each one needs a door opened and a label read.

chip.text: Trips, not data, cost the time

beats.say: A data lake works the same way. Every file costs a request to open, a footer to read, and a line in the catalog. Tiny files make the overhead bigger than the actual reading.
The fix is compaction: tipping the envelopes into a few big boxes. Same data, far fewer trips.

show.sub: many small files become a few big ones

check.q: Why are many tiny files slower to scan than one large file with the same data?
opts: Tiny files hold more data
Each file adds fixed overhead like opening and reading a footer
Large files are compressed and small files are not
check.why: The data volume is the same. The extra time is fixed per-file overhead repeated thousands of times.

work: Count the files and total size of your busiest table.
Ask which jobs write to it and how often.

s02.title: Where small files come from, and the four jobs

beats.say: Ten thousand 50 kilobyte files, or one 500 megabyte file. Same data, so why is one hundreds of times slower to scan?
Each file needs a request to open and a footer read. Ten thousand files means ten thousand requests, mostly waiting, not reading.
They come from three places: streaming micro-batches writing every few seconds, partitions sliced too fine, and Spark writing one file per shuffle partition into every table partition.

show.title: Three sources
items: One file per shuffle partition per table partition

beats.say: Iceberg gives four housekeeping jobs. Rewrite data files compacts small files. Expire snapshots drops old versions. Remove orphan files deletes strays. Rewrite manifests tidies the metadata.

check.q: Which write pattern most directly creates small files?
opts: Streaming micro-batches committing every few seconds
One nightly batch load of 500 MB
Running expire snapshots
check.why: Each frequent commit writes a small file, so the file count grows quickly.

work: List which of your tables get micro-batch writes.
Schedule the four Iceberg jobs in an Airflow DAG per table.

s02.title: Why compaction does not free space yet

beats.say: You compacted a table, so why did your storage bill go up?

show.sub: the old files are still there

beats.say: Compaction writes new big files and a new snapshot. But older snapshots still point at the old small files, so nothing can be deleted yet. For a while you store both.
Space comes back only after expire snapshots runs. But expiring also ends time travel to those versions. So retention is a business decision: how far back might anyone need to roll back or audit?
Remove orphan files cleans up files no snapshot knows about, such as leftovers from failed writes. Use an age threshold, so you never delete a file from a write still in progress.

show.title: Orphan files
items: Only delete files older than a safe age

check.q: After rewrite_data_files finishes, when does storage actually shrink?
opts: Immediately
After expire_snapshots removes snapshots referencing the old files
After rewrite_manifests runs
check.why: Older snapshots still reference the small files, so they stay until those snapshots expire.

work: Agree a snapshot retention period with the data owners.
Run orphan removal with an age threshold, never zero.

s02.title: Prevent small files, do not just mop them

beats.say: Is nightly compaction the real fix for small files, or just a mop?

It is a mop. Prevent at write time. Let adaptive query execution coalesce shuffle partitions, and route all rows for one table partition to one task before writing. Each partition then gets a few large files.
Also question the partitioning. Partitions that are too fine multiply files however well you write. Choose coarser partitions, such as day instead of minute.

Keep maintenance as scheduled Airflow jobs, since compaction costs compute and rewrites data. Streaming tables need it more often. Set retention with the business, balancing audit needs against storage cost.

show.title: Maintenance trade-offs
items: Streaming tables need it more often

check.q: What is the best primary strategy against small files?
opts: Compact more often
Avoid creating them: coalesce shuffle partitions, route rows per partition, partition coarser
Delete old snapshots daily
check.why: Prevention avoids paying compute to rewrite data; compaction stays as a safety net.

work: Review Spark write jobs for shuffle partition count and routing.
Report files per partition and average file size on key tables.

s02.title: A rulebook beside the files

beats.say: Your data lake is just a pile of files. So how can two people change it at once without breaking it?

A table format is a rulebook sitting beside the files. It records which files make up the table right now. Delta Lake keeps a numbered receipt for every change. Hudi keeps an index, like a filing cabinet label for each record. Iceberg keeps a catalogue, like a library.
Readers trust the rulebook, not the folder. A change is either fully written down or it never happened. That is what atomic means.

show.sub: Atomic means a change is fully recorded or not at all

check.q: What does a table format add on top of a pile of data files?
opts: A faster disk
A record of which files make up the table, so changes are all or nothing
A way to compress files into one
check.why: The format is a rulebook of metadata. Readers follow it instead of listing the folder, so a half-finished write is never seen.

work: Explain to a colleague why a plain folder of Parquet files cannot give atomic changes.
List which of your tables are plain files and which sit under a table format.

s02.title: How Delta Lake replays its log

beats.say: How does Delta Lake know what your table looks like right now?

show.text: What is the table right now?

beats.say: Every write adds a numbered JSON file to the delta log folder: zero zero zero one, zero zero zero two, and so on. Each file lists data files added and removed.

To read the table, replay the log from the start. That gets slow after thousands of commits, so every ten commits Delta writes a Parquet checkpoint. Readers load the latest checkpoint, then replay only the few newer files.
Time travel is just replaying to an older number.

show.sub: Replay the log up to commit 7

check.q: Why does Delta write a checkpoint every ten commits?
opts: So readers skip replaying the whole log from commit one
So old data files can be deleted
So two writers never conflict
check.why: A checkpoint is a Parquet snapshot of table state. Readers start from it and replay only newer commits, keeping reads fast.

work: Open a Delta table's log folder and find the latest checkpoint file.
Query an older version of a table and note which commit number you used.

s02.title: Hudi keys, and Iceberg trees

beats.say: Why was Hudi built at Uber? Because millions of trip records changed every day.

show.sub: Trips change after they are written

beats.say: Hudi gives every record a key and keeps an index from key to file. An update goes straight to the right file, with no scan of the whole table.

Copy on write rewrites the whole file on each update, so reads are fast but writes cost more. Merge on read appends changes to a small log file and merges later, so writes are fast but reads do extra work.
Iceberg instead uses a tree of metadata files, so engines can skip data without listing folders.

check.q: A Hudi table gets constant small updates and must write quickly. Which type fits best?
opts: Copy on write, because it rewrites whole files
Merge on read, because it appends changes and merges later
Neither, Hudi cannot do updates
check.why: Merge on read makes writes cheap by appending to log files. You pay later at read time or at compaction.

work: Pick one update-heavy table and estimate how often a typical file would be rewritten under copy on write.
Decide what read delay your users can tolerate before choosing merge on read.

s02.title: Conflicts, compaction and vacuum

beats.say: What happens when two writers commit to a Delta table at the same moment?

Delta uses optimistic concurrency. Both try to write the next numbered file, say number forty two. The storage layer lets only one create it. The loser checks whether the winner touched the same files. If not, it retries as number forty three. If yes, it fails.

Gotchas. Merge on read tables need regular compaction, or reads slow down as log files pile up. Vacuum deletes old data files, and then time travel to those versions breaks. Many tiny commits also create small files, which make every query slower.

show.title: Gotchas
items: Compact merge on read tables or reads slow down
Vacuum removes old files and ends time travel to them
Tiny commits create small files and slow queries

check.q: You ran vacuum with a short retention, and now a query on last week's version fails. Why?
opts: The checkpoint was corrupted
The data files for that version were physically deleted
Optimistic concurrency rolled it back
check.why: The log still names the version, but vacuum removed the data files it points to, so time travel cannot read them.

work: Check the vacuum retention on your tables against how far back you need time travel.
Schedule compaction and watch file counts per table.

s02.title: Choosing a format without picking a winner

beats.say: Delta, Hudi or Iceberg: which one wins? Wrong question.

All three give atomic commits, time travel and row level changes. So the choice follows your engines. Delta where Databricks is the centre. Iceberg where Spark, Trino, Flink and Snowflake must share the same tables. Hudi where record level upserts dominate the workload.

The formats are converging. Snowflake and Databricks now both read and write Iceberg. So the cost of a wrong choice is shrinking. Do not overthink the decision. Pick for today's engines, and keep data in open files so you can change later.

show.title: Decision rules
items: Same core features in all three
Formats are converging on Iceberg support
Pick for today's engines, keep data in open files

check.q: Five teams on Spark, Trino, Flink and Snowflake must share tables. What is the strongest reasoning?
opts: Pick Hudi because it is fastest
Pick Iceberg because wide engine support matters most when many engines share tables
Pick whichever format is newest
check.why: All three cover the core features, so engine support decides. Iceberg is read and written by the widest range of engines.

work: List every engine that reads or writes your core tables before debating formats.
Write a one paragraph decision note that ties the format to engines, not features.

s02.title: A form instead of a letter

beats.say: Why can't a program act on a paragraph written by an AI? Because a program needs boxes to look in, not a letter to read.

chip.text: Prose has no boxes to branch on

beats.say: Picture a hospital. A patient can ramble about their pain for ten minutes. So the nurse hands over a form: pick a type, tick urgent or not, write one line of proof. Now the system knows where to send them.
Structured output is that form for a model. You define the boxes, and you forbid chatting, so the model can only fill them in. A pipeline can then retry, page someone, or route the failure.
Then a clerk checks the form. Is every box filled with an allowed choice? If not, it goes back. And one box says unknown, so odd cases are not squeezed into the wrong answer.

chip.text: Odd cases get an honest label

check.q: Why does the form include an unknown box?
opts: So the model can skip hard work
So odd cases are not forced into a wrong category
So the form looks longer
So the clerk can skip checking
check.why: Without an escape value, every unfamiliar case must be squeezed into the nearest wrong box, and your routing would act on a wrong label.

work: Find one place where your pipeline reads model prose, and list the fields it really needs.
Add an unknown or other value to every closed list of categories you ask a model to pick from.

s02.title: Forcing a model to fill a schema

beats.say: How do you make a model return fields instead of prose? You hand it a fake tool.

show.sub: It exists only to force fields

beats.say: Define a Pydantic class with four fields: category, retryable, evidence line, and confidence between zero and one. Turn it into a JSON schema and register it as a tool. Nothing runs. The tool is only a form.

Next, set tool choice to that tool's name. Now the model cannot reply with text. It must return arguments matching the schema. Send a log tail, and a small, cheap model answers in under four hundred tokens.

Last, validate. Pydantic checks every field. If it fails, send the error back as a tool result, and let the model try again. After two attempts, return unknown, not retryable, so the pipeline never crashes.

items: Fail: send error back, retry once

check.q: What does setting tool choice to the named tool accomplish?
opts: It runs the tool on your server
It makes the model reply only with arguments matching the schema
It guarantees the answer is true
It makes the model cheaper
check.why: Tool choice removes the option of a text reply, so the model must produce arguments in your schema's shape. Nothing runs and truth is not guaranteed, which is why you still validate.

work: Write the Pydantic model first, then generate the tool's input schema from it so the two never drift.
Cap retries at two and make the fallback a safe value such as unknown and not retryable.

s02.title: Valid does not mean true

beats.say: The output passed validation, so why might it still be wrong?

Because a schema checks shape, not truth. A model can pick a valid category that is simply the wrong one, and invent a log line that sounds right. So you ask for the evidence line copied exactly, then check mechanically that it appears in the input. If not, discard the answer.

Second, the closed list needs an unknown value. Without it, a new failure type gets forced into the nearest wrong bucket, and a wrong retry can loop for hours. Also, confidence is the model's own guess, so treat it as a hint, not a probability.

show.title: Two quiet traps
items: No unknown value: new failures land in the wrong bucket
A wrong bucket can trigger endless retries

beats.say: Third, retries are bounded. Feed the validation error back, try twice, then fall back to unknown. Never retry forever, and never let a malformed answer reach your router.

check.q: The model returns a schema-valid answer whose evidence line is not in the log. What should you do?
opts: Accept it because it validated
Raise its confidence threshold
Discard it, because the evidence is not in the input
Add more categories
check.why: Validation proves shape, not truth. An evidence line absent from the log shows the answer is made up, so discard it and retry or fall back.

work: Add a mechanical check that the evidence line appears in the input, and count how often it fails.
Never route on the confidence field alone; treat it as a hint and measure real accuracy on labeled failures.

s02.title: When structured output earns its place

beats.say: When is a schema the wrong tool, and when is a small model the wrong choice?

show.sub: Right for triage, wrong for open reasoning
